question: 12. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Taoiseach if the Central Statistics Office compiles or publishes data on the citizenship or nationality of persons convicted of homicide offences in the State; and if such data is available disaggregated by year since January 2022 to date in 2026. [56030/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of the Taoiseach Referred to CSO for answer The Central Statistics Office does not compile or publish data on the citizenship or nationality of persons convicted of homicide offences in the State. The CSO receives data on homicide offences via the quarterly PULSE extract from An Garda Síochána and this data does not contain information about the citizenship or nationality of suspected offenders. The Garda Commissioner is operationally responsible for PULSE data.

question: 13. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Taoiseach whether the Central Statistics Office collects or publishes data on the reasons cited by Irish citizens for emigration, including housing affordability or housing access; and if any survey instrument captures housing-related factors as a driver of outward migration [56036/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of the Taoiseach Referred to CSO for answer The CSO publishes annual estimates of migration in its Population and Migration Estimates publication. The corresponding figures for 2026 will be published in August 2026. Information on the reasons cited by Irish persons for emigration are not collected or published. Furthermore, the CSO does not compile statistics on the factors driving outward migration.

question: 84. Deputy Brendan Smith asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if there are proposals under consideration in the United States at present in relation to the need to provide a legal pathway for undocumented Irish emigrants such as the inclusion of Ireland in the E-3 non- immigrant visa programme; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [58448/26]
answer: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade Addressing the situation of undocumented Irish emigrants in the United States, and working to secure legal pathways for Irish people seeking to live and work in the US, continues to be important for the Government, as set out in the Programme for Government. Efforts to advance these issues have been made with successive US administrations. Earlier this year, I discussed immigration matters in political meetings on Capitol Hill. This focuses on U.S. immigration policy, its impact on Irish communities and the prospects for immigration reform which could assist, inter alia, undocumented Irish immigrants. It is clear to me from these conversations that the challenges faced by such proposals for reform should not be underestimated. Other members of the Government, including the Taoiseach, have also discussed these matters with high-level American interlocutors. The Government remains supportive of efforts to secure an Irish specific E3 visa programme. This would open up a new legal pathway for more Irish citizens to live and work in the US. However, it is unlikely that undocumented Irish currently in the US would be eligible for such a programme, if secured. The introduction in February 2025 of a bill seeking to add Ireland to the E3 non-immigrant visa program by Congressman Richard Neal and Congressman Mike Kelly, the bipartisan co-Chairs of the Friends of Ireland Caucus was welcome. However, it has not progressed further since then. The vast majority of U.S. legislative proposals related to immigration reform have stalled in Congress, in the last decade. Nonetheless, we continue to take all opportunities to develop immigration pathways for Irish people who wish to live and work in the United States. We will continue to provide funding to Irish community organisations, including those that provide trusted immigration information, legal resources and support for those seeking to regularise their immigration status. Some €4.5 million was provided to organisations in the U.S. last year.

question: 274. Deputy Catherine Callaghan asked the Minister for Defence the timeline envisaged for the development and publication of a National Veterans Policy; the stages of consultation planned with veterans' organisations and other stakeholders; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [56459/26]
answer: Minister for Defence (Deputy Helen McEntee) I propose to take Question 273 and Question 274 together. At the outset, I wish to assure the Deputy that I recognise the outstanding contribution made to the State by our ex-service personnel. The work of the Office of Veterans Affairs, established by the Government last November, has been focused on researching the development of a National Veterans Policy, while also continuing with its other functions of advocating on behalf of veterans and partnership with the associations. The OVA's approach to the development of a Veterans' Policy is guided by the need to fully consider all relevant research and evidence, and includes close consultations with the recognised Veteran Associations and other stakeholders. The regular quarterly meetings with the Veteran Associations provide a forum for these discussions. It is anticipated that formal consultations will take place in the autumn and that the Department will develop a draft policy following the consultation process. This approach will help ensure that any future policy is informed by robust evidence and reflects the full range of issues affecting the veteran community. In this regard, my Department welcomed the recent publication of Óglaigh Náisiúnta na hÉireann's (ONE) research report, ‘Veterans of the Defence Forces’. The report is currently being examined by the OVA and represents an important contribution to the research that will inform a National Veterans Policy. The valuable insights provided by this research into the profile, experiences, and needs of veterans will support the OVA's ongoing work. In parallel, the OVA continues to engage with the Veteran Associations and to work towards ensuring that veterans can access the benefits, services, and supports to which they are entitled.

question: 431. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Transport further to Parliamentary Question No. 190 of 23 June 2026, the reason his Department could have only been notified 17 times by An Garda Síochána of offences pertaining to non-compliant number plates between May 2025 and January 2026, and to not receive any notification of any associated court offences during this period given that Parliamentary Question No. 1325 of 18 March 2026 to the Minister for Justice Home Affairs and Migration shows that 3,304 fixed charge notices were issued for non-compliant number plates in Q4 2025. [56038/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Transport I propose to take Questions Nos. 430 and 431 together. As Minister of State with responsibility for International and Road Transport, Logistics, Rail and Ports, I wish to advise that the statistics provided by my Department in response to Parliamentary Question No. 190 relate only to notifications received by the National Vehicle and Driver File (NVDF) in respect of offences that carry penalty points. As such, these figures should not be regarded as a measure of the overall level of enforcement activity relating to non-compliant vehicle registration plates during the period concerned. Please also note that the timeframe referenced in Parliamentary Question No. 190 of 23 June 2026 was incorrect. The statistics should have been stated as relating to offences notified to the Department between January 2026 and May 2026, rather than between January 2026 and May 2025. This was an error in the original reply, and I apologise for any confusion caused.

question: 435. Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Transport for an update on the way in which he proposes those without off-street parking will be able to access home charging for EVs; and the way in which he envisages the private wires legislation will address this. [56234/26]
answer: Minister for Transport The Government is fully committed to supporting a significant expansion and modernisation of the EV charging network over the coming years and reaching climate targets. Having an effective and reliable charging network is an essential part of enabling drivers to make the switch to electric vehicles. The National EV Charging Infrastructure Strategy outlines the requirements for publicly accessible charging and installing EV Infrastructure that is capable of meeting user needs. This strategy is currently being revised, and a refreshed strategy for 2026-2028 was published for consultation between February and April. Home charging is, and is expected to remain, the primary means by which most drivers charge their vehicles. Public charging infrastructure plays a critical complementary role, not only in supporting enroute journeys, but also in ensuring that those who cannot charge at home are not disadvantaged and can participate fully in the transition to electric vehicles. The Government recognises that the absence of off-street parking presents a particular challenge for some households. Addressing this barrier is a key priority. Work is underway to introduce new legislation establishing a regulated private wires regime. The General Scheme of the Private Wires Bill was approved by Government on 16 December 2025, and the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment has since been engaging with the Office of Parliamentary Counsel to progress drafting of the legislation. Pre-legislative scrutiny has been completed by the Joint Committee on Climate, Environment and Energy, with its report published on 22 April. It is intended that the Bill will complete its passage through the Oireachtas in due course. Separately, officials in the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment, the Department of Transport and the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage are examining options to support EV charging for households that do not have access to off-street parking. This work is being considered as part of the broader development of EV charging policy and infrastructure to ensure that drivers without access to home charging can participate fully in the transition to electric vehicles. Any measures brought forward will need to be safe, practical and appropriate for residential settings.

question: 869. Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation further to Parliamentary Question Nos. 544 and 619 of 30 June 2026, the way in which the forecasted overspends of the Department of Social Protection and the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration will be accommodated for within the Government's fiscal rules; if Supplementary Estimates will be used to cover these overspends; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [55526/26]
answer: Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation I propose to take Questions Nos. 869, 870 and 872 together. Gross voted spending at end June was €54.4 billion. This is €551 million or 1.0% below profile. The majority of Vote Groups are under profile at an overall level at end June. Three of the eighteen vote groups were ahead of profile at end June – Health; Further and Higher Education; and Social Protection. End June spending figures reflect the halfway point of the year. It remains too early to say what spending levels might mean for the overall year end position. Departments may be ahead of profile for a variety of reasons. Deviations from profile may arise due to the timing certain payments earlier than expected and these will likely correct themselves over the course of the year. Other overspends against profile may require mitigating actions to be taken to offset the overrun before year end. In any given year, there can be a range of reasons why Departments might require supplementary funding above the amount included in the original Estimate. Additional allocations may be needed due to Government decisions to provide supports in response to developments during the year – such as the decisions earlier this year on fuel support schemes – or where services or schemes cost more than a Department originally estimated. To ensure the significant level of investment under the Medium Fiscal and Structural Plan delivers on Programme for Government commitments and delivers value for money, there is a need for a strengthened expenditure control environment, a renewed focus on fiscal discipline, and robust oversight mechanisms. It is the responsibility of each Accounting Officer to manage expenditure within their allocations approved by the Dáil. It is essential that Departments actively pursue efficiencies and reforms to identify savings within their allocations, and to ensure that the significant resources allocated to them are used to efficiently and effectively deliver high-quality public services and supports. My Department will continue to monitor and engage with Departments over the second half of the year. The provision of any further supplementary estimates will be a matter for Government decision. Details around the breakdown of current and capital spending figures by Vote Group are available in the fiscal monitor published each month. A copy of the June Fiscal Monitor is attached to this response for information. June Fiscal Monitor

question: 882. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation if the Office of Public Works has received a request from An Garda Síochána or the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration, or initiated an assessment or business case, regarding the provision of a Garda station at Saggart as part of the Citywest campus; the expected timeframe for a decision; if local elected representatives will be updated once an outcome is reached; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [56035/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation The Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration (Department) published their 'Sectoral Investment Plan: Justice Sector' (plan) on the 4th of December 2025. The plan includes capital projects for An Garda Síochána over the period of 2026 to 2030. Some of the capital projects included within the plan are under construction at present, and it is anticipated that they will be complete over the period between 2026 and 2027. The second half of the plan published by the Department aims to bring several other capital projects to construction for An Garda Síochána over the period of 2028 to 2029. Further key projects for An Garda Síochána have been identified and will be progressed following delivery of the priorities included with the plan and outlined above. A new Garda Station for the Citywest area is one of those key projects to be progressed following the delivery of the priority projects listed in the plan. The Office of Public Works has not yet received a Business Case or equivalent from An Garda Síochána in respect of this project.

question: 964. Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment to review a work permit for a person (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [55159/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment Ireland operates a managed employment permits system in accordance with the Employment Permits Act 2024. The system is designed to help employers address identified skills and labour shortages while protecting employment opportunities for Irish and EEA workers. In relation to the case referred to by the Deputy, I am advised that the employment permit held by the person concerned was cancelled on 31 May 2026 after the Department was notified that their employment had ended. Under employment permits legislation, where the employment for which a permit was granted comes to an end, the permit is no longer valid. The person concerned subsequently applied to change employer on 12 June 2026. However, as their employment permit had already been cancelled, they were no longer eligible to use the Change of Employer process. The application was therefore refused on 15 June 2026. The person concerned or their perspective employer can submit a new employment permit application in relation to any new offer of employment. Full details of the process of submitting an employment permit application as well as employment permit application checklists for the most common permit types (including a general employment permit) are available on my Department’s website.

question: 966. Deputy Robert Troy asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if he will examine the current employment permit rules and criteria; if the employment length rule will be examined; his views on whether two years in the initial employment would be a fairer period instead of the current five year rule; his views on whether a change such as this would assist in the protection of work permit holders in their employment. [55200/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment The maximum period a General Employment Permit or Critical Skills Employment Permit holder is required to work with their original employer is 9 months. The protection of employment permit holders remains a key priority of my Department. In this regard, the Employment Permits Act 2024 introduced a significant new Change of Employer provision for holders of General Employment Permits and Critical Skills Employment Permits. As a new provision introduced under this Act, employment permit holders may now move their permit to a new employer after a period of nine months has passed since commencing work on their first employment permit in the State . This Change of Employer provision eliminates the need for the permit holder to apply for a new permit. General Employment Permit holders may change to the same occupation with a new employer, and Critical Skills Employment Permit holders may change within the broader category of employment. This option is intended to provide permit holders with greater freedom of movement to employment offering more attractive terms and conditions, or where they can better utilise their skillsets, while reducing dependency on a single employer. Where the change from initial employment is for a different occupation, a new employment permit is required. In this circumstance, the minimum requirement of nine months with the original employer remains. However, in both cases, the Act provides discretion prior to the nine-month period in cases evidencing a change of circumstances or instances of exploitation. The 2024 Act further supports the employment opportunities of permit holders by facilitating internal promotion or transfer within their current employment as long as the skills, qualifications or experience required for the proposed new role are the same, or substantially the same. Allowing workers to change employers can lead to a more dynamic and competitive labour market, benefiting the economy as a whole. It encourages employers to maintain high standards and good working conditions to retain their staff, which can lead to increased productivity and job satisfaction. My Department is currently reviewing the provisions relating to change of employers to ensure they provide a suitably accessible mechanism in line with employment permit holder and labour market needs. Any resulting recommendations will require careful consideration in the context of employment permit policy, immigration policy, worker protections and labour market requirements.

question: 992. Deputy Noel McCarthy asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the current average processing times for employment permit applications, renewals, and appeals; the actions being taken to reduce the current backlog of applications; the further measures being considered by his Department to reduce processing times for these applications; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [55861/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment (Deputy Alan Dillon) Ireland operates a managed employment permits system designed to maximise the benefits of economic migration while minimising disruption to the domestic labour market. The system facilitates the entry of appropriately skilled non-EEA nationals to address identified skills and labour shortages and to support enterprise and economic growth. The current average processing time for employment permit applications, renewals and appeals is as follows: Critical Skills Employment Permit applications 10 working days New General Employment Permit applications 25 working days All other New Applications (all permit types excluding CSEP, GEPs and I.C.T. applications) 24 working days Intra-Company Transfer Employment Permit Applications (New) 19 working days Intra-Company Transfer Employment Permit Applications (Renewal) 4 months Renewal Applications (All renewable permit types included) 4 months Reviews/Appeals 5 months Up-to-date processing dates are published on the Department’s website, and the Employment Permits Online System provides applicants with real-time updates on the status of their applications. From 01/01/2026 to 30/06/2026 the Department received 24,881 applications which is 47% increase on the number of applications received for the same period in the previous year (16,877). The number of permits issued from the start of the year to 30/06/2026 is 22,527 and this is 32.5% increase for the same period in 2025 (16,994). This year alone the Department has received 1,031 appeals. My Department has implemented a range of measures to improve processing times, including the allocation of additional resources and the introduction of more efficient processing methods, to ensure the system remains responsive to sustained demand across all permit types. My Department continues to monitor processing times closely and is committed to ensuring that the employment permits system remains efficient, modern, and responsive to the needs of a dynamic labour market.

question: 1012. Deputy William Aird asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if he will review the current 50:50 employment permits rule as it applies to the nursing home sector; if he will consider introducing the necessary legislative amendments to provide greater workforce flexibility for nursing homes experiencing recruitment difficulties; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [56722/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment Ireland’s employment permits system is designed to facilitate the targeted entry of appropriately skilled non-EEA nationals to address identified skills and labour shortages in the short to medium term. It is not intended to act as a substitute for, or a means of avoiding, the ongoing need to develop, upskill and fully utilise the resident workforce. The system therefore seeks to maximise the benefits of economic migration while safeguarding the domestic and wider EEA labour market, ensuring that opportunities for Irish and EEA workers are protected and that identified shortages are both genuine and demonstrable. The 50:50 rule is a key component of this framework which underpins Ireland’s obligations under the EU’s Union Preference principle and supports the Government’s broader employment creation strategy by encouraging balanced recruitment from domestic and EEA labour markets. The 50:50 rule requires that, at the time of application for an employment permit, 50% or more of the employees of the employer are Irish/EEA/Swiss/UK nationals. Officials of my Department conducted a review of Ireland’s use of the 50:50 rule, the outcome of which recommended the creation of two new regulation-making powers in the Employment Permits Act 2024. Following the review, Government approval has now been secured to prepare the General Scheme of a Bill to amend the relevant legislation. The forthcoming amendments will consider how best to ensure that the employment permits system remains responsive to labour market needs, with particular regard to the health and social care sector, while continuing to uphold Ireland’s obligations and policy objectives. Officials of my Department are actively developing the first stage of legislative requirements to implement changes to the 50:50 rule. Draft Heads for inclusion in a Bill that will give effect to the 50:50 changes have been commenced and are currently undergoing legal scrutiny. Given the 50:50 rule policy change was only recently approved by Government, the proposed Bill is expected to be on the Government Autumn Legislation Programme. My Department remains committed to delivering these amendments and ensuring that the employment permits system continues to be responsive and aligned with key national priorities and changes in a dynamic labour market.

question: 1049. Deputy Noel McCarthy asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment to provide an update on an employment permit appeal application for a person (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [57488/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment (Deputy Alan Dillon) The Employment Permits Unit of the Department informs me that the application for the person concerned (details supplied) was received by the Department on 12th January 2026 and it was refused on 16th February 2026. A request for a review of the refusal decision was received on 3rd March 2026. The appeal is currently under consideration by the Reviewing Officer. A decision in respect of the appeal will issue in due course.

question: 1052. Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if he will consider adding the occupation of healthcare assistant to the critical skills occupations list, in view of the continuing dependence of the healthcare and social care sectors on internationally recruited workers; if he has undertaken any assessment of the case for reclassifying healthcare assistants as a critical skills occupation; whether consideration has been given to the impact that critical skills employment permit status would have on worker retention and family reunification; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [57640/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment Ireland's economic migration policy is designed to address verified and ongoing skills and labour shortages across the economy. The employment permits system is vacancy-led and is managed through the Critical Skills Occupations List (CSOL) and the Ineligible Occupations List, both of which are reviewed on a regular basis to ensure they remain responsive to labour market needs. The employment permits system is intended to facilitate the recruitment of appropriately skilled non-EEA nationals where shortages exist, but it is not a substitute for investment in the education, training and upskilling of the resident workforce. Any changes to the occupations lists must therefore be balanced with broader workforce development objectives and informed by robust labour market evidence. Health care assistants are not included on the CSOL and are instead eligible for recruitment under the General Employment Permit route. Eligibility is determined through an evidence-based review process which assesses labour market shortages, skills requirements, strategic economic need and wider public policy considerations. The General Employment Permit (GEP) provides employers in this sector with a pathway to recruit internationally, where labour shortages are demonstrated, and health care assistants continue to play a vital role in supporting the delivery of health and social care services. In contrast, the CSOL generally provides for degree-level professional roles, is accompanied by significantly higher minimum annual remuneration requirements, and requires the worker to hold a relevant third-level degree or equivalent qualification. As such, Critical Skills Employment Permits are not the primary mechanism through which health and social care assistant shortages are addressed. Instead, the GEP continues to serve as the main pathway supporting workforce needs for these roles. Employment permit policy is kept under constant review. Reviews of the occupations lists involve public consultation with stakeholders, consideration of research undertaken by the Expert Group on Future Skills Needs and the Skills and Labour Market Research Unit in SOLAS, and engagement through the Economic Migration Interdepartmental Group, which includes representatives from key Government Departments. These reviews take account not only of labour market evidence, educational outputs and sectoral training initiatives, but also wider whole-of-Government considerations, including infrastructure development capacity, healthcare provision and other public services. Any proposal to amend eligibility for a particular occupation must therefore be based on clear evidence of ongoing shortages and workforce needs. While healthcare assistants were not recommended for inclusion on the Critical Skills Occupations List as an outcome the most recent review, this does not preclude the occupation from being considered in future reviews should labour market evidence indicate that such a change is warranted. My Department will continue to monitor labour market developments and engage with relevant stakeholders and Government Departments to ensure that the employment permits system remains responsive to identified skills and labour market needs. I remain committed to ensuring that the employment permits system continues to be responsive, evidence-based, and aligned with key national priorities including, importantly, the provision of health and social care.

question: 1053. Deputy Gillian Toole asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the formal collaborative processes that exist between his Department and the Department of Social Protection, to best match people on jobseeker’s payment with employers making applications for employment permits, across GEP, CSEP and trusted partner applications. [57677/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment The employment permits system is designed to ensure that employment opportunities arising in the State are offered, in the first instance, to suitably qualified workers from Ireland and the wider European Economic Area (EEA), before employers seek to recruit workers from outside the EEA. This policy is reflected in the operation of the Labour Market Needs Test, which is a key employment permit mechanism, facilitated by the engagement of my Department and the Department of Social Protection. Where a Labour Market Needs Test is required, including for General Employment Permit applications, employers must advertise the vacancy through the Department of Social Protection’s Employment Services for a minimum of 28 days before a valid employment permit application can be made. Employers must also advertise the vacancy on at least one additional online platform for a minimum of 28 days. The requirement to advertise vacancies through the Department of Social Protection’s Employment Services ensures that vacancies are made available to jobseekers in the domestic labour market, including persons in receipt of jobseeker payments, before an employer may seek to recruit a non-EEA national through a general employment permit. In addition to this operational role, the Department of Social Protection contributes labour market intelligence and analysis through interdepartmental engagement on economic migration policy and reviews of the employment permits occupations lists. The outcome of the most recent review was published in May 2026. During this review process the Department of Social Protection provided information relating to the connection between submissions and their impact on labour activation and community employment schemes. The Department’s Employer Relations Division was also consulted in order to ensure alignment with the National Employment Services Strategy Pathways to Work 2021-2025, and its successor strategy. This engagement ensures that decisions regarding occupations eligible for employment permits are informed by evidence regarding skills shortages and the availability of workers within the domestic labour market. Collaboration between my Department and the Department of Social Protection takes place both operationally, through the Labour Market Needs Test and through ongoing engagement on labour market conditions, economic migration policy, and reviews of the occupations eligible for employment permits. This structured engagement is integral to the development of economic migration policy while prioritising labour market activation.

question: 1156. Deputy Aindrias Moynihan asked the Minister for Education and Youth the number of schools awaiting approval for prefabricated or modular accommodation for September 2026 in Cork north-west; the number of these applications relating to special education provision; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [55461/26]
answer: Minister for Education and Youth I can confirm that within the school planning areas in Cork North-West, there are currently four modular accommodation projects in train which will deliver between them 4 Mainstream classrooms, 11 Special Education tuition rooms and 5 Special Education classrooms. Furthermore, there are three applications under my department's Additional School Accommodation (ASA) Scheme currently under assessment for mainstream and resource teaching accommodation. Separately there is one National Council for Special Education (NCSE) led project for special education classroom provision at viability report stage with the department’s Project Managers. My department’s approach is to maximise use of the capacity of the existing school estate as much as possible in the first instance and provide necessary additional capacity through targeted and prioritised project rollout over the course of 2026 to 2030 under the National Development Plan (NDP) to meet the most urgent needs. A number of factors are considered by my department in determining the most appropriate construction method to meet a school’s accommodation requirements, including the timing and duration of that accommodation need, and other school-specific factors. Modern methods of construction are an increasingly important feature of the construction landscape. The department’s modular programme is part of this and provides permanent and sustainable accommodation solutions. The Department of Education engages intensely with the NCSE in relation to the forward planning of new special education places. This work involves a detailed review of statistical data in relation to forecasting demand, an analysis of existing school accommodation capacity and a particular focus on the provision of special classes. Approximately 85% of the 584 additional special classes sanctioned by the NCSE for the upcoming school year are being established in repurposed existing classrooms with a further 10% being delivered as part of traditional building rollout and the remaining 5% involving the provision of a new modular classroom. The Deputy will appreciate that the immediate priority of my department is providing the required new and replacement school places each year to ensure that every child has a school place. Special class provision is the focus and priority for modular accommodation projects.

question: 1662. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether his Department has commissioned, funded or received research, including through a programme (details supplied), or the Housing Commission, examining the impact of housing affordability, rental costs or barriers to home ownership on outward migration of Irish citizens; if he will publish any such research; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [56037/26]
answer: Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage (Deputy James Browne) My Department has operated a joint research programme with the Economic and Social Research Institute since 2017. The output of the research programme is a series of published papers concerning housing economics and spatial planning topics with a high degree of policy relevance. These papers have examined a diverse range of matters including housing affordability, price sustainability, conditions in the private residential sector and demographic housing demand. My Department also undertakes and commissions research; the Department's researchers have examined topics including the housing aspirations of renters, the preferences of mature households, and intergenerational dependence on social housing. The papers mentioned above are published on a dedicated page on my Department's website: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-housing-local-government-and-heritage/collections/housing-economics-research-publications/. My Department has not commissioned or undertaken research specifically examining how conditions in housing markets may influence outward migration. The report of the Housing Commission made several references to the housing sector's role in shaping emigration and migration. I note, however, that many of the typical destinations for Irish emigrants also have pronounced housing affordability challenges, which suggests that other factors, such as vibrant labour markets, are also in play.

question: 1831. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether his Department is working with the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration and local authorities to ensure that victims of domestic violence who leave unsafe homes can access emergency and longer-term accommodation in a timely manner; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [58534/26]
answer: Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage Supporting individuals and families experiencing or at risk of experiencing homelessness, including victims and survivors of domestic abuse, is a priority for my Department and Government. The response to Domestic, Sexual and Gender-Based Violence (DSGBV) is a cross-Departmental and multi-agency issue, with overall policy coordinated by the Department of Justice. Responsibility for the development and provision of services to support victims rests with my colleague the Minister for Justice working in conjunction with Cuan, the statutory DSGBV agency under the remit of the Department of Justice. My Department, working with Cuan, supports the development of Domestic Violence Refuges in 18 identified priority areas through the Capital Assistance Scheme (CAS). CAS provides up to 100% capital funding to Approved Housing Bodies to advance Refuge projects in partnership with Domestic Violence groups. My Department and the Housing Agency work closely with the relevant local authorities and Cuan to support, provide technical advice, and advance these projects from initial design through to construction and completion. My Department’s role in relation to homelessness involves the provision of a national framework of policy, legislation and funding to underpin the role of local authorities in addressing homelessness at local level. Statutory responsibility in relation to the provision of accommodation and related services for homeless persons rests with individual local authorities. Decisions on the assessment of households for homeless services, the most appropriate form of such support, and the allocation of that support are a matter for the local authority concerned. Under the Housing Act 1988, it is a matter for each local authority to determine whether a person is regarded as homeless; section 2 of the Act sets out the requirements in this regard. When a household has been assessed as homeless, section 10 of the Housing Act 1988 provides that a local authority may provide accommodation and related services to that household. In 2017, my Department issued policy and procedural guidance to local authorities relating to the role they can play to assist victims of domestic violence. The issuing of this 2017 policy and guidance was a significant action in the second national strategy on DSGBV 2016-2021, and has since played an important role in addressing the housing needs of victims and survivors of DSGBV, providing direction to local authorities in supporting victims of domestic violence. It covers a range of scenarios that may arise for victims of domestic violence currently in receipt of social housing support and those seeking social housing supports. These include provisions around the use of the Housing Assistance Payment scheme, or the Rental Accommodation Scheme, where a victim has a joint interest in the family home, or ownership of alternative accommodation, but would otherwise qualify for social housing support. In June 2022 the Department of Justice published Zero Tolerance, the Third National Strategy on DSGBV 2022-2026. As an action in this strategy, my Department committed to a review of the 2017 Policy and Procedural Guidance for Housing Authorities in relation to assisting victims of domestic violence with emergency and long-term accommodation needs in order to ensure continuing effectiveness and consistency in responses to assist victims of domestic violence. My Department has engaged with Cuan in relation to this review and proposed recommendations arising from the review. Any updates to the policy and guidance will be communicated to local authorities in due course. In the meantime, local authorities operate in accordance with the 2017 Guidance. With regard to social housing support, the qualification criteria for social housing support are set down in Section 20 of the Housing (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2009 and the Social Housing Assessment Regulations 2011, as amended. Decisions on the allocation of social housing support are a matter solely for the local authority concerned. Each application must be considered on its own merits and the individual circumstances taken into account. Local authorities will prioritise allocations to those households they consider to be most in need, which can include victims of domestic violence. A Protocol to allow victims and survivors of domestic, sexual, and gender-based violence (DSGBV) to transfer their time on the social housing waiting list between different local authorities has recently been published by my Department and is currently being implemented by the local authorities. The Protocol gives effect to a commitment contained in Delivering Homes, Building Communities, which recognised that fleeing domestic violence continues to be a significant factor in presentations to homeless services and committed to removing barriers faced by victims and survivors. The Protocol allows victims and survivors of DSGBV assessed as qualified for social housing support, and who satisfy the necessary evidential requirements, to apply to another local authority and, subject to meeting the receiving authority's eligibility criteria, retain their original qualification date for waiting-list purposes. An important feature of the Protocol is that it will be actively monitored as it is rolled out, this monitoring will help ensure that the Protocol is meeting the needs of victims and survivors and will allow any concerns to be identified and addressed quickly should they arise. The HAP Place Finder service assists households in or at immediate risk of homelessness primarily by providing access to deposits and advance rental payments. These elements are the core financial supports and are available to prospective tenants in all local authority areas. To qualify for specific additional supports available to homeless households, a household must have been determined by the relevant local authority to be homeless within the meaning of section 2 of the Housing Act 1988. The operation of local homeless services, including the Place Finder Service, is a matter for each local authority. Since 11 July 2022, each local authority has statutory discretion to agree to a HAP payment up to 35% above the prescribed maximum rent limit, or up to 50% in the case of homeless households in the Dublin region. Local authorities also have additional flexibility to apply a couple HAP rate to single-person households. It is a matter for the local authority to determine, whether, and to what extent, the application of the flexibility is warranted. In addition to the above supports, a new protocol was established in 2020 when the Minister for Social Protection agreed to make rent supplement more accessible to victims of domestic violence. This measure aims to ensure that they are not prevented from leaving their homes because of financial or accommodation difficulties. Local authorities and their service delivery partners work closely with all households in need of emergency accommodation to provide appropriate emergency accommodation, and the ultimate aim is to support them to secure an exit to a tenancy. My Department will ensure sufficient funding is made available for all required homeless services, including the provision of emergency accommodation, to support those at risk of or experiencing homelessness.

question: 1883. Deputy Rory Hearne asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the estimated full year cost of providing emergency accommodation for people experiencing homelessness in Dublin to date in 2026; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [59092/26]
answer: Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage My Department's role in relation to homelessness involves the provision of a national framework of policy, legislation and funding to underpin the role of housing authorities in addressing homelessness at local level. Statutory responsibility in relation to the provision of homeless services rests with individual housing authorities. Section 10 of the Housing Act 1988 sets out the purposes for which costs may be incurred by housing authorities in respect of the provision of homeless accommodation and related services. While responsibility for the provision of accommodation for homeless persons rests with individual housing authorities, the administration of homeless services is organised on a regional basis, with nine administrative regions in place. A homelessness consultative forum has been established in each of the nine homeless regions in accordance with Chapter 6 of the Housing (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 2009. The Dublin Regional Homeless Executive provides a shared service on behalf of the four local authorities in the Dublin region, with Dublin City Council as the lead authority. My Department does not fund any homeless service directly but provides funding to housing authorities towards the operational costs of homeless accommodation and related services. Under Exchequer funding arrangements, housing authorities must provide at least 10% of the cost of services from their own resources. Furthermore, housing authorities may also incur additional expenditure on homeless related services outside of the Exchequer funding arrangements provided by my Department. Therefore, the exact amounts spent by housing authorities on homeless services including emergency accommodation, the amounts paid to private operators, as well as the type and operation of homeless services are a matter for individual housing authorities in consultation with the Management Group of the relevant regional joint Homelessness Consultative Forum. €513.5m in Exchequer funding has been allocated for the provision of homelessness accommodation and associated services. Financial reports from each of the homeless regions setting out their estimated costs and full year expenditure on homeless emergency accommodation and related services are published on my Department's website at the following link. The 2025 end of year reports will be published shortly. www.housing.gov.ie/housing/homelessness/other/homelessness-data. My Department is not in a position to provide the information requested for 2026 at this time.

question: 1937. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Social Protection the number of applicants for international protection and beneficiaries of temporary protection who received employment activation supports that included driving lessons, transport training or licence acquisition assistance in each year since 2020 to date in 2026. [58308/26]
answer: Minister for Social Protection I propose to take Questions Nos. 1937 and 1938 together. The Training Support Grant is a non-repayable grant, designed to support quick access to short-term training where the training is not delivered by a state provider. The grant can be provided to individuals where an immediate skills gap is identified that represents an obstacle to taking up a job offer or accessing other opportunities. Under the Training Support Grant a contribution of up to €250 can be awarded for Essential Driver Training, which refers to training course teaching and fundamental driving skills to learner car drivers’ B licence. There is no qualifying period to access this grant, and the support is available to all Jobseekers. The grant payment is paid directly to the training provider or organisation on completion of the course. While the primary focus of the scheme is on jobseekers and on supporting the activation policy of the Department, the grant is also available for individuals in receipt of other qualifying payments, who may be looking to up-skill when seeking employment. There is no qualifying period to access this grant, apart from Illness Benefit - you must be in receipt of Illness Benefit for a minimum of 6 months to be eligible for the Training Support Grant. The following table shows the number of Non-EEA Nationals and International Protection Applicants that availed of B Licence Driving Interventions under the Training Support Grant in total since 2021. Segregated data for Beneficiaries of Temporary Protection is not available, however, they are included within the Non-EEA Nationals figures. Disaggregated data from 2020 is not available. The Department is unable to provide a list of the individual training providers and the amount paid per organisation within the timeframe of a PQ response. The estimate assumes each intervention was awarded the maximum €250. question: 2119. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if his Department has engaged, or plans to engage, with the Jordanian authorities in relation to the ongoing Garda investigation into the death of a person (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [54937/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2119, 2120, 2137 to 2139, inclusive, and 2142 together. The investigation of alleged/suspected offences is an operational matter for An Garda Síochána. Decisions relating to prosecutions are a matter for the Director of Public Prosecutions, who is independent in the exercise of her functions. It would not be appropriate for me to comment on the details of any individual case. Within the European Union, the surrender of persons for the purpose of criminal prosecution or to serve a criminal sentence is governed by the European Arrest Warrant system which, in Ireland, is implemented in accordance with the European Arrest Warrant Act 2003, as amended. The European Arrest Warrant system provides a streamlined process of judicial cooperation based on the principle of mutual recognition of judicial decisions and mutual trust and respect between Member States. Ireland operates similar systems with the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland as well as Norway and Iceland, respectively. With countries outside the European Union, Norway, Iceland, and the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, extradition to/from Ireland is conducted in accordance with the Extradition Act 1965, as amended. Extradition in this regard may be carried out, where appropriate, in accordance with an applicable bilateral or multilateral treaty or other legal basis for extradition such as a reciprocal agreement. I can confirm that there is not at present a bilateral treaty between Ireland and the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan in respect of extradition or mutual legal assistance. International cooperation may also take place through a range of other mechanisms, depending on the legal framework applicable in the requested jurisdiction. These may include police-to-police cooperation, cooperation through INTERPOL channels, and requests for mutual legal assistance. The exact particulars of each case are considered in terms of any decision as to which possible legal avenue to engage. Ireland currently has bilateral treaties with a small number of states including the United States of America, Australia, Hong Kong (suspended) and the United Arab Emirates. For operational reasons, it would not be appropriate to release any details regarding any other bilateral treaties planned and/or in development. My Department keeps Ireland’s framework for international judicial cooperation under constant review.

question: 2122. Deputy Robert Troy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration in cases in which an employee is issued with an IRP card, when they apply for their atypical skills permit and the location changes but not the company, if they need to change their IRP card to match their new location on their critical skills permit. (details supplied) [56097/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I can advise the Deputy that an Irish Residence Permit (IRP) card does not include the details of an individuals location of employment. In the scenario referred to by the Deputy, such people should contact the Registration Office of my Department using the Customer Service Portal, where a note will be put on their file to reflect this change. Such individuals do not need to submit a new online renewal application or obtain a new IRP card. The Customer Service Portal can be accessed at the following link: www.portal.irishimmigration.ie/en/ .

question: 2123. Deputy Robert Troy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will ensure that a long stay spousal visa application is approved without further delay (details supplied). [56670/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I can advise the Deputy that the Join Family (Irish nat.)(spouse) visa application referred to was created on 26 March 2025. Supporting documentation was received in the Dublin Visa Office on 11 April 2025 where it awaits examination and processing. While I acknowledge the personal difficulties an applicant might be experiencing; it is not possible to give a definitive date as to when this application will be finalised. All applications are processed in chronological order, based on date order of receipt. While every effort is made to process applications as soon as possible, processing times will vary having regard to the volume and complexity of applications, the possible need for the Immigration Service Delivery function of my Department to investigate, inquire into, or seek further information, and the resources available. The current processing times for Dublin visa decisions is available here: www.irishimmigration.ie/visa-decisions/ The date published on the website is the oldest date of application currently being processed under a given category. However, it should be noted that the Visa team continue to process and make decisions on applications received after the published processing date. If a particular application takes longer to consider this may result in the published processing date remaining unchanged. I can assure you that this does not indicate the processing of these applications has halted overall. I am acutely aware that join family applications are very important for the people impacted. I understand that people are eager to have their families join them in Ireland, and I am committed to improving the service my Department provides. The person concerned can now directly check the status of their visa application on the Immigration Service’s Customer Service Portal. They can register for, or log in to their existing account, at: www.portal.irishimmigration.ie As an Oireachtas member, you can also request the status of individual immigration cases by e-mail, using the Oireachtas Mail facility at: IMoireachtasmail@justice.ie, which has been specifically established for this purpose. This service enables up to date information on such cases to be obtained without the need to seek information by way of the Parliamentary Question process.

question: 2124. Deputy Fionntán Ó Súilleabháin asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if the Government will revisit its Migrant Integration Strategy 2017-2020; to commission the Irish naturalisation and immigration service to carry out a piece of research to include a review of civics and language testing; to include a mapping exercise on international activity and best practice; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [58427/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2389, 2124, 2125, 2126, 2387, 2388, 2390, 2391, 2395, 2396 and 2397 together. The granting of Irish citizenship through naturalisation is governed by the provisions of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956, as amended. All applications for a certificate of naturalisation are processed and assessed individually in accordance with the provisions of the Act, including the requirement that applicants satisfy the good character criterion under Section 15. As part of a naturalisation application, each applicant is required to detail any offences, regardless of where an incident occurred, or how long ago, including “spent” convictions. All adult applicants must also undertake Garda vetting. As part of the good character assessment, An Garda Síochána is requested to make enquiries into the applicant’s background, the detail and extent of which is a matter for An Garda Síochána. Last November I secured Government approval to introduce new policies and legislative changes to strengthen Ireland’s migration and asylum system to ensure it is rules-based, efficient and more aligned with EU Member States. As part of this my Department is reviewing aspects of Ireland’s citizenship legislation and developing proposed amendments. This includes examining the possibility of language and civics testing as a requirement for naturalisation and reviewing research in this area that the Department commissioned from the Economic and Social Research Institute. My Department is committed to supporting evidence-informed policymaking. My Department has also supported public information programmes on migration and integration, including a national digital, social media and community information campaign on migration in 2024, and in 2026, supporting a series of community engagement sessions in each Local Authority area to hear community stakeholders' and service providers' experience of migration and integration. These meetings are ongoing at this time. This work will also be supported by the forthcoming National Migration and Integration Strategy, which will provide a long-term framework to guide Ireland's approach to migration and integration, based on evidence, collaboration across Government, and engagement with stakeholders. To that end, a Strategic Migration Policy Group (SMPG) was established in December 2024 to support that work which now consists of ten Government Departments, meeting at senior official level. The key objective of the Strategy and the SMPG is to develop a whole-of-government approach to migration policy that is coherent across Departments and responsive in seeking to address Ireland’s current and future demographic, economic and social policy needs.

question: 2127. Deputy Peter Roche asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether the Government has conducted an assessment of the risks posed by artificial intelligence to national security, public services, democratic processes and critical infrastructure; the measures being taken across Government to mitigate such risks. [58777/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2127 to 2129, inclusive, together. This Government recognises the benefits that artificial intelligence (AI) can bring, while also acknowledging that it can present risks which require careful consideration. The recently published National Digital and AI Strategy identified secure and trustworthy AI, cyber resilience and digital security as strategic priorities. The Strategy includes commitments to undertake a national AI cyber risk assessment, strengthen the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), enhance the capabilities of the Joint Cyber Defence Command, update the National Cyber Emergency Response Plan, implement the EU AI Act and strengthen governance arrangements for the use of AI across the public service. The NCSC which is an operational arm of my department monitors developments in AI-enabled cyber capabilities on a continuous basis and collaborates with our international partners in the EU and globally. The latest National Cyber Risk Assessment (NCRA), published last December, highlighted how AI drives systemic risk by increasing the speed, scale and sophistication of cyberattacks. In June 2026, the NCSC published Securing AI Adoption in the Public Sector, providing guidance to public bodies on identifying and managing cyber security risks associated with AI systems. This complements the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation's Responsible Use of AI in the Public Service framework which sets out governance, risk management, transparency and human oversight requirements for the use of AI by public bodies. In relation to risks to democratic processes and the information environment, the Department of Communication, Culture and Sport published the National Counter Disinformation Strategy in 2025, which analyses the rise of Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference (FIMI) and the role played by the amplification of harmful online content. The drafting of a new National Cyber Security Strategy, which is being led out by my department and currently open for consultation, aims to build resilience against AI-enabled threats by tasking the NCSC to develop AI readiness across government, small businesses, and critical national infrastructure (CNI). It further proposes leveraging AI to enhance national defence capabilities, which the NCSC will progress through the development of an AI readiness plan. This strategy will complement the work of Government as part of a suite of complementary strategies including the upcoming National Security Strategy.

question: 2130. Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will provide a current assessment on the dangers faced by the State from possible hybrid and cyberattacks on communications infrastructure in the State; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [59158/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) is an operational arm of my Department. The NCSC is tasked with protecting and defending against threats in the cyber domain and embedding cyber resilience throughout the country. In late 2025 the NCSC published its updated National Cyber Risk assessment, available at the following link - www.gov.ie/en/department-of-justice-home-affairs-and-migration/publications/ncsc-2025-national-cyber-risk-assessment/ The specific risk referenced by the Deputy is categorised under the Digital section in the National Critical Functions heading (Annex I) and assessed in Annex II. The analysis conducted as part of the assessment included a comprehensive review of the global threat landscape, an in-depth examination of cyber incidents observed here in Ireland, and active engagement with partner agencies. Within this risk assessment, the likelihood of a successful cyberattack is ‘Likely or Probable’. This has increased since the previous risk assessment (2022) to reflect the growing number of cyberattacks targeting digital infrastructure, due to its centrality in the daily life of the country. The Digital sector underpins all critical sectors, through the provision of high-capacity, data-driven networks, 24 x 7 communications via a host of global cloud providers, and high-tech data centres. It inherently poses as a high-value target for those intent on causing direct or indirect cross-sectoral disruption. However, it is important to note that there is maturity in this sector regarding resilience and business continuity planning, supporting its preparedness to recover from successful cyber-attacks. The impact from a successful attack has also been revised since 2022. In the context of the NCRA methodology, impact has moved to the upper end of ‘moderate’. As organisations, industry and public services advance digital transformation plans, dependencies on this sector increase. Consequently, any impact to operational stability will have increased consequences. The wider report underscores the need for a co-ordinated national approach to cyber security, including taking a whole-of-society approach to increasing resilience. The NCSC will continue to work to maintain Ireland’s position as a digitally advanced, secure, and trusted partner within the European and global cyber domain.

question: 2131. Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will detail the recent engagement his Department has had with the EU regarding migration in Europe; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [59322/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration My Department is committed to playing its part in delivering a successful Irish Presidency of the Council of the European Union. One of the key priority themes that has been identified for the Presidency is advancing a fair, firm, rules-based approach to migration, asylum and returns. In this context, my Department and I engage regularly with EU counterparts on migration issues across a wide range of working groups and other formats, including at the Justice and Home Affairs Council. I recently chaired the informal meeting of Home Affairs Ministers on 16 July 2026 in Dublin Castle. The meeting allowed Home Affairs Ministers from across the EU to engage in informal and open discussions on important migration issues. Meaningful conversations took place on how restricting visa-free travel can contribute to the internal security of the European Union and on the possibility of increasing information exchange with trusted third countries to support decision making related to internal security and migration management. I will also chair meetings of the JHA Council in Luxembourg in October, and in Brussels in December, and I expect migration to feature on the agenda for both. Officials in my Department are also chairing a large number of working parties. It is currently estimated that up to 200 such meetings will be chaired by Department officials during the Presidency, and a substantial number of these will relate to migration and asylum matters. Areas of particular focus in all of these discussions are likely to include the implementation of the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum and the recently agreed Returns Regulation, the extension of the activation of the Temporary Protection Directive, the availability of EU funding to support asylum and migration-related activities, the development of large-scale IT systems to support asylum and migration management across the EU, and of course emerging trends relating to migration, asylum and returns.

question: 2132. Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if the disposable income threshold to access Civil Legal Aid of €18,000 will be increased; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [54790/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Legal Aid Board is the statutory, independent body responsible for the provision of civil legal aid and advice to qualifying individuals. The Civil Legal Aid Scheme has two parts: a legal advice element and a legal representation element. Eligibility for the scheme is determined by reference to a financial assessment and the merits of the case being taken. In accordance with the provisions of the Civil Legal Aid Act 1995 (as amended) and associated Regulations, the Legal Aid Board calculates financial eligibility with reference to the applicant’s disposable income and disposable assets after certain allowances are applied to both. In June 2022, a Civil Legal Aid Review Group under the chairmanship of former Chief Justice Frank Clarke, SC, was established to review the current operation of the Civil Legal Aid Scheme. The outputs of the review were published in July 2025 and contained recommendations relating to eligibility for the Scheme including income threshold and allowances, as well as recommendations aimed at improving access to justice for people. In particular, the majority report recommends increasing the disposable income threshold from €18,000 to €23,500. Having the Civil Legal Aid Scheme and a Legal Aid Board which is equipped to meet the changing needs of society is critical to ensuring access to justice, particularly for those who have very modest means. However, any changes must be considered in the round and the potential implications that such changes might have on the operation of the Scheme. A critical aspect will therefore be the careful sequencing of reforms. Officials in my Department are examining the recommendations and are working closely with the Legal Aid Board to ensure any proposed reforms are developed as part of the annual budgetary Estimates process. Potential implications on the operation of the Scheme and broader government policy will be taken into account. The recommendations from the Review will also have to be considered with due regard to the findings from Ireland’s first legal needs survey, recently completed with the support of the European Commission and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). This survey will provide invaluable insights into the extent of legal need in Ireland. While preliminary results of the survey have been released on gov.ie, further analysis is underway, with officials in my Department working closely with the OECD on final outputs. I will revert to Government in due course with proposals to reform the Scheme.

question: 2133. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the reason biometric data of migrants is not shared with authorities in Britain; and the plans he has to address this. [54835/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Ireland and the United Kingdom have a shared responsibility and a shared interest in protecting the Common Travel Area (CTA). It offers great advantages to our people on a social and economic level. The invisible border on the island of Ireland is among the most tangible gains of the peace process and is essential to the continuing normalisation of relationships. For security reasons and to protect the integrity of the immigration system, both I and my Department do not comment on specific operational channels of communication with UK immigration authorities. However, I can advise the Deputy that there is extensive engagement and cooperation at all levels between my Department officials and their Home Office counterparts, as well as significant operational cooperation between the Gardaí, UK Border Force, UK policing services and the Police Service of Northern Ireland. This strong practical engagement and cooperation serves the mutual interests of both Ireland and the UK and will continue. At the UK Ireland Summit in March it was agreed that further steps would be taken to ensure that the CTA remains secure by working together to expand immigration data sharing arrangements, particularly in preventing abuse of CTA free movement by those not entitled to its benefits. In June, I discussed the importance of cross border cooperation in protecting the CTA for both Ireland and the UK by phone with the Northern Ireland Minister for Justice, Naomi Long and the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland, Hillary Benn. I also spoke with UK Home Secretary, Shabana Mahmood; we discussed recent events across Northern Ireland, the ongoing need for cross border cooperation and our shared focus on protecting the Common Travel Area. Furthermore, I intend to meet with the Home Secretary at the earliest opportunity to discuss relevant matters, including returns.

question: 2135. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the current status of the family reunification-spouse visa application by a person (details supplied) submitted on 28 October 2025; and when a decision is expected. [54894/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2135 and 2136 together. I can advise the Deputy that the Join Family visa applications referred to were created on 1 October 2025. Supporting documentation was received in the Dublin Visa Office on 29 October 2025 where they await examination and processing. My Departments business target for join family visa applications is 12 months. It must be made clear that these are business targets for the immigration service and some applications can take longer than others. The business target reflects the detailed and often complex assessment that is required to be carried out in relation to applications for family reunification. While I acknowledge the personal difficulties an applicant might be experiencing; it is not possible to give a definitive date as to when these applications will be finalised. All applications are processed in chronological order, based on date order of receipt. While every effort is made to process applications as soon as possible, processing times will vary having regard to the volume and complexity of applications, the possible need for the Immigration Service Delivery function of my Department to investigate, inquire into, or seek further information, and the resources available. The current processing times for Dublin visa decisions is available here: www.irishimmigration.ie/visa-decisions/ The date published on the website is the oldest date of application currently being processed under a given category. However, it should be noted that the Visa team continue to process and make decisions on applications received after the published processing date. If a particular application takes longer to consider this may result in the published processing date remaining unchanged. I can assure you that this does not indicate the processing of these applications has halted overall. I am acutely aware that join family applications are very important for the people impacted. I understand that people are eager to have their families join them in Ireland, and I am committed to improving the service my Department provides. The people concerned can now directly check the status of their visa applications on the Immigration Service’s Customer Service Portal. They can register for, or log in to their existing accounts, at: www.portal.irishimmigration.ie/ As an Oireachtas member, you can also request the status of individual immigration cases by e-mail, using the Oireachtas Mail facility at: IMoireachtasmail@justice.ie, which has been specifically established for this purpose. This service enables up to date information on such cases to be obtained without the need to seek information by way of the Parliamentary Question process.

question: 2137. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if there is an extradition treaty in place between Ireland and the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan; if his Department has ever initiated or considered initiating negotiations for such a treaty; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [54921/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2119, 2120, 2137 to 2139, inclusive, and 2142 together. The investigation of alleged/suspected offences is an operational matter for An Garda Síochána. Decisions relating to prosecutions are a matter for the Director of Public Prosecutions, who is independent in the exercise of her functions. It would not be appropriate for me to comment on the details of any individual case. Within the European Union, the surrender of persons for the purpose of criminal prosecution or to serve a criminal sentence is governed by the European Arrest Warrant system which, in Ireland, is implemented in accordance with the European Arrest Warrant Act 2003, as amended. The European Arrest Warrant system provides a streamlined process of judicial cooperation based on the principle of mutual recognition of judicial decisions and mutual trust and respect between Member States. Ireland operates similar systems with the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland as well as Norway and Iceland, respectively. With countries outside the European Union, Norway, Iceland, and the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, extradition to/from Ireland is conducted in accordance with the Extradition Act 1965, as amended. Extradition in this regard may be carried out, where appropriate, in accordance with an applicable bilateral or multilateral treaty or other legal basis for extradition such as a reciprocal agreement. I can confirm that there is not at present a bilateral treaty between Ireland and the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan in respect of extradition or mutual legal assistance. International cooperation may also take place through a range of other mechanisms, depending on the legal framework applicable in the requested jurisdiction. These may include police-to-police cooperation, cooperation through INTERPOL channels, and requests for mutual legal assistance. The exact particulars of each case are considered in terms of any decision as to which possible legal avenue to engage. Ireland currently has bilateral treaties with a small number of states including the United States of America, Australia, Hong Kong (suspended) and the United Arab Emirates. For operational reasons, it would not be appropriate to release any details regarding any other bilateral treaties planned and/or in development. My Department keeps Ireland’s framework for international judicial cooperation under constant review.
