question: 2140. Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he is aware of the policy currently being enforced in an IPAS centre (details supplied) which prohibits food from being consumed in rooms as well as the use of fridges to store food items and vital medicines; if he will instruct his Department to review this policy and ensure IPAS residents are able to store and consume food in their rooms. [54936/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration IPAS Accommodation is provided in a range of different locations and types of accommodation, including both self-catering and catered accommodation. While the Department cannot provide information about individual cases, correspondence relating to the location and details supplied has been received by officials who are giving it attention. As per the IPAS House Rules, the use of unauthorised electrical equipment such as fridges in residents’ rooms is not permitted in any accommodation centre, because of the significant fire and health and safety risks they pose. Additionally, due to the health and safety risks posed, those accommodated may not store, cook or prepare food in their room. IPAS directs centres, where necessary, to provide a fridge in a shared space or add a secure box to a shared fridge for medicines which may require refrigeration. Where there are medically mandated dietary requirements, the resident can inform centre management in order for them to provide for this appropriately. If a person applying for international protection has any concerns in relation to their accommodation, they can also contact IPAS directly via a dedicated helpdesk at ipasinbox@justice.ie.

question: 2141. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration given that emergency Covid powers were exercised on an unprecedented scale, his views on whether it is acceptable that neither his Department nor the Garda Commissioner can provide basic statistics on prosecutions, convictions and fines arising from those powers. [54939/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Operational Policing is a matter for the Garda Commissioner, who is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Siochana under section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024. The Commissioner is independent in the exercise of his operational policing functions under section 34 of that Act. I can inform the Deputy that An Garda Siochana maintained operational records relating to the enforcement of the emergency Covid- 19 legislation. However, the specific information sought by the Deputy, including statistics on prosecutions, convictions and fines, is not held in a readily extracted format. Compiling this information would require the examination of a significant volume of operational and Court records and would involve a disproportionate amount of time and resources. The management of the courts, operational matters and logistical functions are the responsibility of the judiciary and Courts Service, which are independent in exercising their functions under the Courts Service Act 1998 and the Constitution. As Minister, I have no role in these matters and my Department does not record data relating to convictions, as this is a function of the courts. The Deputy may also wish to note that the Courts Service has a dedicated email address for the provision of information to members of the Houses of the Oireachtas: oireachtasenquiries@courts.ie.

question: 2144. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of complaints relating to anti-social behaviour involving e-scooters in Tallaght and Citywest, County Dublin since May 2024; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [54971/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2144, 2145 and 2146 together. Gardaí have significant legislative powers to combat the antisocial and dangerous misuse of e-scooters, e-bikes, scramblers and other such vehicles. I can assure the Deputy that Gardaí respond to reports of anti-social behaviour and conduct operations on a continuous basis, targeting people engaged in anti-social activities involving the misuse of scramblers, electric motorbikes and e-scooters in public places. To be of assistance to the Deputy I had requested information from the Garda Authorities on the number of complaints relating to anti-social behaviour involving e-scooters. An Garda Síochána respond to all calls for service and calls are routed through a regional control room and prioritised for response. I am informed by the Garda Authorities that they are unable to establish the exact number of complaints received in respect of e-scooters from Garda records, either from PULSE or from GardaSafe. Consequently, An Garda Síochána are therefore not in a position to provide a response on the number of complaints relating to anti-social behaviour involving e-scooters in Tallaght and Citywest. An Garda Síochána has taken significant action against the illegal use of e-scooters, e-bikes and other powered personal transporters. There have been 793 prosecutions for possession of e-scooters so far this year. Operation Meacán within the Dublin Metropolitan Region (DMR) aims to tackle the use of electric motorbikes, e-scooters and e-bikes which are being used illegally in our public spaces and for criminal activity including drug distribution, money laundering, transporting firearms, Drug Related Intimidation (DRI) and other serious offences. On 21 July, Gardaí conducted a Day of Action in the DMR West with aerial support and the use of a drone from the newly established Garda Drone Unit. As part of this operation one scrambler, two e-bikes and 11 e-scooters were seized by Gardaí from individuals driving in contravention of regulations and/ or in a dangerous manner on public roads and pedestrianised streets. I am advised by An Garda Síochána that since the introduction of the Road Traffic (Electric Scooters) Regulations on 20 May 2024, there have been 853 Fixed charge notices issued involving electric powered personal transporter (ePPT) vehicles. The below table provides a breakdown of incidents by year where a fine was issued involving electric powered personal transporter (ePPT) vehicles in the Dublin region from 1 May 2024 to 30 June 2026. question: 2147. question: 2148. Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the options available for a person from Belarus who has an expired passport but cannot return to Belarus to renew it due to new rules introduced there, but who needs a current passport for their IRP Stamp 4 card; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [54989/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration An in-date national passport is a requirement to support any application for the renewal of an immigration permission. Where an applicant is not in possession of an in-date passport, but they can provide evidence that they have applied for a new passport, the Registration Office may provide a short-term permission, up to six months, to give them time to obtain a new passport. In exceptional circumstances, if an applicant can provide evidence that applying for a new passport would present a danger to themselves or their family, the requirement to provide a current in-date passport can be waived for that renewal period. Each request of this nature is considered on a case by case basis. Further information on the renewal process as well as the list of documents required for each stamp type are available on the ISD website at the following link: www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/how-to-register-your-immigration-permission-for-the-first-time/required-documents/ .

question: 2149. Deputy John Lahart asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration with regard to the recent meeting held in Brussels between European Commission officials, representatives of EU Member States and the Taliban concerning migration and returns to Afghanistan who represented the EU side (details supplied); if any Irish officials attended the meeting; if the Government had been informed, who attended on behalf of the European Commission and the Member States; if women were present representing the EU or Ireland during these discussions; the safeguards that were discussed to ensure that any returns to Afghanistan comply with international human rights obligations, particularly the principle of non-refoulement; if the Government requested that the European Commission publish the attendee list, agenda and meeting record in the interests of transparency; the way in which these discussion were conducted; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [55015/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The meeting referred to by the Deputy was held during the Cyprus Presidency of the Council of the European Union. While my Department was aware of the meeting, there was no representative from Ireland in attendance and documentation, including the agenda, location of the meeting or the list of attendees, was not shared with Ireland. Ireland’s position on returns in a broader sense is well articulated at European Union level. Ireland is supportive of utilising voluntary returns provided that return is voluntary, safe, dignified and durable. Ireland is open to consideration of all options regarding enforced returns, provided that any proposed option is practical, represents value for money, and would be carried out in full compliance with respect for fundamental rights, including the principle of non-refoulement.

question: 2150. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the catchment area size population for each Garda station in the country, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [55026/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under Section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which includes the distribution and stationing of Garda personnel throughout the State. An Garda Síochána police on a Divisional basis using all resources in a Community Engagement area, supported by Divisional resources and units. This Operating Model has been designed to enable An Garda Síochána to meet the challenges of modern-day policing more consistently around the country by enabling specialisation in the delivery of key services and freeing up more Gardaí to focus on front line policing. Under this structure, each Division is organised into four Functional Areas: Community Engagement, Crime, Performance Assurance, and Business Services. The Operating Model, coupled with some realignment of responsibilities, is helping to deliver a consistent, community-focused policing service. I regularly engage with the Garda Commissioner to ensure our Gardaí have the resources they need. I am informed that when allocating and transferring Garda members to and from any Division, consideration is given to commitments and undertakings outlined in the Annual Policing Plan and priorities as determined in delivering ‘A Policing Service for The Future’. The Deputy may be interested to note that Garda authorities advise that the requirements of all Garda Divisions nationwide are also taken into account, which include: • Local and national crime trends and workloads; • Policing arrangements and operational strategies; • Minimum establishment statistics; • Local population and trends, geographical area and size; • Transfer applications, including welfare, personnel issues and concerns. An Garda Síochána publishes information in relation to the allocation of Gardaí nationally, including a breakdown of Garda allocated to divisions and stations nationwide. Data for 2026 can be found here: Human Resources Statistics - Garda (www.garda.ie/en/information-centre/garda-statistics/human%20resources/) . The Deputy should select the relevant month and access the file called 'Garda Members by Division District Station' on the allocation of Gardaí by station. Historical data on the allocation of Gardaí can be found here: www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/human-resources-and-people-development/garda-hr-directorate/garda-strength-breakdown-2025/garda-strength-breakdown-2025.html The Deputy should select December 2025 and then select 'Garda Members by Division District Station'. The historical data is included in this file.

question: 2151. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for an update on the working group on establishing a new Garda college; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [55027/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Garda Training Review Group was established to identify delivery options to increase the scale and capacity of high-quality education, training and continuous professional development in An Garda Síochána. This will help ensure that the skills needs of the organisation are met over the next decade. A former Secretary General was Chair of the Group, with senior officials representing the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration, An Garda Síochána, the Department of Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science, the Office of Public Works and the Higher Education Authority. The Group convened for the first time on 30 January and subsequently met eight times to progress its work. I received the final report from the Chair on 30 June and will be considering its contents.

question: 2152. Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the timeframe in which his Department is obliged to process the renewal of a residency permit; his Departments targeted timeframe; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [55034/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2447, 2152, 2162 and 2400 together. The Registration Office of my Department continues to experience an exceptionally high demand for first time registration appointments and immigration permission renewal applications. I understand that the extended wait times can be frustrating for applicants, and I can assure the Deputy that my Department is utilising every avenue available to facilitate as many applicants as quickly as possible and to increase processing capacity. The Registration Office is open seven days a week to facilitate customers to process both first time registration appointments and online renewals, with significant additional staff assigned to this work. This is having an impact and wait times are reducing, and I expect times to reduce further over the summer months. In the meantime, I can advise the Deputy that I recently published an updated interim employer notice and a notice to facilitate customers travelling during the summer months to alleviate pressure on applicants while the Department continues to reduce the wait times. Where an employee’s Irish Residence Permit (IRP) card has expired and they are unable to obtain a new one by the expiry date of their current IRP card, they are still permitted to work and to remain in the State until 31 August 2026. This applies to all expired IRP cards regardless of the number of weeks elapsed, but is subject to the applicant submitting their renewal application prior to their current IRP card expiring. Further information on this notice can be found at the following www.irishimmigration.ie/minster-announces-interim-notice-to-employers-regarding-renewal-of-registration/ It is important to note that the existing www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/how-to-renew-your-current-permission/notice-to-employers/.will continue to apply after 31 August 2026. Furthermore, the previous travel arrangements made for people awaiting a renewal of their IRP card who intend to travel has been reinstated until 31 August 2026. People may use their recently expired IRP card to travel until the end of August 2026, provided an application to renew their registration permission was submitted in advance of the expiry date of their IRP Card. Further information can be found on the ISD website at the following www.irishimmigration.ie/minster-announces-interim-notice-to-employers-regarding-renewal-of-registration/. While the Registration Office endeavours to process applications as quickly as possible, processing times for each stamp category may vary due to a number of factors, such as the number of applications on hand, individual circumstances, the complexity of applications, whether further information is required, and peak application periods. The objective is to reducing the timelines across all categories to more sustainable levels. The Registration Office provide a live application processing date broken down by stamp category, which is updated every Monday, and is available at the following link: www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/how-to-renew-your-current-permission/renewing-your-registration-permission-if-you-live-in-the-republic-of-ireland/. Applicants can now directly check the status of their immigration application on the Immigration Service’s Customer Service Portal. They can register for, or log in to their existing account, at www.portal.irishimmigration.ie/en/. It is also open to any person to request to have their renewal application expedited due to extenuating circumstances, and they can do so by contacting the Registration team of the Department via the Customer Service Portal. They will need to explain their circumstances and the urgent need to travel. All such requests are considered on a case by case basis. I can advise that as of 27 July 2026, there are approximately 59,000 renewal applications awaiting examination. The information requested on the number of Stamp 4 renewal applications submitted within 16 weeks that are yet to be processed is not readily available.

question: 2153. Deputy Danny Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide an update on a matter (details supplied; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [55051/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration It is a central priority for me as Minister that our immigration laws are robust and enforced. The State is required to examine the application of anyone who presents at the borders of the State, or is in the State, and indicates that they wish to make an application for international protection. This is in accordance with our obligations under international and EU asylum law and the Government takes those commitments very seriously. Each application for international protection is examined in detail on its individual merits, taking all factors into account. Where an applicant has been refused and has exhausted all appeal avenues for international protection, they have the option of voluntary return, which if not accepted will in the normal course lead to the making of a deportation order. The only barrier to that course of action is the provisions of section 50 of the International Protection Act 2015 on the prohibition of refoulement. If a person does not remove themselves from the State following the issuance of a deportation order, they will be removed. A deportation order is a legal order to leave the State, and the enforcement of a deportation order is an operational matter for the Garda National Immigration Bureau (GNIB). My Department works closely with the GNIB to progress arrangements for the removal of people subject to deportation orders. Any person who is the subject to a deportation order is ineligible for social assistance payments and a range of other public services such as accommodation.

question: 2154. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if international protection applicants are permitted to retain their passports while an application or appeal is pending; the date on which any change to this policy took effect; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [55091/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2154, 2155 and 2156 together. It is a central priority of this Government that our immigration laws are robust and enforced. Since taking office, I have worked to ensure integrity, efficiency and public confidence in our migration system. Passports and identity documents are surrendered by international protection applicants to the International Protection Office (IPO) at the time of their initial application. For those in the International Protection process, under section 16(3)(a) of the International Protection Act 2015, they or any dependents on whose behalf an application has been made, must not attempt to leave the State without the express permission of the Minister. This consent is only granted in exceptional circumstances. Passports are not returned to those who have been granted Refugee Status. Anyone given a refugee declaration under section 55 of the International Protection Act 2015 or who is a beneficiary of international protection under the International Protection Act 2026 (other than a person to whom section 207(2) of that Act applies) is entitled to a 1951 UN Convention Travel Document, sometimes referred to as a Refugee Travel Document, which is used in lieu of a passport to travel from and into the State. Aside from those provisions rooted in the Qualification Regulation, which relate to the criteria to be recognised as a refugee or to be granted subsidiary protection, the vast majority of the provisions of the 2026 Act do not apply retrospectively to those who made their applications prior to 12th June.

question: 2161. Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the actions being taken to reduce overcrowding in the Irish prison system. [55106/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I am acutely aware of the capacity constraints in our prisons and the resulting challenges faced by those who work and live in our prisons. The Irish Prison Service (IPS) must accept into custody all people committed to prison by the courts and has no control over the numbers committed to custody at any given time. I am pursuing a dual approach to address the issue of prison overcrowding by both increasing prison capacity and pursuing further measures to support increased use of non-custodial sanctions. Since 2024, 265 spaces have been constructed across the Prison Estate, with 126 finished in 2024, 106 in 2025 and a further 33 so far in 2026. A further 32 spaces will be built this year, and 70 in 2027 The Government has allocated funding for a significant building programme in the prison estate. On conclusion of the NDP Review in July 2025, I secured a record capital investment of €528 million from 2026 to 2030, of which €495 million is being invested in building projects to further increase capacity, with an overall target of delivering over 1,500 spaces by 2031. This will include a large extension to the existing Cork Prison, a new block in Wheatfield, and an additional block extension at Midlands prison. This is in addition to spaces created at Castlerea, Mountjoy and the Dóchas Centre. Last year, a total of 304 Recruit Prison Officers were recruited by the Irish Prison Service. The pay budget, totalling €383m in 2026, will fund the IPS staffing plans which include a target of 250 prison officers onboarded in 2026. Additionally, the IPS will work with the Department to onboard 26 additional permanent clinical and allied health posts, in response to the challenges of managing prisoners with major mental illness. Measures to support non-custodial sanctions are also important. The Criminal Law, Civil Law and Defence (Miscellaneous Provisions) Bill 2026 has been passed by both Houses and will amend the Criminal Justice (Community Service) Act 1983 to support and encourage greater use of community service orders (CSOs). It includes an amendment to oblige the courts to consider a CSO in lieu of a prison sentence of up to 24 months’ duration (the current such threshold being 12 months) and to give reasons where they consider that a CSO should not be imposed in such a case. This amendment will oblige judges to demonstrate that they have considered this alternative. The Bill will further amend the 1983 Act to increase the maximum community service hours that a judge may order from 240 to 480. Budget 2026 also provides for a 13% increase in funding for the Probation Service. This additional funding will be used to increase the use of supervised community sanctions in the criminal courts, expand restorative justice services, and expand supervised temporary release schemes nationally. The Programme for Government commits to implement electronic tagging for appropriate categories of people, including those on temporary release and on bail. Under Budget 2026, I secured funding of €2.1 million for the project and anticipate electronic monitoring will be operational in 2026. Additionally, a Prison Overcrowding Response Group (PORG) was established in July 2023, composed of officials from my Department and representatives from relevant agencies. The Group considers measures to address capacity issues in the prison estate. In June 2024, following a report from this Group, a range of actions was agreed. Actions agreed by the PORG include developing new responses to deliver structured temporary release for suitable prisoners, actions to encourage greater use of community service, and advancing legislative changes to support delivery of community-based sanctions. The PORG continues to meet and work to implement these actions is ongoing.

question: 2162. Deputy Joanna Byrne asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of renewal applications for Stamp 4 submitted within the recommended 16-week lead time are yet to be processed. [55112/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2447, 2152, 2162 and 2400 together. The Registration Office of my Department continues to experience an exceptionally high demand for first time registration appointments and immigration permission renewal applications. I understand that the extended wait times can be frustrating for applicants, and I can assure the Deputy that my Department is utilising every avenue available to facilitate as many applicants as quickly as possible and to increase processing capacity. The Registration Office is open seven days a week to facilitate customers to process both first time registration appointments and online renewals, with significant additional staff assigned to this work. This is having an impact and wait times are reducing, and I expect times to reduce further over the summer months. In the meantime, I can advise the Deputy that I recently published an updated interim employer notice and a notice to facilitate customers travelling during the summer months to alleviate pressure on applicants while the Department continues to reduce the wait times. Where an employee’s Irish Residence Permit (IRP) card has expired and they are unable to obtain a new one by the expiry date of their current IRP card, they are still permitted to work and to remain in the State until 31 August 2026. This applies to all expired IRP cards regardless of the number of weeks elapsed, but is subject to the applicant submitting their renewal application prior to their current IRP card expiring. Further information on this notice can be found at the following www.irishimmigration.ie/minster-announces-interim-notice-to-employers-regarding-renewal-of-registration/ It is important to note that the existing www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/how-to-renew-your-current-permission/notice-to-employers/.will continue to apply after 31 August 2026. Furthermore, the previous travel arrangements made for people awaiting a renewal of their IRP card who intend to travel has been reinstated until 31 August 2026. People may use their recently expired IRP card to travel until the end of August 2026, provided an application to renew their registration permission was submitted in advance of the expiry date of their IRP Card. Further information can be found on the ISD website at the following www.irishimmigration.ie/minster-announces-interim-notice-to-employers-regarding-renewal-of-registration/. While the Registration Office endeavours to process applications as quickly as possible, processing times for each stamp category may vary due to a number of factors, such as the number of applications on hand, individual circumstances, the complexity of applications, whether further information is required, and peak application periods. The objective is to reducing the timelines across all categories to more sustainable levels. The Registration Office provide a live application processing date broken down by stamp category, which is updated every Monday, and is available at the following link: www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/how-to-renew-your-current-permission/renewing-your-registration-permission-if-you-live-in-the-republic-of-ireland/. Applicants can now directly check the status of their immigration application on the Immigration Service’s Customer Service Portal. They can register for, or log in to their existing account, at www.portal.irishimmigration.ie/en/. It is also open to any person to request to have their renewal application expedited due to extenuating circumstances, and they can do so by contacting the Registration team of the Department via the Customer Service Portal. They will need to explain their circumstances and the urgent need to travel. All such requests are considered on a case by case basis. I can advise that as of 27 July 2026, there are approximately 59,000 renewal applications awaiting examination. The information requested on the number of Stamp 4 renewal applications submitted within 16 weeks that are yet to be processed is not readily available.

question: 2163. Deputy Mark Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of community Gardaí allocated to the Garda stations in Clondalkin, Ronanstown, Lucan and Rathcoole in each year since 2020 to date in 2026, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [55138/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2163 and 2164 together. Under the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, the Garda Commissioner is responsible for the distribution and stationing of Garda personnel throughout the State. I engage regularly with the Commissioner and I am assured that the resourcing of each Garda Division is fully considered within the overall context of the needs and requirements of Garda Divisions throughout the country. As Minister, my priority is getting more Gardaí into all our communities by supporting increased recruitment and appropriate civilianisation where possible. A Garda budget of €2.74 billion in 2026 is funding the recruitment of up to 1,000 new Gardaí, 200 more Garda staff and additional members of the Garda Reserve. The Garda Commissioner and his senior management team keep the distribution of resources under ongoing review and I understand that when allocating and transferring Garda members to and from any Division, consideration is given to commitments and undertakings outlined in the Annual Policing Plan. The Commissioner also takes the requirements of all Garda Divisions nationwide into account, which include: • Local and national crime trends and workloads; • Policing arrangements and operational strategies; • Minimum establishment statistics; • Local population and trends, geographical area and size; • Transfer applications, including welfare, personnel issues and concerns. An Garda Síochána publishes information in relation to the allocation of Garda personnel nationally. This includes a breakdown of Gardaí assigned to the Community Policing Units by Division from 2008 to the end of June 2026, the latest date for which figures are available. This can be found at the following links: Information for 2026 can be found at the following link: www.garda.ie/en/information-centre/garda-statistics/human%20resources/ . Information for previous years can be found at the following link: www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/human-resources-and-people-development/garda-hr-directorate/garda-strength-breakdown-2025/december-2025.html .

question: 2168. Deputy Joe Cooney asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of domestic violence incidents reported in County Clare during each of the past five years. [55154/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Combatting all forms of domestic, sexual and gender-based violence (DSGBV) is a priority for this Government, for me as Minister, and for the Garda Commissioner. 'Zero Tolerance,' the Third National Strategy on Domestic, Sexual and Gender-based Violence (DSGBV), set out an ambitious five-year programme of reform to achieve a society that does not accept DSGBV or the attitudes underpinning these crimes. A Garda Síochána prioritise and proactively respond to incidents of domestic abuse. The nationwide roll out of Divisional Protective Service Units (DPSUs) ensures that when victims of crimes such as domestic abuse and sexual violence present to Gardaí, they are met with a consistently high standard of specialist, sensitive, professional and expert assistance. I can confirm that there is now a DPSU in every Garda Division. In relation to the specific information sought by the Deputy, An Garda Síochána has advised that it is not possible to provide a breakdown by county. A divisional breakdown is provided in line with the new An Garda Síochána Operating Model. The table below shows the number of domestic abuse incidents reported in the Clare/Tipperary Division. Figures have been provided for the past five full years in addition to figures for the first two quarters of 2026. 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 2026 1955 2148 2456 2395 2745 1543 I am further advised by AGS that these figures are based on incident data available on the Pulse database as at 16 July 2026 and are operational and subject to change. Domestic Abuse incidents have been defined as any incident with an incident type of: • Breach of Barring Order • Breach of Emergency Barring Orders • Breach of Interim Barring Order • Breach of Protection Order • Breach of Safety Order • Breach of Barring/Protection Orders • Coercive Control • Domestic – No Offence Identified or any incident with a domestic abuse motive. My Department is continuing to work with agencies in the criminal justice system to strengthen trust and confidence in the system, so that victims will feel more assured in coming forward to report what has happened to them. I want to reassure anyone who is subject to, or at risk of, domestic or sexual abuse that practical help is always available. I urge anyone who is in fear or danger due to domestic abuse or any other crime, to please contact the Gardaí as soon as it is safe to do so.

question: 2170. Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will devise a policy whereby payments made to the Criminal Assets Bureau, arising from the proceeds of crime, will be ring-fenced and made entirely available, via bursary schemes, to community groups; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [55161/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2170, 2171, 2194, 2283 and 2301 together. CAB is a multi-agency statutory body established under the Criminal Assets Bureau Act, 1996. I am advised that all monies seized by CAB are remitted to the Central Fund of the Exchequer after the appropriate statutory time frame under the Proceeds of Crime Acts. I was pleased to secure an 8.2% increase on the Criminal Assets Bureau budget allocation for 2026. The Bureau’s budget allocation in 2026 is €13.8m, of which €11.25m is for Pay and €2.55m is for Non-Pay. A 15% uplift on the Criminal Assets Bureau’s total budget would equate to €2.07m additional in funding. This would provide a total budget in 2027 totalling €15.15m. I am committed to ensuring that the Criminal Assets Bureau have the powers and resources to continue their important work. The Proceeds of Crime and Related Matters Bill is making its way through the Oireachtas currently. Once passed into law, the Criminal Assets Bureau will have stronger investigative powers and will be able to dispose of assets much more quickly than is currently the case. Figures relating to asset recovery under the Proceeds of Crime Acts by CAB are available publicly in Chapters 3 and 4 of the annual reports published on the Bureau's website: www.cab.ie/annual-reports/ . The Criminal Assets Bureau have advised that they do not collate statistics by County. Statistics for 2026 are not yet available and can not be provided at this point in time. The disbursement of monies collected by the Criminal Assets Bureau is controlled by the Central Exchequer. However, the Deputy may be interested to note that the Community Safety Fund re-directs a portion of the proceeds of crime, seized by the Criminal Assets Bureau (CAB) and An Garda Síochána, back into communities in order to fund innovative local projects aimed at building stronger, safer communities. In 2025, €4.4 million was allocated through the Community Safety Fund to 42 community safety projects nationwide. This represented a 33% increase on the €3 million awarded to 33 community safety projects in 2024. I secured a further increase in funding to €4.75 million for 2026, which is reflective of the continued success of An Garda Síochána and CAB. The Fund has supported 127 community safety projects to date all across Ireland. Putting this money back into the community is a tangible way of showing that there can be a direct link between the activities of law enforcement and building stronger, safer communities. The below table provides a breakdown of the number of projects funded by the Community Safety Fund since it launched in 2022. Year Number of Funded Projects 2022 22 2023 30 2024 33 2025 42 Total 127 In 2025, the Community Safety Fund was transferred to the newly established National Office for Community Safety. The National Office for Community Safety, an office of my Department, is a central coordinating body to the new whole of government, collaborative, problem-solving approach to community safety. The final elements of this new community safety infrastructure are being established including: • The establishment of all 36 Safety Partnerships. • The publishing of the National Strategy for Improving Community Safety The National Office is currently conducting a review of the current operating model and criteria for the Community Safety Fund to ensure that projects funded in the future are consistent with the National Strategy for Community Safety and support the work of Local Community Safety Partnerships.

question: 2174. Deputy Noel McCarthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the status of a visa application (details supplied) given the urgent need to provide family assistance in Ireland; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [55178/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I can advise the Deputy that the Visit visa application referred to was created on 21 June 2026. Supporting documentation was received in the Dublin Visa Office on 17 July 2026 where it awaits examination and processing. Requests to expedite an application or for an emergency visa can be made through my Department's Customer Service Portal, which can be accessed at the following link: portal.irishimmigration.ie/en Expediting a visa application is usually confined to time-sensitive instances, such as, if a family member has been hospitalised, in a life-threatening situation, or in the unfortunate event of a bereavement. Each request is considered on its merits; the person concerned should also engage with the relevant Embassy of Ireland, explaining the nature of the emergency and provide any documentary evidence that may be available to them. A full list of Irish embassies is available at the following link: ireland.ie/en/dfa/embassies/ Emergency visa applications and requests will be dealt with on a case-by-case basis but will, wherever possible, be processed speedily and sympathetically. In order to be fair to all those who have applied, not all requests to expedite an application can be granted. The current processing times for Dublin visa decisions is available here: irishimmigration.ie/visa-decisions/ This webpage is updated weekly. Please note, the processing date published on the above page is the oldest date of application currently being processed under a given category. However, it should be noted that the Visa team continue to process and make decisions on applications received after the published processing date. If a particular application takes longer to consider this may prevent the published processing date from advancing. Applicants are advised not to pay for airline or other travel tickets without having first been issued with a visa. The person will be notified as soon as a decision has been reached by a Visa Officer. The person concerned can now directly check the status of their visa application on the Immigration Service’s Customer Service Portal. They can register for, or log in to their existing account, at: portal.irishimmigration.ie/en. As an Oireachtas member, you can also request the status of individual immigration cases by e-mail, using the Oireachtas Mail facility at: IMoireachtasmail@justice.ie, which has been specifically established for this purpose. This service enables up to date information on such cases to be obtained without the need to seek information by way of the Parliamentary Question process.

question: 2175. Deputy Ciarán Ahern asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of sentences made under Section 8 of the Criminal Justice (Hate Offences Act) 2024 since its initiation; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [55183/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Criminal actions carried out based on prejudice against the inherent characteristics or identity of a person are abhorrent to the basic values of our Republic. The introduction of the Criminal Justice Hate Offences Act 2024 strengthens the law by ensuring that perpetrators face tougher penalties where hatred is proven to be a motivating factor, or where hatred is demonstrated based on the identity of the victim. The management of the courts, operational matters and logistical functions are the responsibility of the judiciary and Courts Service, which are independent in exercising their functions under the Courts Service Act 1998 and the Constitution. The Courts Service has a dedicated email address for the provision of information to members of the Houses of the Oireachtas at: oireachtasenquiries@courts.ie. To be of assistance to the Deputy, I have sought information from the Courts Service. I am informed by the Courts Service that Section 8 of the Criminal Justice (Hate Offences) Act 2024 provides that a Court shall, without prejudice to any other enactment or rule of law and subject to subsections (2) and (3), treat as an aggravating factor hatred against a person or a group of persons on account of their protected characteristics or any of those characteristics on the part of a person in the commission of an offence to which the section applies for the purposes of determining the sentence to be imposed on the person for that offence. I’m further informed that while the judge must have regard to this in sentencing, it is not possible to provide data on instances when this has been considered or what characteristics /protected characteristics of the person/group of persons concerned were relevant to the offence.

question: 2176. Deputy Ciarán Ahern asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the status of each action in the National Action Plan Against Racism 2023-2027, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [55184/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration As the Deputy is aware, Ireland’s National Action Plan Against Racism (NAPAR) 2023 – 2027 represents a national level, State-led, coordinated approach to eliminating racism in all its forms in Ireland. This includes antisemitism, Islamophobia, racism that impacts the Traveller and Roma people and communities, and racism affecting people of African Descent. Ireland is taking a broad approach to this issue, by considering all facets of racism. The NAPAR is being implemented over the five-year period 2023-2027 and it will have a significant positive impact on all minority ethnic communities and faith-based groups in Ireland. Monitoring the progress of the NAPAR is multifaceted. The NAPAR undergoes independent monitoring in the form of the Special Rapporteur for Racial Equality and Racism’s annual report. The Special Rapporteur’s first annual report was published in February 2026. My Department publishes an annual NAPAR Implementation Report which provides significant updates from Government Departments and Agencies on the progress of the NAPAR actions. Publication of the 2025 NAPAR Implementation Report to the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration website is expected in the coming weeks and will include updates on the implementation status of NAPAR actions.

question: 2177. Deputy Ciarán Ahern asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for an update on the Migration and Integration Strategy; when it will be published; to provide a list of stakeholders he has engaged with to-date; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [55185/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Programme for Government contains a commitment to publish a National Migration and Integration Strategy detailing how Government intends to meet the demands and the opportunities facing Ireland’s society and economy over the next decade. My Department is currently working collaboratively with a wide range of other Government departments to develop this strategy with the aim to publish Ireland’s first overarching whole-of-government National Migration and Integration Strategy later this year. The scope of the Strategy will include issues such as labour market needs, legal pathways, international education and planning for public service provision including housing, amongst other issues relating to migration. To that end, a Strategic Migration Policy Group (SMPG) was established in December 2024 to support that work which now consists of ten Government Departments meeting at senior official level. The ten Departments represented on the SMPG are: • Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration (Chair) • Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment • Department of Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science • Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage • Department of Finance • Department of Social Protection • Department of an Taoiseach • Department of Health • Department of Education and Youth • Department of Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht Each Department is in a position to convey the perspectives of the agencies under their remit which have also provided inputs to the Group as required. The SMPG and its working group has now met on 14 occasions for detailed discussions on different aspects of the Strategy. The key objective of the Strategy and the SMPG is to develop a whole-of-government approach to migration policy that is coherent across Departments and responsive in seeking to address Ireland’s current and future demographic, economic and social policy needs. With specific regard to integration, work previously undertaken, including a detailed consultation process with stakeholders, will be taken into account in the development of this strategy. The first phase of consultation consisted of a public survey, stakeholder submissions, and stakeholder workshops to gather insights into the needs, challenges, and opportunities for supporting migrant integration. Over 7,000 submissions were received to the public survey on migrant integration, while 82 stakeholders provided written submissions, and two stakeholder workshops were held. There was a second phase of consultation in 2024 which consisted of 11 focus groups with migrants and Irish citizens with a migrant background, and 74 people participated. The second phase targeted migrant communities who were underrepresented in phase one and participants were recruited through migrant organisations. In addition to this, focus groups were held with the Local Authority Integration Teams. My Department is also continuing the work of the Community Engagement team during 2026, including engagement meetings that are being convened in each Local Authority area. These meetings are being convened in partnership with each Local Authority, and participants are a mix of statutory service providers and community and voluntary sector representatives. The feedback received through community engagement meetings is supporting my Department's work to complete the Migration and Integration Strategy.

question: 2179. Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the further measures planned to support families experiencing drug-related intimidation; and whether additional resources will be provided to expand community-based interventions. [55330/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration There are a number of actions being taken to support families experiencing drug related intimidation. An Garda Síochána is committed to continuing to build and maintain relationships with communities, agencies and groups in the fight against drug related intimidation and violence within all communities. An Garda Síochána continues to maintain the Drugs Related Intimidation Reporting Programme by assigning nominated Inspectors in each Division throughout the country to assist those who are victims of intimidation. An Garda Síochána in dealing with any complaint of drug related intimidation or advice sought in relation to this issue, will do so by the safest and most effective means in order to afford the person or family subject to the threat of the best level of security, advice and support which can be offered. In 2025, alongside my colleague Minister Murnane O’Connor, I launched the DRIVE (Drug related intimidation & violence engagement) project. DRIVE is an interagency project which outlines systems and structures to respond to drug-related intimidation and associated violence. It focuses on responding to incidents, supporting those affected, and preventing future occurrences. DRIVE promotes interagency collaboration by bringing together law enforcement, health services, social services, and community organisations to tackle Drug Related Intimidation from multiple perspectives. It operates on a national scale across Ireland, ensuring consistent and comprehensive support in all regions. There are over 400 publicly funded drug services, including family support services, across the country which can advise and support people affected by Drug Related Intimidation. Family support services are critical because drug-related violence nearly always becomes an issue for the whole family. There is a comprehensive national network of family support services to which people can turn.

question: 2180. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if the international protection appeal status of a person of interest in an ongoing homicide investigation has any bearing on that person's immigration status or re-entry rights to the State should they return; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [55416/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration It is a central priority for me as Minister that our immigration laws are robust and enforced. As the matter referred to is the subject of an ongoing criminal investigation by An Garda Síochána, I cannot comment on the details of the specific case. More generally, each application for international protection is examined in detail on its individual merits, taking all factors into account. When processing international protection applications, criminal convictions are always considered. Character and conduct checks are also carried out before applicants can be granted any permission to remain in the State. An Garda Síochána notifies my Department of matters which may be relevant to its considerations. If an applicant is not granted protection, they no longer have a right to remain in the State and are not allowed to so remain. The removal of people who are involved in criminality and those who are a danger to society is a priority for me as Minister and my Department works closely with An Garda Síochána and the Irish Prison Service to ensure high risk persons are prioritised for removal from Ireland.

question: 2181. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of gardaí currently trained and authorised to pursue scramblers and e-scooters following risk assessment, broken down by Garda division; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [55448/26]

question: 2182. Deputy David Cullinane asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will report on the evaluation carried out on the recommendations of the report of the Joint Committee on Assisted Dying which are relevant to his Department, in tabular form; the status of consideration, intention, or implementation for each recommendation; if research has been undertaken on international systems to evaluate a potential framework for the State; his view on the introduction of assisted dying in the State; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [55479/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The issue of assisted dying is very complex, requiring careful consideration of medical, ethical and cultural issues. It also gives rise to challenging issues in the areas of criminal justice and constitutional law. The Joint Committee on Assisted Dying was established in January 2023 to consider and make recommendations for legislative and policy change in relation to assisted dying. The Committee published its Final Report on 20 March 2024. The Committee’s report recommends that the Government introduce legislation to allow for assisted dying in certain restricted circumstances. On 23 October 2024, the Dáil voted by 76 to 53 to note the Committee’s Report. It is a matter for Government, on foot of the Dáil vote, to determine how to progress this issue, including with regard to which Department will take a lead role in relation to it. No decision has been taken, as of yet, as regards any proposed legislative, or other actions, to be taken.

question: 2183. Deputy Ann Graves asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the estimated cost in 2027 if the number of horses in the Garda mounted unit were doubled. [55484/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under Section 33 of the Policing Security and Community Safety Act 2024. This includes responsibility for the allocation and deployment of resources available to him, such as the Mounted Unit. The Garda Mounted Unit is based at Áras an Uachtárain, Phoenix Park, Dublin 8 and has a national remit. I am informed that there are currently twelve horses attached to the Garda Mounted Unit. The cost of purchasing a horse is approximately €16,000. Therefore, the estimated cost to purchase an additional twelve horses for the Garda Mounted Unit would cost approximately €192,000. It should also be noted however that the cost of providing additional facilities as well as the cost additional Garda personnel and the associated operational requirements to support such an expansion would be significant.

question: 2186. Deputy Cormac Devlin asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if his attention has been drawn to the case of a person (details supplied); if he can assist in this case; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [55514/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I can advise the Deputy that the Preclearance - Join Family application referred to was created on 7 March 2026. I can assure you that this does not indicate the processing of these applications has halted overall. The person concerned can now directly check the status of their visa application on the Immigration Service’s Customer Service Portal. They can register for, or log in to their existing account, at: www.portal.irishimmigration.ie. question: 2187. Deputy Cormac Devlin asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if his attention has been drawn to the case of a person (details supplied); if he can assist in this case; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [55515/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The person referred to by the Deputy applied to renew their immigration permission on 29 April 2026 and this application is currently in the queue for consideration. The Registration Office within Immigration Service Delivery (ISD) of my Department provide a live application processing date broken down by stamp category, which is updated every Monday, and is available at the following link: Renewing your registration permission if you live in the Republic of Ireland - Immigration Service Delivery[ ] (www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/how-to-renew-your-current-permission/renewing-your-registration-permission-if-you-live-in-the-republic-of-ireland/0). I understand that the extended wait times can be frustrating for applicants, and I can assure the Deputy that my Department is utilising every avenue available to facilitate as many applicants as quickly as possible and to increase processing capacity. The Registration Office is open seven days a week to facilitate customers to process both first time registration appointments and online renewals, with significant additional staff assigned to this work. This is having an impact and wait times are reducing, and I expect times to reduce further over the summer months. In the meantime, I can advise the Deputy that I recently published an updated interim employer notice and a notice to facilitate customers travelling during the summer months to alleviate pressure on applicants while the Department continues to reduce the wait times. Where an employee’s Irish Residence Permit (IRP) card has expired and they are unable to obtain a new one by the expiry date of their current IRP card, they are still permitted to work and to remain in the State until 31 August 2026. This applies to all expired IRP cards regardless of the number of weeks elapsed, but is subject to the applicant submitting their renewal application prior to their current IRP card expiring. Further information on this notice can be found at the following link (www.irishimmigration.ie/minster-announces-interim-notice-to-employers-regarding-renewal-of-registration/). It is important to note that the existing Notice to Employers (www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/how-to-renew-your-current-permission/notice-to-employers/) will continue to apply after 31 August 2026. Furthermore, the previous travel arrangements made for people awaiting a renewal of their IRP card who intend to travel has been reinstated until 31 August 2026. People may use their recently expired IRP card to travel until the end of August 2026, provided an application to renew their registration permission was submitted in advance of the expiry date of their IRP Card. Further information can be found on the ISD website at the following link (www.irishimmigration.ie/isd-announces-initiative-to-facilitate-customers-travelling-during-the-summer-months/). The naturalisation application referred to by the Deputy continues to be processed by my Department. Citizenship Division is doing everything possible to progress applications as quickly as possible. It is important to note, however, that no two naturalisation applications are the same and some take longer than others to process. Given the importance of citizenship, robust and comprehensive checks must take place on each application. Unfortunately, some checks, such as international checks, can take a considerable amount of time and these are largely outside of the control of the Immigration Service. Applicants can now directly check the status of their immigration application on the Immigration Service’s Customer Service Portal. They can register for, or log in to their existing account, at www.portal.irishimmigration.ie/en/ . As an Oireachtas member, you can also request the status of individual immigration cases by e-mail, using the Oireachtas Mail facility at: IMoireachtasmail@justice.ie, which has been specifically established for this purpose. This service enables up to date information on such cases to be obtained without the need to seek information by way of the Parliamentary Question process.

question: 2192. Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration further to Parliamentary Question No. 588 of 14 July 2026, the changes made to District Court criminal legal aid fees in each year since 2015, outlining further for each year what the changes due to the reversal of FEMPI cuts were through fee restoration; the date on which each of those changes came into effect, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [55633/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Under the Criminal Justice (Legal Aid) Act 1962, it is the Courts, through the judiciary, that are responsible for the granting of legal aid. The Criminal Legal Aid Scheme is demand-led and it is for the courts to decide in any given case if legal aid is to be granted, therefore it is not possible to accurately predict the cost of the Scheme in any given year. However, I can advise that the total criminal legal aid expenditure for 2025 was €120.6 million including appearance fees and other fees and expenses. As the Deputy will be aware, the then Minister introduced a 10% increase in fees on 1 January 2024. A further increase of 8% was applied to fees on 1 January 2025. Since then I have introduced a final 8% increase in criminal legal aid fees payable to solicitors and barristers in the Circuit Court and higher courts from 1 July 2026. This represents a full restoration of the so-called FEMPI cuts in line with the Programme for Government commitment. I also introduced a flat fee of €520 for District Court criminal cases under the criminal legal aid scheme. This figure represents the current fee paid for five appearances in the District Court plus an 8% increase. The information is not recorded in such a way to provide the Deputy with the increase in expenditure in the District Court due to fee changes including those resulting from the reversal of so-called FEMPI cuts since 2015.

question: 2194. Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the estimated cost in 2027 if the budget for Criminal Assets Bureau increased by 15%. [55679/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2170, 2171, 2194, 2283 and 2301 together. CAB is a multi-agency statutory body established under the Criminal Assets Bureau Act, 1996. I am advised that all monies seized by CAB are remitted to the Central Fund of the Exchequer after the appropriate statutory time frame under the Proceeds of Crime Acts. I was pleased to secure an 8.2% increase on the Criminal Assets Bureau budget allocation for 2026. The Bureau’s budget allocation in 2026 is €13.8m, of which €11.25m is for Pay and €2.55m is for Non-Pay. A 15% uplift on the Criminal Assets Bureau’s total budget would equate to €2.07m additional in funding. This would provide a total budget in 2027 totalling €15.15m. I am committed to ensuring that the Criminal Assets Bureau have the powers and resources to continue their important work. The Proceeds of Crime and Related Matters Bill is making its way through the Oireachtas currently. Once passed into law, the Criminal Assets Bureau will have stronger investigative powers and will be able to dispose of assets much more quickly than is currently the case. Figures relating to asset recovery under the Proceeds of Crime Acts by CAB are available publicly in Chapters 3 and 4 of the annual reports published on the Bureau's website: www.cab.ie/annual-reports/ . The Criminal Assets Bureau have advised that they do not collate statistics by County. Statistics for 2026 are not yet available and can not be provided at this point in time. The disbursement of monies collected by the Criminal Assets Bureau is controlled by the Central Exchequer. However, the Deputy may be interested to note that the Community Safety Fund re-directs a portion of the proceeds of crime, seized by the Criminal Assets Bureau (CAB) and An Garda Síochána, back into communities in order to fund innovative local projects aimed at building stronger, safer communities. In 2025, €4.4 million was allocated through the Community Safety Fund to 42 community safety projects nationwide. This represented a 33% increase on the €3 million awarded to 33 community safety projects in 2024. I secured a further increase in funding to €4.75 million for 2026, which is reflective of the continued success of An Garda Síochána and CAB. The Fund has supported 127 community safety projects to date all across Ireland. Putting this money back into the community is a tangible way of showing that there can be a direct link between the activities of law enforcement and building stronger, safer communities. The below table provides a breakdown of the number of projects funded by the Community Safety Fund since it launched in 2022. Year Number of Funded Projects 2022 22 2023 30 2024 33 2025 42 Total 127 In 2025, the Community Safety Fund was transferred to the newly established National Office for Community Safety. The National Office for Community Safety, an office of my Department, is a central coordinating body to the new whole of government, collaborative, problem-solving approach to community safety. The final elements of this new community safety infrastructure are being established including: • The establishment of all 36 Safety Partnerships. • The publishing of the National Strategy for Improving Community Safety The National Office is currently conducting a review of the current operating model and criteria for the Community Safety Fund to ensure that projects funded in the future are consistent with the National Strategy for Community Safety and support the work of Local Community Safety Partnerships.

question: 2196. Deputy Máire Devine asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the steps being taken by his Department to address ongoing serious delays in the processing and issuance of Irish Residence Permit (IRP) cards for beneficiaries of temporary protection; the number of individuals currently awaiting the issue or renewal of an IRP card; the average processing time for the issue of an IRP card following registration or renewal; the advice available to individuals who applied for temporary protection registration or renewal, including those who applied as far back as February 2025, but who have yet to receive either an IRP card or confirmation that their application is being processed; the procedures available to individuals who have received confirmation that their temporary protection registration has been approved and have received a temporary protection certificate but have not yet received their IRP card; whether his Department provides confirmation that an IRP card application is being processed; whether consideration has been given to introducing an expedited process for the issuance of IRP cards in urgent cases relating to employment, education, medical treatment or essential travel; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [55749/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2196, 2197 and 2198 together. The Registration Office of my Department continues to experience an exceptionally high demand for first time registration appointments and immigration permission renewal applications. I understand that the extended wait times can be frustrating for applicants, and I can assure the Deputy that my Department is utilising every avenue available to facilitate as many applicants as quickly as possible and to increase processing capacity. The Registration Office is open seven days a week to facilitate customers to process both first time registration appointments and online renewals, with significant additional staff assigned to this work. This is having an impact and wait times are reducing, and I expect times to reduce further over the summer months. In the meantime, I can advise the Deputy that I recently published an updated interim employer notice and a notice to facilitate customers travelling during the summer months to alleviate pressure on applicants while the Department continues to reduce the wait times. Where an employee’s Irish Residence Permit (IRP) card has expired and they are unable to obtain a new one by the expiry date of their current IRP card, they are still permitted to work and to remain in the State until 31 August 2026. This applies to all expired IRP cards regardless of the number of weeks elapsed, but is subject to the applicant submitting their renewal application prior to their current IRP card expiring. Further information on this notice can be found at the following link (www.irishimmigration.ie/minster-announces-interim-notice-to-employers-regarding-renewal-of-registration/). It is important to note that the existing Notice to Employers (www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/how-to-renew-your-current-permission/notice-to-employers/) will continue to apply after 31 August 2026. Furthermore, the previous travel arrangements made for people awaiting a renewal of their IRP card who intend to travel has been reinstated until 31 August 2026. People may use their recently expired IRP card to travel until the end of August 2026, provided an application to renew their registration permission was submitted in advance of the expiry date of their IRP Card. Further information can be found on the ISD website at the following link (www.irishimmigration.ie/isd-announces-initiative-to-facilitate-customers-travelling-during-the-summer-months/). Information in this regard has been issued to airlines. The Registration Office provide a live application processing date broken down by stamp category, which is updated every Monday, and is available at the following link: Renewing your registration permission if you live in the Republic of Ireland - Immigration Service Delivery (/www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/how-to-renew-your-current-permission/renewing-your-registration-permission-if-you-live-in-the-republic-of-ireland/) Applicants can check the status of their immigration application on the Portal, which can be accessed at the following link: www.portal.irishimmigration.ie/en/ It is also open to any person to request to have their renewal application expedited due to extenuating circumstances, and they can do so by contacting the Registration team of the Department via the Customer Service Portal. They will need to explain their circumstances and the urgent need to travel. All such requests are considered on a case by case basis. Details on how to submit a query to the registration office can be found here: www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/submitting-registration-or-renewal-queries/ Once an individual reaches 16 years of age and are in possession of a valid temporary protection certificate, they can book a first time registration appointment with my Department and register their immigration permission in the normal manner. Further information is available at the following link: www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/how-to-register-your-immigration-permission-for-the-first-time/information-on-registering-your-immigration-permission-for-the-first-time/ All temporary protection certificates valid up to 4 March 2026 are now valid until 4 March 2027 and as such can be used when applying for an IRP card. It should be noted that the Temporary Protection certificate is the permission to be in the State and grants Beneficiaries of Temporary Protection access to all services and also the right to work. Information on the number of reported cases in which Beneficiaries of Temporary Protection have been unable to commence employment, renew employment contracts or access education is not recorded by my Department.

question: 2197. Deputy Máire Devine asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the measures being taken to ensure that delays in the issuance of Irish Residence Permit (IRP) cards do not prevent beneficiaries of temporary protection from accessing employment and education; whether his Department provides employers with official confirmation that holders of a valid temporary protection certificate have the legal right to work in the State while awaiting the issuance or renewal of an IRP card; if not, whether he plans to introduce such a mechanism; the number of reported cases in which beneficiaries of temporary protection have been unable to commence employment, renew employment contracts or access education due to delays in receiving an IRP card; the procedures in place for young persons who reach the age of 16 years and are required to register through the online portal and attend Citywest to obtain an IRP cards; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [55750/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2196, 2197 and 2198 together. question: 2199. Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to open a dedicated immigrant investor programme in respect of schools, healthcare facilities and sport, with rules and regulations in place; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [55789/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Immigrant Investor Programme (IIP) was established over a decade ago during a time of unprecedented economic difficulty to stimulate investment in Ireland that would be of strategic and public benefit to the State. Since its inception, the Programme has brought significant investment to Ireland and has been operated by the Department to the highest professional standards. However, it is important that we keep all programmes under review and having taking into account both internal and external reviews including implications for wider public policy, such as the continuing appropriateness and suitability of this programme for cultural, social and economic use, the Government agreed to close the IIP to further applications from 15 February 2023.
