question: 2200. Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the steps he is taking to address delays in the processing of short-stay (C) tourist visa applications for individuals seeking to visit family members resident in Ireland, particularly in cases where visas have previously been granted for visits; the current average processing time for such applications, by country where available; the reasons for the delays being experienced in recent months; the measures he plans to implement to reduce waiting times and ensure that families are able to reunite for short visits in a timely manner; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [55863/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I can assure the Deputy that while processing times can vary across the different Visa Offices and Irish Embassies, the majority of visas are processed within stated target times. The average processing time for a Type C short stay visa processed in 2025 was 37 days. My Department’s website recommends that a visa application is submitted three months before an applicant intends to travel. A person may submit an application prior to this three month recommendation, however, they are advised to make sure that supporting documentation is as up to date as possible. Applicants may use my Department's Customer Service Portal to upload updated documents after the initial application has been submitted. The Customer Service Portal can be accessed at the following link: www.portal.irishimmigration.ie/en/ In 2025, approximately 206,000 visa applications, of all types, were received by the Visa Division of my Department. This reflects an increase of 2% compared to 2024, with over 3,900 additional applications received. This follows a 21% increase in applications in 2024 compared to 2023. In the first six months of 2026, my Department's Visa Division received approximately 102,000 visa applications and has issued approximately 85,200 decisions. Processing times for all applications are influenced by a number of factors. The time it can take varies depending on the type and complexity of application; individual circumstances; peak application periods; such as holidays or the start of the school year; and, crucially, the quality and completeness of the application lodged. Verifying an application is an important part of our immigration system and the checks involved can take time to complete. Processing times and decisions at the Dublin Visa Office and the Overseas Visa Offices can be checked at the following link: www.irishimmigration.ie/visa-decisions/ In December 2025, the Immigration Service of my Department introduced online payment functionality to my Department's online visa system. This allows applicants to pay visa fees as part of the online application process. The initiative is being rolled out on a phased basis and is currently live in 40 countries, with South Africa added in January 2026. This reduces the administrative burden on Irish Missions and visa teams, and allows visa officers to dedicate more time to core application processing and decision-making, contributing to improved processing efficiency over time.

question: 2201. Deputy Aindrias Moynihan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number and proportion of staff who have completed AI-related training programmes since January 2024; the levels of training, introductory or advanced use; to confirm the associated expenditure on each level of training provided, by his Department and public body; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [55878/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration My Department complies with the Guidelines for the Responsible Use of AI in the Public Service issued by the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation, as well as guidance from the National Cyber Security Centre. My Department continues to review its training, risk assessment and oversight arrangements to support the responsible use of AI technologies and work tools. To assist in achieving its strategic objectives, my Department is fully committed to enhancing the capacity and capability of staff and provides access to a comprehensive programme of learning and development resources to meet the needs of both staff and the organisation. My Department provides a central learning and development offering via the Civil Service’s OneLearning platform. OneLearning provides staff with access to core skills and capability development across the Civil Service. This includes self-paced and virtual learning programmes that support the responsible and effective use of artificial intelligence. There are two Civil Service-specific eLearning programmes on AI, available on OneLearning. These are ‘AI in the Public Service’, which is included as part of compliance training for all staff, and ‘Navigating the Guidelines for the Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Public Service’ which staff in my Department are encouraged to complete. Staff may also, in consultation with their line manager and where appropriate to their role and organisational need, undertake external AI-related training and development. Specialist units, including the National Cyber Security Centre, have access to additional and specific subject matter training and expertise. The information requested by the Deputy is presented in the attached appendix. Please refer to the first tab for a full list of relevant training undertaken by staff in my Department and the agencies for which my Department provides HR services. The second tab lists staff in the other agencies under my Department's remit which I am informed have received relevant training in the past year. It may also be relevant to note that, as part of a series of events for Senior Leaders (at Principal Officer/ Director/Assistant Secretary level) a session was provided in July 2025 which had a focus on Artificial Intelligence (AI). This session involved presentations from the Department’s Change Technology and Information (CTI) Function as well as guest speakers including the National Cyber Security Centre. 62 senior staff attended the session. My Department will continue to assess emerging digital tools, including AI, but any future adoption will remain subject to appropriate governance processes, including risk assessment and human oversight. question: 2205. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if his Department has reviewed, or plans to review, the operation of section 26 of the International Protection Act 2015 insofar as it affects the reporting of ongoing criminal proceedings; if his Department has received correspondence from media organisations, the Courts Service or other parties regarding the practical application of the section; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [56027/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration It is a central priority of this Government that our immigration laws are robust and enforced. Since taking office, I have worked to ensure integrity, efficiency and public confidence in our migration system. Nothing in the International Protection legislation prevents An Garda Síochána communicating information in the course of an investigation, including personal details of a person where necessary, so long as they have due regard to the requirement not to publish information likely to lead members of the public to identify that person as an international protection applicant without the consent of that person. The confidentiality principle is a principle of asylum law which is reflected both in the Asylum Procedures Regulation and in our domestic law, the International Protection Act 2015, which applies to asylum applications made before 12th June 2026, and the International Protection Act 2026, which applies to applications made after that date. An asylum-seeker’s claim inherently supposes a fear of persecution by the authorities of their home country and therefore may also mean that their family or friends still living in the country from which they have sought protection, can be jeopardised if their personal information is not confidential. Therefore my officials and I are legally obliged to ensure that the identity of any person who applied for international protection is kept confidential. For applicants whose applications were made prior to 12th June 2026, section 26(1) of the 2015 Act sets out that: “the Minister and the Tribunal and their respective officers shall take all practicable steps to ensure that the identity of applicants is kept confidential”. As regards applications made after 12th June 2026, Article 7 of the Asylum Procedures Regulation states that “1. The authorities applying this Regulation shall be bound by the principle of confidentiality in relation to any personal information they acquire in the performance of their duties, including any exchange of information in accordance with Union or national law which is relevant for the application of this Regulation between authorities of the Member States. 2. Throughout the procedure for international protection and after a final decision on the application has been taken, the authorities shall not: (a) disclose information regarding the individual application for international protection or the fact that an application has been made, to the alleged actors of persecution or serious harm; (b) obtain any information from the alleged actors of persecution or serious harm in a manner that would result in such actors being informed of the fact that an application has been made by the applicant in question.” In line with this, section 278(1) of the International Protection Act 2026 (in similar terms to section 26 of the 2015 Act) provides that: “A person shall not publish or broadcast, or cause to be published or broadcast, information likely to lead members of the public to identify that a person is an applicant without the consent of that person”. A person who contravenes this section themselves commits an offence. The confidentiality requirements contained in both Acts apply to all international applicants including those charged or convicted of criminal offences. This does not mean that cases cannot be covered by the media, but rather that it must be covered in a manner that does not lead to the person being identified as an applicant for international protection. An applicant can themselves consent to being so identified.

question: 2209. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of District Court cases adjourned since 1 July 2026 arising from the withdrawal of solicitors from the Criminal Legal Aid panel; the number of persons who appeared before the courts without legal representation in that period; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [56143/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2209 and 2238 together. Under the Criminal Justice (Legal Aid) Act 1962, it is the Courts, through the judiciary, that are responsible for the granting of legal aid. The Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration has no involvement in the granting of free legal aid or the assignment of solicitors. These matters are handled entirely by the courts. Management of the courts, operational matters such as allocation of court business, the scheduling of cases and logistical functions are the responsibility of the judiciary and Courts Service, which are independent in exercising their functions under the Courts Service Act 1998 and given the separation of powers in the Constitution. The Courts Service has a dedicated email address for the provision of information to members of the Houses of the Oireachtas, at oireachtasenquiries@courts.ie. Due to a number of applications under Article 40.4 of the Constitution and the recent High Court challenge, the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration does not comment on matters before the Courts. The changes to the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme in the District Court that came into effect on Wednesday 1 July are designed to make the system more efficient and effective. For cases in the District Court, regardless of the number of appearances, a set fee is payable to solicitors, replacing the previous appearance-based sliding scale. The new structure also provides for a full separate set fee for each defendant in court on a given day. In considering the need for reform, it is important to note that, while criminal case volumes in the District Court have decreased, expenditure on criminal legal aid in the District Court has nearly doubled, from €19 million in 2015 to €37 million in 2024. My Department reviewed more than 350,000 District Court cases which took place during 2022 and 2023. The reforms aim to address structural issues identified during this review, such as unnecessary adjournments resulting from the payment per appearance model. The Department continues to keep the operation of the new criminal legal aid arrangements in the District Court under review following their introduction, including monitoring claims for fees, entries to and exits from the panel of solicitors and overall operations within the courts.

As you will recall, I sought the information from the Garda authorities and undertook to contact you again once the information was to hand. The tables below have been provided to me by the Garda authorities and outlines the number of Cars and Vans allocated and removed from the Dog unit in 2024, 2025, and to date in 2026. Dog Unit Vehicle Allocations - Marked Cars Unmarked Cars Marked Vans Unmarked Vans 2024 0 0 0 1 2025 0 1 0 0 2026 0 0 0 0 Dog Unit Vehicle Removals - Marked Cars Unmarked Cars Marked Vans Unmarked Vans 2024 0 0 1 0 2025 0 0 1 1 2026 0 0 0 0 The purchase and allocation of vehicles by An Garda Síochána is made on the basis of identified operational demands, the availability of resources and is reviewed on a continual basis.

question: 2218. Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of people who have applied for the ex gratia Stardust recognition payment scheme; the number of successful applicants who have not yet received payment; the reasons for any delays in issuing payments; and the expected timeframe for all outstanding payments to be completed. [56301/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration On 16 February, I announced the details of the Stardust Recognition Payment Scheme. The scheme is available to all survivor beneficiaries of the original Stardust Victims Compensation Tribunal established in 1985. The Stardust Recognition Scheme can be accessed online at www.stardustrecognitionpayment.ie and applications can be made online or by post. A Stardust Recognition Payment Helpline has also been set up that is available during office hours, for those who wish to request an application form to be sent to their home address. Since the Stardust Recognition Payment Scheme opened in February, over 500 applications have been made. Completed applications are reviewed by the Stardust Recognition Payment Unit for completeness. In making an application, applicants consent to providing any relevant information requested by the Stardust Recognition Payment Unit that is required to validate their application. Once all criteria are met, the applicant is then contacted to finalise arrangements and information for payment. Progress is continuing in the processing of applications. As of 22 July 2026, 94 applications have been authorised for payment. Payments to these applicants have been made to their designated bank account. Further applications are proceeding towards final validation, and I expect the number of payments to increase further in the coming weeks. As the scheme remains open for applications up until 5pm 17 August 2026, it is not possible at this time to provide a definitive timeline for final payments to be made.

question: 2219. Deputy Holly Cairns asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to confirm the correct immigration pathway for a Ukrainian temporary protection beneficiary moving to a Stamp 1G as the spouse of a critical skills employment permit holder. [56308/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration In the situation referred to by the Deputy, such people can submit an online renewal application and select the ‘Stamp 1G’ stamp type, then the ‘Spouse of Employment Permit holder’ category. Further information on the renewal process as well as the list of documents required for each stamp type are available on the ISD website at the following link: www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/how-to-register-your-immigration-permission-for-the-first-time/required-documents/.

question: 2220. Deputy Tom Brabazon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration further to Parliamentary Question No. 1376 of 9 June 2026, if his Department has since been provided with the relevant information. [56324/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I understand that in Parliamentary Question No. 1376 of 9 June 2026 you sought: “To ask the Minister for Justice; Home Affairs and Migration the number of stop and search incidents recorded for each of the years 2015 to 2025, and to date in 2026; the locations at which such stop and searches occurred; and the number of these stop and searches that resulted in successful prosecutions, in each years 2015 to 2025.; and if he will make a statement on the matter”. question: 2221. Deputy Micheál Carrigy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration his plans to open a physical domestic violence refuge house in County Longford; and if not, if this will be considered. [56325/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration This Government has taken unprecedented actions to confront the scourge of domestic, sexual, and gender-based violence (DSGBV). This includes increasing funding to almost €80 million under Budget 2026, to support Cuan and services working to tackle DSGBV and the implementation of the Zero Tolerance Strategy. The increased funding for Cuan and community organisations that support victims and survivors will accelerate the delivery of safe accommodation, while also providing stronger supports for victims. Cuan is collaborating with various stakeholders, including domestic violence services, Approved Housing Bodies, the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage, the Housing Agency and Local Authorities to facilitate local action and support service development and delivery of safe accommodation and ancillary services. Cuan provides funding to Longford Women’s Link for the provision of safe home and related support service provision. Longford has been identified as a priority area for Refuge Development. Cuan is engaging with all key stakeholders to progress refuge development in this area. Once complete, this domestic violence refuge will have 8 units available. Cuan is collaborating with Longford Women’s Link to expand the number of Safe Homes in County Longford, which currently has one unit, and is actively seeking potential properties for the purpose.

question: 2222. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of return orders issued by his Department that have not been actioned in each of the past five years within the legal timeframe. [56373/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2222, 2223 and 2224 together. I can advise the Deputy that Section 51A of the International Protection Act 2015 provides for the making of a return order where an international protection application has been determined as inadmissible. An international protection application may be determined as inadmissible where certain conditions are met in accordance with section 21 of the same Act. This situation will typically arise where the relevant applicant holds an international protection status in another EU Member State, where a country, other than an EU Member State, is a first country of asylum for the person, or where the person arrived from a State that is a safe third country. The UK has been designated as a safe third country for the purpose of the Act of 2015. I can also advise that before such an order can be made, I, as Minister, must be satisfied that the making of the order would not result in a breach of the prohibition of refoulement, as enshrined in section 50A of that Act. The Deputy should note that sections 50A and 51A are relatively new provisions on the Irish legislative landscape, having only come into effect on the first working day of 2021. During this time, there was a moratorium on returns and deportations in place during the Covid 19 pandemic. As a result, it was not until the second half of 2022 that the first return order was made under section 51A of the 2015 Act. Furthermore, in the period between March 2024 and March 2025, the ability to issue return orders in circumstances where a person arrived from a safe third country was affected by a High Court judgment [2024] IEHC 183 which identified shortcomings in the procedures set out in the Act of 2015. This has since been remedied by amendments brought forward in the Courts, Civil Law, Criminal Law and Superannuation (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2024, and the subsequent re-designation of the UK as a safe third country in March 2025. Arrangements for re-operationalising an agreement for reciprocal returns of international protection applicants between Ireland and the UK, on foot of the re-designation of the UK as a safe third country, are being put in place in consultation with the UK. People issued with return orders are required to remove themselves from the State. Many people comply with their return order and leave the country without informing my Department; as such it is not always possible to record these departures definitively and confirm that the return order was executed within the statutory timeframe. As there are no routine exit checks at Irish borders, it is not possible to provide the number of people who have or have not complied with an order. If a person issued with a return order does not leave the State independently then they are required to present to the GNIB in accordance with the conditions of their return order. There are many reasons returns may be prevented, including due to a person evading, due to legal challenges or due to complications with obtaining identification documentation for a returnee. The table below details the number of return orders issued and those that have not been actioned in each of the past five years within the legal timeframe from 2022 to 17 July 2026. Year Number of Return Order issued Number of return orders issued that have not been actioned within the legal timeframe 2022 <5 <5 2023 6 6 2024 42 40 2025 309 233 2026 (to 17 July) 112 0 * Please note, figures are correct at time of issue, however, all statistics may be subject to data cleansing. ** The Department does not release figures where there are less than 5, as there is a possibility that a person may be identifiable by releasing such information. Information on Return Order appeals costs are not compiled in such a way as to provide the specific data requested by the Deputy.

question: 2225. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of persons who presented at each airport and each seaport in the State with false, fraudulent or altered travel documents, or who were recorded as imposters, in each year from 2020 to 2025 and to 30 June 2026, broken down by port of entry, in tabular form; to confirm whether this category is recorded separately from persons presenting without documentation; whether these figures are collated nationally across all ports of entry or held separately by the Border Management Unit and An Garda Síochána; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [56450/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2266, 2225, 2226, 2267, 2268, 2269 and 2270 together. Implementing effective border security arrangements is a priority for me as Minister. The Programme for Government commits to developing a border security strategy to deliver stronger border security, ensuring technology supports border screening and to reviewing the potential of extending pre-clearance mechanisms, such as electronic travel authorisation, for travel from designated third countries. This work is underway. The Border Management Unit (BMU) of my Department is responsible for frontline Immigration at Dublin Airport only, as such the below figures reflect the position at Dublin Airport. Other airports and other ports of entry are the responsibility of An Garda Síochána. When any non-EEA national presents at a border, an Immigration Officer must determine whether that person should be granted leave to land and gain entry to the State. In performing their duties, an Officer is required to consider all of the circumstances of the individual at the time of entry in line with the provisions of the Immigration Act 2004. The establishment of a person’s identity and nationality is an important feature of our immigration process. Section 4(3) of the Immigration Act 2004 sets out the full range of grounds on which a person may be refused. People can be refused for more than one reason. These include, but are not limited to, persons arriving without correct documentation. When a person is refused leave to land at Dublin airport, the Immigration Officer will arrange for the person to be referred to the Garda National Immigration Bureau (GNIB) for removal from the State. The priority is to return them on the next available return flight to the last point of embarkation. The operational policy in this regard has not changed. Arrangements for the removal of those refused leave to land are operational matters for the GNIB. If a person indicates or is identified as being in need of international protection they are admitted to the international protection process. However, they will still be recorded as a refusal of leave to land. My Department and the GNIB are working closely with airlines on a range of measures to ensure that passengers have such documentation when boarding. This includes delivering in-person training to relevant airline ground-handling staff on immigration requirements and false travel documentation. BMU officials are available 24/7 to assist airlines with any immigration queries. An Garda Síochána has responsibility for issuing carrier liability notices and warnings, and for the imposition of carrier liability fines on carriers who permit a non-national to travel with their airline or ferry without the necessary documentation i.e. no documents, false document, no visa or improper use of genuine documents. The fines payable by carriers in such instances were increased by way of the Courts, Civil Law, Criminal Law and Superannuation (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2024. The effect of these changes is to increase the fines payable by carriers on summary conviction to a maximum of €5,000 from the previous maximum of €3,000. The Act also provides that carriers which make a payment of €2,500 within 28 days will avoid prosecution for an offence under the Act, which was an increase from the previous payment of €1,500; in practice many carriers avail of this option. The visa requirements to travel to Ireland have been strengthened and remain under review by my Department. BMU and GNIB have an ongoing intelligence-led programme of operations at airplanes to detect passengers who destroyed documents inflight and to identify the point of embarkation of undocumented passengers. To the end of June this year, the BMU have carried out 3,408 doorstop operations at Dublin Airport. The table below outlines the number of people refused leave to land and those who presented without a valid travel document at Dublin Airport from 2018 onwards, as the civilianisation process was completed that year. The figures for those who have claimed asylum at Dublin Airport have only been recorded since 2022. While systems do not allow for the extraction of the precise data requested with regard to the number of refusals who subsequently claimed asylum, it is the case that the majority of those who present without appropriate documentation and are refused leave to land seek to enter the international protection process. It is also the case that some people with valid travel documents seek to enter the international protection process, hence the number of applicants for asylum below include persons who presented with valid documents. I have written to the Garda Commissioner in relation to records in relation to other ports of entry and I will write to the Deputy directly should the information be available. Table 1. Dublin Airport immigration control Year Total Arriving Passengers Total Refusals Undocumented Arrivals False Documents + Imposters Claimed Asylum 2018 15,634,300 3,999 895 891 N/A 2019 16,318,300 6,151 1,579 1,849 N/A 2020 3,636,256 2,077 712 169 N/A 2021 4,118,027 3,210 2,082 279 N/A 2022 13,930,041 7,662 4,968 832 6,765 2023 16,628,545 5,826 3,287 872 4,712 2024 17,310,841 5,267 2,297 1080 4,320 2025 18,202,584 4,928 2,067 1034 3,993 2026 (to 30/06) 8,945,664 2130 894 465 1,669 * Please note, figures are correct at time of issue, however, all statistics may be subject to data cleansing

question: 2227. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of persons subject to a deportation order signed between 2020 and 2025 whose whereabouts are not known to his Department; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [56452/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2227, 2228, 2394 and 2404 together. It is a central priority for me that Ireland’s immigration system is robust and rules based. The enforcement aspects of our laws, including deportation orders, are an essential requirement for the system to work effectively and to ensure that there is confidence in the application of our legislation in this area. Deportations are costly and complex to enforce. It is the preferred option to return people voluntarily and my Department has a voluntary return programme to assist people to return prior to the issuance of a deportation order. A person can only avail of voluntary return before a deportation order is issued and I have increased resources into this programme to enable individuals who wish to return before a deportation order is issued to them. If a person does not remove themselves from the State following the issuance of a deportation order, they will be removed, and my Department has taken action to significantly improve immigration enforcement measures and increase removals. The number of deportation orders signed in 2024 (2,403) increased by 180% compared to 2023 (857). In 2025, 4,700 deportation orders were signed, an increase of 96% compared to 2024. 2,650 deportation orders have been signed up to 24 July 2026. In 2024, 1,122 people departed from the State under various mechanisms (i.e. enforced deportation, voluntary return etc.). In 2025, 2,111 people had their departure confirmed through these pathways, an increase of 88% compared to 2024. Up to 24 July 2026, 1,294 people have departed the State through these pathways. Tables 1 and 2 below detail the number of deportation orders signed, as well as the number enforced, from 2020 up to 24 July 2026. Table 1 Year 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 2026 (up to 24 July) Deportation orders signed 598 33 549 859 2,403 4,700 2,650 *Please note, figures are correct at time of issue, however, all statistics may be subject to data cleansing. Table 2: Deportation Enforcement 2020 to 24 July 2026 Year 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 2026 (up to 24 July) Enforced Deportations 42 5 24 51 134 185 148 Removed by Charter N/A N/A N/A N/A N/A 182 104 Otherwise Confirmed Deportation (1) 97 33 93 28 28 67 45 Total Deportations 139 38 117 79 162 434 297 Other Removals (2) 40 46 39 24 26 61 102 Number of Voluntary Returns 201 132 91 215 934 1,616 895 Total Removed 380 216 247 318 1,122 2,111 1,294 *Please note, figures are correct at time of issue, however, all statistics may be subject to data cleansing. ** During the COVID- 19 Pandemic there was a moratorium on deportations. This was effective during the latter part of 2020, 2021 and for the first 8 months of 2022. During the moratorium only people who whose presence in Ireland would be contrary to the public interest were deported. This moratorium was lifted in July 2022. *** A deportation order effected in any year may relate to an order signed in a previous year. 1. question: 2230. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of persons serving a sentence for a sexual offence who were granted enhanced remission under Rule 59(2) of the Prison Rules 2007 in each of the years 2020 to 2025 and to date in 2026; the number of applications for enhanced remission from such persons that were refused in the same period; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [56461/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration All prisoners with a sentence to which remission applies qualify for one quarter remission on their sentence on the basis of good behaviour. In addition, prisoners who have engaged in authorised structured activity may apply to receive enhanced remission of greater than one quarter, but not more than one third, of their sentence. There is no automatic entitlement to enhanced remission and the principles governing the awarding of it are contained in the Prison Rules, as set out in the relevant Statutory Instruments. In order for a prisoner to be granted enhanced remission, the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration must be satisfied that the prisoner is less likely to re-offend and is better able to re­integrate into the community. All applications are assessed having regard to a range of criteria set out in the legislation. Other factors taken into consideration include the manner and extent to which the prisoner has engaged constructively in authorised structured activities and the extent to which the prisoner has taken steps to address his or her offending behaviour. The nature and gravity of the offence, the sentence of imprisonment concerned and any recommendations of the Court that imposed the sentence are also taken into account. Other criteria include the period of the sentence already served by the prisoner and the potential threat to the safety and security of members of the public, including to the victim of the offence. Finally, applications are also assessed having regard to any previous convictions; the conduct of the prisoner while in custody or during a period of temporary release; as well as any report or recommendation made by the Governor, the Garda Síochána, Probation Officer or any other person who may be of assistance in making a decision on the application. I can confirm that from 2020 to 2026 to date there was a total of 764 prisoners approved for enhanced remission and a total of 1374 refused enhanced remission. From the total number of prisoners who were approved enhanced remission, I can confirm no prisoner who was serving a sentence for a sexual offence was granted enhanced remission. The vast majority of persons approved for enhanced remission were those who were already in an Open Centre or those who had completed the Community Return Scheme neither of which prisoners convicted of a sex offence would be deemed suitable for. The Irish Prison Service does not record the data in a way that allows for an annual breakdown.

question: 2231. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if prison capacity or overcrowding is a factor considered by the Irish Prison Service when assessing applications for temporary release; if so, the manner in which that factor is recorded and weighted in the decision making process; if any policy document, circular or operational instruction governs the consideration of capacity in such decisions; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [56462/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Irish Prison Service must accept into custody all people committed to prison by the Courts. As such, the Irish Prison Service has no control over the numbers committed to custody at any given time. Where the number of prisoners exceeds the maximum capacity in any prison, the Irish Prison Service make every effort to address the issue through prisoner Temporary Release in accordance with the Criminal Justice Act 1960, as amended by the Criminal Justice (Temporary Release of Prisoners) Act 2003. All applications for temporary release are assessed by the Irish Prison Service on a case-by-case basis, and before a final determination is made a range of factors are considered including: • the nature and gravity of the offence to which the sentence relates; • the sentence concerned and any recommendation made by the Court in relation to the sentence imposed; • the prisoners behaviour and engagement with the various therapeutic services while in custody; • the prisoners family support situation; • the person's previous criminal record; • the potential threat to the safety and security of the public should the person be released; • the risk that the person might commit an offence during any period of temporary release; • the risk of the person failing to comply with any of the conditions of temporary release. Any prisoner who breaches his or her conditions, including by committing a criminal offence, may be arrested and returned to prison immediately by Gardaí or may be refused another period of reviewable temporary release. The Irish Prison Service has two supervised early release schemes, the Community Return Scheme for prisoners in the one to eight-year sentence category and the Community Support Scheme for prisoners with sentences of less than 18 months. Measures to support non-custodial sanctions are also important. The Criminal Law, Civil Law and Defence (Miscellaneous Provisions) Bill 2026 has been passed by both Houses and will amend the Criminal Justice (Community Service) Act 1983 to support and encourage greater use of community service orders (CSOs). It includes an amendment to oblige the courts to consider a CSO in lieu of a prison sentence of up to 24 months’ duration (the current such threshold being 12 months) and to give reasons where they consider that a CSO should not be imposed in such a case. This amendment will oblige judges to demonstrate that they have considered this alternative. The Bill will further amend the 1983 Act to increase the maximum community service hours that a judge may order from 240 to 480.

question: 2233. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of persons convicted of a sexual offence who were charged with a further offence while on temporary release in each of the years 2020 to 2025 and to date in 2026. [56464/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I can assure the Deputy that this Government remains focused on reducing re-offending, including by diverting people, where appropriate, from the criminal justice system and ensuring the underlying causes of offending behaviour are addressed. The Irish Prison Service (IPS) uses temporary release to support the reintegration of prisoners back into their communities following a period of imprisonment. All applications for temporary release are assessed on a case-by-case basis in respect of all relevant information available and the safety of the public is paramount when decisions on temporary release are made. Before a final determination is made to grant temporary release, a number of factors are considered including inter alia: • the nature and gravity of the offence to which the sentence being served by the person relates • the potential threat to the safety and security of the public should the person be released • the risk that the person might commit an offence during any period of temporary release • the risk of the person failing to comply with any of the conditions of temporary release • any report or recommendation made by the Governor, An Garda Síochána or the Probation Service. All temporary releases are subject to a number of stringent conditions. Any person who breaches their conditions may be arrested and returned to prison immediately by the Gardaí, or they may be refused a further period of temporary release. I am advised by An Garda Síochána that the information requested by the Deputy regarding those who have been charged with a criminal offence while on temporary release is not available in the format requested.

question: 2237. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of criminal legal aid certificates issued in the Cork District Court area in each month from January 2026 to date, the number of solicitors who have resigned from the criminal legal aid panel since 1 June 2026; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [56478/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Under the Criminal Justice (Legal Aid) Act 1962, it is the Courts, through the judiciary, that are responsible for the granting of legal aid. The Criminal Legal Aid Scheme is demand-led and it is for the courts to decide in any given case if legal aid is to be granted. My Department has no involvement in the granting of free legal aid or the assignment of solicitors. These matters are handled entirely by the courts. Management of the courts, operational matters such as allocation of court business, the scheduling of cases and logistical functions are the responsibility of the judiciary and Courts Service, which are independent in exercising their functions under the Courts Service Act 1998 and given the separation of powers in the Constitution. The Courts Service has a dedicated email address for the provision of information to members of the Houses of the Oireachtas, at oireachtasenquiries@courts.ie. Solicitors may apply to be placed on the Criminal Legal Aid panel for any county using a single application form, which is processed by a centralised courts office in Castlebar, Co. Mayo. This system, introduced in 2021, replaced the previous requirement to apply separately to individual local court offices. My Department significantly simplified the procedures for Criminal Legal Aid panel membership both for solicitors and counsel last year by waiving the requirement to apply yearly to be retained on panels, with the commencement on 26 November 2025 of S.I. 539 of 2025. It is common practice for solicitors to apply to be included on more than one county panel, and some solicitors apply to be included on all panels. As a result, a solicitor may appear on multiple county panels. I am advised that the Courts Service cannot currently generate a single consolidated report from its tracking systems showing the names of all solicitors on the Criminal Legal Aid panels on a specific date. The Courts Service is examining how this information can be generated in that format in future. I can inform the Deputy that the total number of resignations received by close of business on 27 July 2026 was 218.

question: 2238. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of accused persons who have appeared before the District Court without legal representation since 1 July 2026; the number of cases adjourned or remanded by reason of the unavailability of a legal aid solicitor; the number of such cases involving a person in custody; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [56479/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2209 and 2238 together. Under the Criminal Justice (Legal Aid) Act 1962, it is the Courts, through the judiciary, that are responsible for the granting of legal aid. The Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration has no involvement in the granting of free legal aid or the assignment of solicitors. These matters are handled entirely by the courts. Management of the courts, operational matters such as allocation of court business, the scheduling of cases and logistical functions are the responsibility of the judiciary and Courts Service, which are independent in exercising their functions under the Courts Service Act 1998 and given the separation of powers in the Constitution. The Courts Service has a dedicated email address for the provision of information to members of the Houses of the Oireachtas, at oireachtasenquiries@courts.ie. Due to a number of applications under Article 40.4 of the Constitution and the recent High Court challenge, the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration does not comment on matters before the Courts. The changes to the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme in the District Court that came into effect on Wednesday 1 July are designed to make the system more efficient and effective. For cases in the District Court, regardless of the number of appearances, a set fee is payable to solicitors, replacing the previous appearance-based sliding scale. The new structure also provides for a full separate set fee for each defendant in court on a given day. In considering the need for reform, it is important to note that, while criminal case volumes in the District Court have decreased, expenditure on criminal legal aid in the District Court has nearly doubled, from €19 million in 2015 to €37 million in 2024. My Department reviewed more than 350,000 District Court cases which took place during 2022 and 2023. The reforms aim to address structural issues identified during this review, such as unnecessary adjournments resulting from the payment per appearance model. The Department continues to keep the operation of the new criminal legal aid arrangements in the District Court under review following their introduction, including monitoring claims for fees, entries to and exits from the panel of solicitors and overall operations within the courts.

question: 2242. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of offences involving the use, possession, production or threatening display of a knife or other bladed weapon recorded by An Garda Síochána in each of the years from 2016 to 2025, by county, in tabular form. [56500/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2242 to 2245, inclusive, together. Ireland has a comprehensive and robust legal framework in place to address knife crime, with penalties for knife-related offences strengthened in recent years. In 2024, legislation increased the maximum penalty for offences including possession of a knife with intent to cause injury, trespassing with a knife and producing a knife to unlawfully intimidate another person from five years to seven years imprisonment. In addition, the Government doubled the maximum penalty for assault causing harm to ten years imprisonment in 2023. The Central Statics Office is the national statistics agency, established under the Statistics Act 1993. Recorded crime statistics are published quarterly and are available from the CSO website at www.cso.ie/en/statistics/crimeandjustice/ An Garda Síochána's report on Knife Related Crime for 2015-2024 provides detailed analysis of incidents involving the use and/ or possession of a knife. The report is publicly available on the Garda website and I am informed by Garda authorities that it will be updated later in 2026. The report can be viewed at the below link: www.garda.ie/en/about-us/publications/general-reports/knife-related-crime-2015-to-2024.pdf The report shows that assaults causing harm involving a knife accounted for, on average, less than 7% of all assault causing harm incidents over the past decade. The analysis also identified a 40% reduction in robberies involving a knife in retail spaces and a 35% reduction in robberies involving a knife in public spaces since 2020. An Garda Síochána continues to undertake a range of proactive measures to tackle assaults in public places, including those involving knives. This is informed by a pro-arrest, early-investigation and high-visibility policing approach. An Garda Síochána are currently developing a new Crime Prevention and Reduction Strategy 2026-2029. Knife related crime will be encompassed with all violent crime within this new strategy. Management of the courts, along with related operational matters and logistical functions, are the responsibility of the judiciary and Courts Service, which are independent in exercising their functions. The Courts Service has a dedicated email address for the provision of information to members of the Houses of the Oireachtas at: oireachtasenquiries@courts.ie The Courts Service has advised that it is not possible to provide the specific data on convictions requested as data is only available by offence type.

question: 2246. Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the timeframe between submission of an application for citizenship and the application’s registration on the system; if the registration of such applications is delayed, if he will clarify if the processing timeframe begins from submission or registration of an application; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [56504/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The processing timeline for citizenship applications begins from the date an application is submitted. There can, however, be a period between the submission of an application and its registration. The Citizenship division of my Department is currently registering applications from November 2025. As part of the registration process, applications are checked to ensure the required documentation has been provided. Where further documents are required, applicants are given an opportunity to submit them. Once an application has been registered, the applicant is issued with a personal ID and citizenship application number, allowing them to track their application. It is important to note that no two naturalisation applications are the same and some take longer than others to process. Given the importance of citizenship, robust and comprehensive checks must take place on each application. Unfortunately, some checks, such as international checks, can take a considerable amount of time and these are largely outside of the control of the Immigration Service. Citizenship Division have taken a significant number of steps to improve the process for applicants. These included introducing an online digital application, online payments, and the introduction of eVetting. Applicants can now directly check the status of their immigration application on the Immigration Service’s Customer Service Portal. They can register for, or log in to their existing account, at: www.portal.irishimmigration.ie/en/.

question: 2248. Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the measures that are in place to ensure consistency in the issuing of hunting licences by Garda stations around the country. [56596/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration While my Department is the competent authority for the import and export of firearms and the licensing of firearms dealers, An Garda Síochána has a range of functions with regard to the operation of firearms legislation, including the issuing of firearms certificates and authorisations and is the competent authority for the licensing of firearms within the State. Under the Wildlife Act 1976, as amended, applications for deer hunting licences within the State fall under the remit of the National Parks and Wildlife Service. The Firearms Act 1925-2023 and the Firearms (Firearm Certificates for Non-Residents) Act 2000 both give the authority for granting licences to Superintendents and Chief Superintendents of An Garda Síochána. Licensing Officers, when considering firearms licence applications, are considered 'persona designata' and cannot have their decision-making process fettered in any way. Neither I, as Minister, nor my Department, have any role in the issuing or otherwise of firearms certificates. Nevertheless, reform of the firearms licensing system has been under consideration for a number of years, and extensive consultation has been undertaken and is continuing with various firearms stakeholders, including representative firearms organisations. My Department also regularly holds meetings with individual firearms organisations on request.

question: 2249. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of persons who have arrived in Ireland at any port of entry, including Dublin Airport, without valid travel documents for each of the years from 2018 to 2025 and to date in 2026; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [56662/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Border Management Unit (BMU) of my Department is responsible for frontline Immigration at Dublin Airport only. Other airports and other ports of entry are the responsibility of An Garda Síochána. The establishment of a person’s identity and nationality is an important feature of our immigration process. Immigration officials conduct passport checks, and run operations as required, to ensure passengers arriving in the State are properly documented in accordance with Section 11 of the Immigration Act 2004. The table below details the total number of people who have been refused leave to land at Dublin Airport, and of that total, the numbers refused due to presenting false identity documents or no identity documents. In relation to other ports of entry, I have sought the information requested from the Garda Commissioner and I will write to the Deputy directly should the information be available. My Department and the Garda National Immigration Bureau (GNIB) are working closely with airlines on a range of measures to ensure that passengers have such documentation when boarding. This includes delivering in-person training to relevant airline ground-handling staff on immigration requirements and false travel documentation. BMU officials are also available 24/7 to assist airlines with any immigration queries. An Garda Síochána has responsibility for issuing carrier liability notices and warnings, and for the imposition of carrier liability fines on carriers who permit a non-national to travel with their airline or ferry without the necessary documentation i.e. no documents, false document, no visa or improper use of genuine documents. The fines payable by carriers in such instances were increased by way of the Courts, Civil Law, Criminal Law and Superannuation (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2024. The effect of these changes is to increase the fines payable by carriers on summary conviction to a maximum of €5,000 from the previous maximum of €3,000. The Act also provides that carriers which make a payment of €2,500 within 28 days will avoid prosecution for an offence under the Act, which was an increase from the previous payment of €1,500; in practice many carriers avail of this option. The visa requirements to travel to Ireland have been strengthened and remain under review by my Department. BMU and GNIB have an ongoing intelligence-led programme of operations at airplanes to detect passengers who destroyed documents inflight and to identify the point of embarkation of undocumented passengers. To the end of June this year, the BMU have carried out 3,408 doorstop operations at Dublin Airport. Table 1. question: 2250. Deputy Martin Kenny asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will examine an ongoing situation with a citizenship application (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [56710/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The granting of Irish citizenship through naturalisation is governed by the provisions of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956, as amended. All applications for a certificate of naturalisation are processed and assessed individually in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The person referred to by the Deputy made their first application as the spouse of an Irish national, and the application was deemed ineligible as the applicant did not have the reckonable residence required. The applicant has since made a new application, which was returned to them as a number of documents were missing. These have since been submitted by the applicant. When an application is returned to an applicant and subsequently resubmitted, it will rejoin the queue on the date that it is resubmitted, not the date of the original application. My Department has recently launched a new webpage to help people better understand the naturalisation application process, including the key documents required for identity and residency. The page also provides guidance on how to have documents certified. Your constituent can view it here: How to Become an Irish Citizen Guide - Immigration Service Delivery (www.irishimmigration.ie/how-to-become-an-irish-citizen-guide/). Given the importance of citizenship, robust and comprehensive checks must take place on each application. Unfortunately some checks, such as international checks, can take a considerable amount of time and these are largely outside of the control of the Immigration Service. Applicants can check the status of their immigration applications and submit queries on the Immigration Service’s Customer Service Portal at the following link: www.portal.irishimmigration.ie/en/ As an Oireachtas member, you can also request the status of individual immigration cases by e-mail, using the Oireachtas Mail facility at IMoireachtasmail@justice.ie, which has been specifically established for this purpose. This service enables up to date information on such cases to be obtained without the need to seek information by way of the Parliamentary Question process.

question: 2251. Deputy Ciarán Ahern asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the practical supports that will be put in place to help Ukrainian families currently living in a hotel (details supplied) secure suitable accommodation within such a short timeframe; who is co-ordinating communication and case management for families with complex medical, educational or disability needs; the measures being taken to minimise disruption to children's education, particularly where they have established school placements and specialist supports; the way in which the needs of working families are being considered, particularly where relocation could result in parents losing employment because they can no longer reasonably travel to work; the arrangements being made to ensure continuity of healthcare for those receiving ongoing treatment or specialist services; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [56715/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration As previously communicated to all residents, Citywest Hotel accommodation for those granted Temporary Protection will terminate on 18th September 2026. Recognising that this is a significant change for residents, my Department, the Irish Red Cross and the International Organisation for Migration undertook dedicated engagement with those affected. Information and practical support regarding available options was made available to all residents. This included supports to facilitate independent living where appropriate. My Department also recognises that there are some Temporary Protection beneficiaries who have a continued requirement for state-supported accommodation due to individual circumstances. For this reason an application process was available to those who could demonstrate that they continued to require temporary accommodation following the commercial accommodation wind-down at Citywest Hotel. The application process opened on 30 June 2026 and closed at 5pm on 17 July 2026. Support was provided to applicants throughout the application process by the Irish Red Cross, the International Organisation for Migration and staff from my Department. Applications received are being assessed, and those found to require continued accommodation will be offered places in Designated Accommodation Centres (DACs), which may include Punchestown (Co. Kildare), Kill Equestrian (Co. Kildare), Inchmore (Co. Offaly) and St Malachy’s (Dundalk), with transfers commencing from August onwards. Residents who did not submit an application within the application period will not receive a further offer of state-supported accommodation as part of this process. These residents will be required to vacate Citywest Hotel by mid-September. The Irish Red Cross (IRC) and the International Organization for Migration (IOM) are conducting a series of information sessions for people granted Temporary Protection living in UCTAT (Ukrainian Crisis Temporary Accommodation Team) accommodation. These sessions will take place online every Tuesday and Thursday. My Department is endeavouring to ensure that people with HSE care plans are relocated within the same Community Health Organisation Area, to ensure continuity of care.

question: 2256. Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of Garda members assigned to County Kerry on 1 July of each year from 2020 to 2026, broken down by Garda station. [56837/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2256 and 2259 together. An Garda Síochána publishes information in relation to the allocation of Garda personnel nationally. This includes a breakdown of Gardaí assigned to County Kerry by Garda Station from 2010 to the end of June 2026, the latest date for which figures are available. This can be found at the following links: Information for 2026 can be found at the following link: www.garda.ie/en/information-centre/garda-statistics/human%20resources/ Information for previous years can be found at the following link: www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/human-resources-and-people-development/garda-hr-directorate/garda-strength-breakdown-2025/december-2025.html The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which includes the distribution and stationing of Gardaí throughout the State. The Deputy should note that An Garda Síochána is not structured or aligned operationally to county boundaries and, as a result, figures by county are not available. I am also informed that when allocating Gardaí to and from any Division or station, consideration is given to commitments and undertakings outlined in the Annual Service Plan. The requirements of all Garda Divisions nationwide are also taken into account, which include: Local and national crime trends and workloads; Policing arrangements and operational strategies; Minimum establishment statistics; Local population and trends, geographical area and size; and Transfer applications, including welfare, personnel issues and concerns. It should also be noted that, with the completion of the roll-out of the Garda Operating Model, Divisions no longer operate on a District model and are now organised into Functional Areas. Under this model, An Garda Síochána do not police on a station basis, but rather on a Divisional basis and see stations as locations within communities for people to attend, and for resources to be accommodated. Policing for an area will be delivered using all resources in a Community Engagement Area and supported by Divisional resources and units.

question: 2257. Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of Garda stations in County Kerry operating with reduced public opening hours; and the breakdown of the location of these stations. [56838/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which includes operational policing matters such as the opening hours of Garda stations. The Commissioner is independent in the performance of his functions under section 34 of the Act. I am informed by the Garda authorities that information regarding Garda station contact details and public opening hours is available through the Garda Station Directory at: www.garda.ie/en/contact-us/station-directory/ The Deputy may select the relevant Garda Division and review the information using either the map or list function. Where a member of the public needs to speak with their local Gardaí, contact can be made through the relevant Garda District Headquarters, which is open 24 hours and is identified in the Station Directory. It is important to emphasise that the hours during which a Garda station is open for public business are not equivalent to the operational hours of the station or the availability of Gardaí patrolling in the community. Outside these public business hours, members of An Garda Síochána continue to operate from Garda stations, are on patrol in their local communities, are involved in community engagement and investigations and are available to respond to assist the public. It is also important to emphasise that An Garda Síochána does not police on a station basis, but rather on a Divisional basis. Policing services are delivered using all resources within a Community Engagement Area, supported by Divisional resources and specialist units. I am advised that An Garda Síochána operates a Regional Control Room strategy which ensures that Garda resources are available to respond to calls for service from the public, including situations where a local resource is not immediately available. Calls for service, whether received through a local Garda station or the 999 Emergency Call Answering Service (ECAS), are routed through the Regional Control Rooms and prioritised for response. Higher priority calls will always take priority over lower priority calls. The Garda authorities inform me that An Garda Síochána aims to answer 80% of 999 calls within 7 seconds and deploy resources immediately, giving an estimated time of arrival. An Garda Síochána will take appropriate steps to deal with all incidents and ensure that emergency and life-threatening calls receive priority. They will endeavour to reach callers within 15 minutes in urban locations and as soon as possible, given the distance to be travelled, in more rural areas.

question: 2261. Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of Garda members assigned to community policing duties in County Kerry in each of the years 2020 to 2025 and to date in 2026, in tabular form. [56876/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration This Government is committed to ensuring that An Garda Síochána has the resources it needs to fight crime and a strengthened, well-resourced Garda organisation is central to this policy. The Programme for Government also includes a commitment to ensure each community policing area has a dedicated community Garda, so everyone knows their local officer and how to contact them. The Garda Vote in Budget 2026 includes unprecedented funding of over €2.74 billion which will support the continued recruitment of Gardaí and Garda staff. Increasing the overall strength of An Garda Síochána will, in turn, increase the number of Gardaí available to work in areas like community policing. Community Gardaí play a pivotal role in building trust between Gardaí and the public, through visible, responsive policing and open dialogue in neighbourhoods, schools and diverse community groups. It is through this engagement that communities and Gardaí work together to prevent crime and strengthen local resilience. It is essential to point out however that, whilst not every Garda member is designated as a 'Community Garda', community policing is at the heart of An Garda Síochána and all Gardaí have a role to play in community policing in the course of carrying out their duties. An Garda Síochána publishes figures in relation to the allocation of Gardaí nationally. This includes a breakdown of Community Garda from 2008 to the end of June 2026, the latest date for which figures are available. This can be found at the following links: Information for 2026 can be found at the following link: www.garda.ie/en/information-centre/garda-statistics/human%20resources/ The Deputy should select 2026, June 2026 and then select the file titled ‘Community Garda by Division June 2026’. Information for previous years can be found at the following link: www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/human-resources-and-people-development/garda-hr-directorate/garda-strength-breakdown-2025/december-2025.html The Deputy should select the file titled ‘Community Garda by Division 2008 to 31 December 2025’.

question: 2262. Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of Gardaí assigned to each Garda division, together with the population of each division, in each of the years 2021 to date in 2026, in tabular form; the number of Gardaí included in the strength figures for the Cork city division who are assigned to national or regional units rather than to divisional policing duties; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [56903/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024. By law, he is responsible for all stationing and deployment decisions, including the designation to, and/or assignment of Garda members and staff to specialist and national units. Under section 34 of the Act, he is independent in these matters. As Minister, it is my role to support the Commissioner in ensuring he has the resources he needs. Budget 2026 provides unprecedented funding of €2.74 billion to support recruitment and staffing. An Garda Síochána publishes information in relation to the allocation of Gardaí nationally. This includes a breakdown of the number of Gardaí by rank assigned to each Garda Division as at 30 June 2026, the latest date for when figures are available. The information for 2026 can be found at the following link: www.garda.ie/en/information-centre/garda-statistics/human%20resources/ The Deputy should select the statistics for 2026, June 2026 and then select the file titled ‘Garda Members by Division District Station" to access a breakdown of Garda members assigned to each Division. Information for 2021 to 2025 can be found at the following link: www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/human-resources-and-people-development/garda-hr-directorate/garda-strength-breakdown-2025/december-2025.html I am assured by the Garda Commissioner that the allocation of Garda resources is kept under continued review to ensure their optimum use. It is important to note that ratios such as the number of Gardaí per head of population are not an appropriate tool to use when considering the allocation of Garda resources as they fail to take account of, among other things, the fact that crime levels and types can vary significantly among communities of similar population size. When allocating resources, consideration is also given to commitments and undertakings outlined in the Annual Policing Plan. The requirements of all Garda Divisions nationwide are also taken into account, which include: • Local and national crime trends and workloads; • Policing arrangements and operational strategies; • Minimum establishment statistics; • Local population and trends, geographical area and size; • Transfer applications, including welfare, personnel issues and concerns. It should also be noted that, with the completion of the roll-out of the Garda Operating Model, Divisions are now organised into Functional Areas. Under this model, An Garda Síochána do not police on a station basis, but rather on a Divisional basis and see stations as locations within communities for people to attend, and for resources to be accommodated. Policing for an area will be delivered using all resources in a Community Engagement Area and supported by Divisional resources and units. An Garda Síochána acknowledges that they have previously published details in respect of national and regional units, however, for operational reasons and given the current geopolitical situation it is not appropriate for detailed data on individual sections to be shared.

question: 2266. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of persons refused leave to land at each port of entry in each of the years 2015 to 2025 and to date in 2026, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [56969/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2266, 2225, 2226, 2267, 2268, 2269 and 2270 together. Implementing effective border security arrangements is a priority for me as Minister. The Programme for Government commits to developing a border security strategy to deliver stronger border security, ensuring technology supports border screening and to reviewing the potential of extending pre-clearance mechanisms, such as electronic travel authorisation, for travel from designated third countries. This work is underway. The Border Management Unit (BMU) of my Department is responsible for frontline Immigration at Dublin Airport only, as such the below figures reflect the position at Dublin Airport. Other airports and other ports of entry are the responsibility of An Garda Síochána. When any non-EEA national presents at a border, an Immigration Officer must determine whether that person should be granted leave to land and gain entry to the State. In performing their duties, an Officer is required to consider all of the circumstances of the individual at the time of entry in line with the provisions of the Immigration Act 2004. The establishment of a person’s identity and nationality is an important feature of our immigration process. Section 4(3) of the Immigration Act 2004 sets out the full range of grounds on which a person may be refused. People can be refused for more than one reason. These include, but are not limited to, persons arriving without correct documentation. When a person is refused leave to land at Dublin airport, the Immigration Officer will arrange for the person to be referred to the Garda National Immigration Bureau (GNIB) for removal from the State. The priority is to return them on the next available return flight to the last point of embarkation. The operational policy in this regard has not changed. Arrangements for the removal of those refused leave to land are operational matters for the GNIB. If a person indicates or is identified as being in need of international protection they are admitted to the international protection process. However, they will still be recorded as a refusal of leave to land. My Department and the GNIB are working closely with airlines on a range of measures to ensure that passengers have such documentation when boarding. This includes delivering in-person training to relevant airline ground-handling staff on immigration requirements and false travel documentation. BMU officials are available 24/7 to assist airlines with any immigration queries. An Garda Síochána has responsibility for issuing carrier liability notices and warnings, and for the imposition of carrier liability fines on carriers who permit a non-national to travel with their airline or ferry without the necessary documentation i.e. no documents, false document, no visa or improper use of genuine documents. The fines payable by carriers in such instances were increased by way of the Courts, Civil Law, Criminal Law and Superannuation (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2024. The effect of these changes is to increase the fines payable by carriers on summary conviction to a maximum of €5,000 from the previous maximum of €3,000. The Act also provides that carriers which make a payment of €2,500 within 28 days will avoid prosecution for an offence under the Act, which was an increase from the previous payment of €1,500; in practice many carriers avail of this option. The visa requirements to travel to Ireland have been strengthened and remain under review by my Department. BMU and GNIB have an ongoing intelligence-led programme of operations at airplanes to detect passengers who destroyed documents inflight and to identify the point of embarkation of undocumented passengers. To the end of June this year, the BMU have carried out 3,408 doorstop operations at Dublin Airport. The table below outlines the number of people refused leave to land and those who presented without a valid travel document at Dublin Airport from 2018 onwards, as the civilianisation process was completed that year. The figures for those who have claimed asylum at Dublin Airport have only been recorded since 2022. While systems do not allow for the extraction of the precise data requested with regard to the number of refusals who subsequently claimed asylum, it is the case that the majority of those who present without appropriate documentation and are refused leave to land seek to enter the international protection process. It is also the case that some people with valid travel documents seek to enter the international protection process, hence the number of applicants for asylum below include persons who presented with valid documents. I have written to the Garda Commissioner in relation to records in relation to other ports of entry and I will write to the Deputy directly should the information be available. Table 1. Dublin Airport immigration control Year Total Arriving Passengers Total Refusals Undocumented Arrivals False Documents + Imposters Claimed Asylum 2018 15,634,300 3,999 895 891 N/A 2019 16,318,300 6,151 1,579 1,849 N/A 2020 3,636,256 2,077 712 169 N/A 2021 4,118,027 3,210 2,082 279 N/A 2022 13,930,041 7,662 4,968 832 6,765 2023 16,628,545 5,826 3,287 872 4,712 2024 17,310,841 5,267 2,297 1080 4,320 2025 18,202,584 4,928 2,067 1034 3,993 2026 (to 30/06) 8,945,664 2130 894 465 1,669 * Please note, figures are correct at time of issue, however, all statistics may be subject to data cleansing
