question: 2271. Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will consider establishing a transfer or lateral-entry pathway for Irish citizens who are currently working as police officers in the United Kingdom to join An Garda Síochána without having to apply as new recruits, in recognition of their existing policing experience; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [56975/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Section 94 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act allows the Garda Commissioner, at the request of the Chief Constable of the PSNI, to appoint a member of the PSNI as a member of An Garda Síochána on secondment for a period of not more than three years. There is currently no provision for the direct transfer on a permanent basis of serving PSNI officers at the rank of sergeant or below into An Garda Síochána. The position regarding direct transfer will, in consultation with our UK and Northern Irish counterparts, be kept under review. It may be noted that any suitably qualified member of the PSNI can apply to join open positions at the rank of Superintendent and above within An Garda Síochána under the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024 (Appointment to the Ranks of Assistant Garda Commissioner, Chief Superintendent and Superintendent) Regulations 2025 and section 26 and 27 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024. Any Regulations made under the Act will continue to honour Ireland’s commitments under the 2002 Agreement between the Government of Ireland and the Government of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland on Police Co-operation.

question: 2272. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether a complaint or referral has been received by his Department or An Garda Síochána alleging a contravention of section 26(3) of the International Protection Act 2015 in each of the years from 2015 to 2025 and to date in 2026, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [56990/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2272 and 2273 together. As the Deputy will be aware, the prosecution of offences in these instances are a matter for An Garda Síochána and the Director of Public Prosecutions, who are independent in the exercise of their functions in this regard; as Minister I have no role in the taking of such prosecutions. I am advised by the Garda Commissioner that there were <10 proceedings initiated in relation to Section 26(3) of the International Protection Act 2015 between 1 January 2015 and 30 June 2026. In accordance with standard practice An Garda Síochána do not provide specific figures relating to incidents of fewer than ten for data protection reasons. I am advised by the Courts Service that the information requested on the number of convictions for this offence is not recorded in a manner that allows it to be extracted from the relevant databases. The confidentiality requirements contained in the International Protection Acts apply to all international protection applicants including those charged or convicted of criminal offences. It is important to note that this does not mean the cases cannot be covered by the media, but rather that it must be covered in a manner that does not lead to the person being identified as an applicant for international protection.

question: 2274. Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if Ireland will be forced to take in a certain quota of asylum seekers each year; if so, the number; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [57030/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2274, 2275 and 2276 together. Ireland is under no obligation to accept a quota of asylum seekers each year. The State is required to examine the application of anyone who presents at the borders of the State, or is in the State, and indicates that they wish to make an application for international protection. Each application for international protection is examined in detail on its individual merits, taking all factors into account. This is in accordance with our obligations under international and EU asylum law. There has been a significant increase in investment into the international protection system over the last number of years which, combined with digitisation and process reengineering, has facilitated a major increase in processing capacity and demonstrates a strong commitment to reducing cases on hand. As the Deputy will be aware, the International Protection Act 2026 gives effect to the EU Migration and Asylum Pact and came into effect on 12 June 2026. The EU Migration and Asylum Pact has been designed to establish a common approach to migration and asylum that is based on the concepts of solidarity and responsibility amongst Member States. The Asylum and Migration Management Regulation (AMMR) introduces an annual mandatory, but flexible, solidarity mechanism for the European Union Under the Solidarity Mechanism, Member States must provide solidarity support to those Member States determined to be "under migratory pressure". Member States, however, have flexibility as to the form of solidarity which they pledge. The solidarity provided can be in the form of relocations of asylum applicants, in the form of financial support, or alternative solidarity measures. Member States pledge solidarity to the Annual Solidarity Pool in line with their fair share based on the size of their population and the strength of their economy. For the first Annual Solidarity Pool set in 2025, Ireland pledged financial support of up to €9.26 million in respect of 2026 to support the Member States determined to be "under migratory pressure". As Ireland was determined to be ‘At Risk of Migratory Pressure’ it will have priority access to an EU Migration Support Toolbox, including funding.

question: 2278. Deputy Mark Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of scramblers, e-scooters, e-bikes and quad-bikes seized by an Garda Síochána to date in 2026; the number of each that were seized in transit; the number that were returned to their owners; the number that were destroyed, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [57042/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration On 1 April, the Road Traffic (Control of Certain Vehicles) Regulations 2026, known as Grace's Law, were signed into law by the Minister for Transport. These regulations prohibit the use of an off-road motorcycle, such as a scrambler or a quadbike, in any place, except on private land. They impose a requirement of consent where restricted vehicles are used on private land and will make enforcement easier. The seriousness with which the Government views this issue is reflected in the fact the mere use of scramblers is now explicitly an offence, assisting An Garda Síochána operationally by ensuring that members no longer have to form a reasonable belief about dangerous use of the vehicle. Gardaí also have additional, and significant, legislative powers to combat the antisocial and dangerous misuse of e-scooters, scramblers, quad bikes, e-bikes and other such vehicles including under the Road Traffic Act 1961, the Non-Fatal Offences Against the Person Act 1997, and the Criminal Law Act 1997 and the Road Traffic and Roads Act 2023. I am assured that An Garda Síochána continues to adopt a proactive approach in addressing the illegal use of e-scooters, scramblers, quad bikes and e-bikes and have been informed of a substantial increase in the seizure of these types of vehicles during the first quarter of 2026 when measured against the full year 2025. The table below sets out the number of incidents where an e-scooter, scrambler, e-bike and quad bike was seized or detained, nationally, in 2024, 2025 and in Quarter 1 in 2026. Data related to the number of vehicles seized while in transit, the number of vehicles returned to owners and the number of vehicles destroyed is not currently available. - 2024 2025 Q1 2026 Incidents where e-scooters were seized or detained 310 931 754 Incidents where scramblers were seized or detained 165 159 94 Incidents where quad bikes were seized or detained 39 40 17 Incidents where e-bikes were seized or detained 144 237 140

question: 2279. Deputy Mark Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if there will be an increase in funding for the bail supervision scheme in the Budget 2027; if this service will be rolled out to additional counties; if so, the counties in question; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [57045/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Bail Supervision Scheme (BSS) offers courts an alternative option to detaining a young person who comes before them. It provides for the possibility of granting bail with intensive supervision. By reducing the need for remand places, this also provides an opportunity to focus on developing successful community resources designed to prevent young people being detained in a youth justice facility and reduce the risk of them going further down the path of criminality. On 1 January 2026, governance for the Bail Supervision Scheme (BSS) transferred from my Department to the Probation Service. This transition forms part of a broader effort to ensure the ongoing, effective management of children subject to bail conditions, which is integral to the delivery of youth justice services. The Probation Service recognises the significant value the scheme has, both in providing the judiciary with options to strengthen confidence in use of bail for children; but also in ensuring that detention is only used as a last resort. An annual budget of €2.1 million has been allocated to the scheme for 2026. Over the next six months, the Probation Service will conduct a review of BSS provision, with considerations around national expansion, budget requirements and delivery/service model being explored.

question: 2280. Deputy Mark Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the Garda staffing levels throughout Dublin by DMR area; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [57046/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2280, 2281 and 2282 together. Under the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, the Garda Commissioner is responsible for the distribution and stationing of Garda personnel throughout the State. I engage regularly with the Commissioner and I am assured that the resourcing of each Garda Division is fully considered within the overall context of the needs and requirements of Garda Divisions throughout the country. An Garda Síochána police on a Divisional basis using all resources in a Community Engagement area, supported by Divisional resources and units. This Operating Model has been designed to enable An Garda Síochána to meet the challenges of modern-day policing more consistently around the country by enabling specialisation in the delivery of key services and freeing up more Gardaí to focus on front line policing. Under this structure, each Division is organised into four Functional Areas: Community Engagement, Crime, Performance Assurance, and Business Services. The Operating Model, coupled with some realignment of responsibilities, is helping to deliver a consistent, community-focused policing service. As Minister, my priority is getting more Gardaí into all our communities by supporting increased recruitment and appropriate civilianisation where possible. A Garda budget of €2.74 billion in 2026 will fund the recruitment of up to 1,000 new Gardaí, 200 more Garda staff and additional members of the Garda Reserve. The Garda Commissioner and his senior management team keep the distribution of resources under ongoing review and I understand that, when allocating and transferring Garda members to and from any Division, consideration is given to commitments and undertakings outlined in the Annual Policing Plan. The Commissioner also takes the requirements of all Garda Divisions nationwide into account, which include: • Local and national crime trends and workloads; • Policing arrangements and operational strategies; • Minimum establishment statistics; • Local population and trends, geographical area and size; • Transfer applications, including welfare, personnel issues and concerns. An Garda Síochána publishes information in relation to the allocation of Garda personnel nationally. This includes a breakdown of Garda Staff by Division and Garda Station from 2010 to the end of June 2026 and Garda Members by Division from 2006 to the end of June 2026 assigned to the DMR Garda Divisions. question: 2281. Deputy Mark Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for a breakdown of Gardaí, per Garda station in Dublin mid-west; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [57058/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2280, 2281 and 2282 together. Under the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, the Garda Commissioner is responsible for the distribution and stationing of Garda personnel throughout the State. I engage regularly with the Commissioner and I am assured that the resourcing of each Garda Division is fully considered within the overall context of the needs and requirements of Garda Divisions throughout the country. An Garda Síochána police on a Divisional basis using all resources in a Community Engagement area, supported by Divisional resources and units. This Operating Model has been designed to enable An Garda Síochána to meet the challenges of modern-day policing more consistently around the country by enabling specialisation in the delivery of key services and freeing up more Gardaí to focus on front line policing. Under this structure, each Division is organised into four Functional Areas: Community Engagement, Crime, Performance Assurance, and Business Services. The Operating Model, coupled with some realignment of responsibilities, is helping to deliver a consistent, community-focused policing service. As Minister, my priority is getting more Gardaí into all our communities by supporting increased recruitment and appropriate civilianisation where possible. A Garda budget of €2.74 billion in 2026 will fund the recruitment of up to 1,000 new Gardaí, 200 more Garda staff and additional members of the Garda Reserve. The Garda Commissioner and his senior management team keep the distribution of resources under ongoing review and I understand that, when allocating and transferring Garda members to and from any Division, consideration is given to commitments and undertakings outlined in the Annual Policing Plan. The Commissioner also takes the requirements of all Garda Divisions nationwide into account, which include: • Local and national crime trends and workloads; • Policing arrangements and operational strategies; • Minimum establishment statistics; • Local population and trends, geographical area and size; • Transfer applications, including welfare, personnel issues and concerns. An Garda Síochána publishes information in relation to the allocation of Garda personnel nationally. This includes a breakdown of Garda Staff by Division and Garda Station from 2010 to the end of June 2026 and Garda Members by Division from 2006 to the end of June 2026 assigned to the DMR Garda Divisions. Information in relation to the Garda fleet, the number of cars currently assigned in the DMR Garda Divisions, is publicly available and can be found at the following link: www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/finance-services/finance-fleet-management.html The Deputy should select Finance Fleet Management and access the file titled Fleet Management Report to the most recent date for a breakdown of vehicles currently assigned to the area.

question: 2283. Deputy Mark Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to outline any changes to the Community Safety Fund for 2027; to outline any proposed changes to the application process; the funding that will be allocated; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [57060/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2170, 2171, 2194, 2283 and 2301 together. CAB is a multi-agency statutory body established under the Criminal Assets Bureau Act, 1996. I am advised that all monies seized by CAB are remitted to the Central Fund of the Exchequer after the appropriate statutory time frame under the Proceeds of Crime Acts. I was pleased to secure an 8.2% increase on the Criminal Assets Bureau budget allocation for 2026. The Bureau’s budget allocation in 2026 is €13.8m, of which €11.25m is for Pay and €2.55m is for Non-Pay. A 15% uplift on the Criminal Assets Bureau’s total budget would equate to €2.07m additional in funding. This would provide a total budget in 2027 totalling €15.15m. I am committed to ensuring that the Criminal Assets Bureau have the powers and resources to continue their important work. The Proceeds of Crime and Related Matters Bill is making its way through the Oireachtas currently. Once passed into law, the Criminal Assets Bureau will have stronger investigative powers and will be able to dispose of assets much more quickly than is currently the case. Figures relating to asset recovery under the Proceeds of Crime Acts by CAB are available publicly in Chapters 3 and 4 of the annual reports published on the Bureau's website: www.cab.ie/annual-reports/ . The Criminal Assets Bureau have advised that they do not collate statistics by County. Statistics for 2026 are not yet available and can not be provided at this point in time. The disbursement of monies collected by the Criminal Assets Bureau is controlled by the Central Exchequer. However, the Deputy may be interested to note that the Community Safety Fund re-directs a portion of the proceeds of crime, seized by the Criminal Assets Bureau (CAB) and An Garda Síochána, back into communities in order to fund innovative local projects aimed at building stronger, safer communities. In 2025, €4.4 million was allocated through the Community Safety Fund to 42 community safety projects nationwide. This represented a 33% increase on the €3 million awarded to 33 community safety projects in 2024. I secured a further increase in funding to €4.75 million for 2026, which is reflective of the continued success of An Garda Síochána and CAB. The Fund has supported 127 community safety projects to date all across Ireland. Putting this money back into the community is a tangible way of showing that there can be a direct link between the activities of law enforcement and building stronger, safer communities. The below table provides a breakdown of the number of projects funded by the Community Safety Fund since it launched in 2022. Year Number of Funded Projects 2022 22 2023 30 2024 33 2025 42 Total 127 In 2025, the Community Safety Fund was transferred to the newly established National Office for Community Safety. The National Office for Community Safety, an office of my Department, is a central coordinating body to the new whole of government, collaborative, problem-solving approach to community safety. The final elements of this new community safety infrastructure are being established including: • The establishment of all 36 Safety Partnerships. • The publishing of the National Strategy for Improving Community Safety The National Office is currently conducting a review of the current operating model and criteria for the Community Safety Fund to ensure that projects funded in the future are consistent with the National Strategy for Community Safety and support the work of Local Community Safety Partnerships.

question: 2284. Deputy Mark Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of Gardaí recruited to date in 2026; the total number recruited in 2025; the total number of Gardaí in the State; the number of Gardaí at the start of 2025; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [57061/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2284, 2289 and 2290 together. The government is committed to building stronger, safer communities, and strengthening An Garda Síochána is at the core of that. This is reflected in the unprecedented allocation of over €2.74 billion to An Garda Síochána in Budget 2026. This funding allows for the continued recruitment of Garda members and staff. Three Garda recruitment campaigns have been held in the last 18 months with over 15,000 people applying to enter An Garda Síochána. 206 new Gardaí attested at the Garda College in Templemore on 24 July, the third Garda attestation this year. A further 193 Gardaí attested on 1 May 2026, and 167 attested in February 2026. Overall, 619 probationer Gardaí attested in 2025. An Garda Síochána have advised there are currently over 604 Garda recruits undergoing the training programme at the Garda College. The most recent intake of Garda recruits, which numbered over 200, entered the Garda college on 27 July. This intake brings the number of Garda trainees that have entered the college since 2022 to nearly 3,000. Garda recruit intakes continue to enter the Garda College every 11-12 weeks. The number of graduates expected to pass out of Templemore this year is based the on three attestations this year so far which totals 566, and the February intake of 215 which is due to attest in October this year. On that basis, I am advised by the Garda authorities that between 770 and 780 trainees, approximately will attest this year. An Garda Síochána publishes information in relation to the allocation of Gardaí nationally. This includes a breakdown of the number of Gardaí by rank assigned to each Garda Division as at 30 June 2026, the latest date for when figures are available. Information for 2025 can be found at the following link: [ www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/human-resources-and-people-development/garda-hr-directorate/garda-strength-breakdown-2025/december-2025.html ]

question: 2285. Deputy Seán Crowe asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of peace commissioners registered on the most recent roll maintained by his Department. [57072/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration In line with the provisions of section 88 of the Courts of Justice Act 1924, Peace Commissioners are appointed, and may be removed from that appointment, by the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration. A list of individuals appointed to the office of Peace Commissioners is maintained by my Department. That list is referred to as the Roll (or Register) of Peace Commissioners. I can inform the Deputy that the total number of Peace Commissioners recorded throughout the country is currently just over 4000. While my Department maintains the Roll of Peace Commissioners and every effort is made to keep it accurate, the data currently on the Roll may include Peace Commissioners who are no longer active or, indeed, some whom have died. My Department relies on Peace Commissioners themselves, or others familiar with their circumstances (such as family members), to let us know of any changes in circumstances of individual Peace Commissioners since their appointment. My Department is currently working on the Roll of Peace Commissioners, with a view to making it as accurate as possible, and good progress has been made to date in this regard. Consideration is being given to making the Roll of Peace Commissioners available online which would be of assistance to members of the public and is in line with the move to increase digital delivery of certain services. Once the work to update the data on the Roll has been completed, the question of publishing the Roll in an accessible, online format will be considered in the context of any legal, technical or other constraints.

question: 2286. Deputy Seán Crowe asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the average waiting time for successful naturalisation applications to be processed at present; and the number of applications currently being considered. [57073/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2286 and 2453 together. I can assure the Deputy that the Citizenship Division of my Department has taken a significant number of steps to speed up the process for applicants. These included introducing an online digital application, online payments, and the introduction of eVetting. This digitisation has facilitated a record number of citizenship decisions made last year. The Citizenship Division of my Department has gone from processing around 12,000 applications a year, to processing over 20,000 applications in 2023, and more than 31,000 decisions in both 2024 and 2025. There are currently 61,000 applications on hand. Approximately 6,000 of the applications on hand are adults who attended the June citizenship ceremonies and minors whose naturalisation certificates will issue in the coming weeks. These applications will be finalised once the certificates have issued. The median processing time for a decision on an application in 2024 and 2025 was approximately 8 months. This was a significant improvement from the median processing time of 15 months in 2023, 19 months in 2022, and 24 months in 2021. It is important to note that no two naturalisation applications are the same and some take longer than others to process. Given the importance of citizenship, robust and comprehensive checks must take place on each application. Unfortunately, some international checks can take a considerable amount of time, and these are largely outside of the control of my Department.

question: 2287. Deputy Seán Crowe asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of garda personnel seconded to duties relating specifically to and for the duration of the EU Presidency. [57074/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under Section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024 which includes the distribution and stationing of Garda personnel throughout the State. Since January 2024, An Garda Síochána has been actively preparing to meet the policing and security requirements associated with the Presidency of the EU. I am informed that a comprehensive command, control and coordination framework is in place to support the delivery of Presidency-related policing operations, together with all other major and significant policing operations and events, while ensuring the continued provision of effective day-to-day policing services. I am advised by An Garda Síochána that specific operational arrangements and the deployment of Garda resources associated with Operation Brehon remain confidential for operational and security reasons. I understand that a small number of Gardaí have been temporarily transferred to Dublin Castle to effectively support and implement a robust policing and security operation for the duration of the EU Presidency, however the attestation of 1,185 Gardaí since March 2025 will ensure that An Garda Síochána have the necessary resources to maintain policing services in divisions nationwide while also providing for the security needs of the Presidency. While certain events may necessitate the deployment of a greater number of Garda personnel than others, I am assured that sufficient Garda resources will remain available to ensure the continued delivery of effective and consistent Garda services throughout the Presidency period. Continuity of core policing services across all functional areas remains a key organisational priority. Resource requirements for Presidency events are subject to continuous assessment through established governance, planning and coordination processes. Every effort is made to ensure that the delivery of normal policing services is maintained in parallel with the operational demands associated with the Presidency programme. The protection of frontline policing services, community engagement, crime prevention activity and emergency response capability remains a core consideration in all operational planning associated with the Presidency.

question: 2288. Deputy Tom Brabazon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will consider legislating to allow bars, late bars and night clubs to extend their opening hours; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [57088/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Programme for Government commits to updating our licensing laws. Other legislative projects, including work on intoxicating liquor legislation, will be taken forward in subsequent iterations of the legislative programme, to be determined by Government in due course

question: 2293. Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if there is an individual or team in his Department overseeing the implementation of Local Community Safety Partnerships; and if so, if contact details will be made available. [57141/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which I commenced in April 2025, provides for the establishment of Local Community Safety Partnerships (Safety Partnerships) within each local authority area. Safety Partnerships once established, are independent, community-led bodies mandated to design tailored safety plans based on local priorities. They make their own decisions as to their day-to-day activity, operating in accordance with Statutory Regulations and having regard to Guidance from the National Office for Community Safety. The National Office for Community Safety, an office of my Department, is providing support and guidance to Safety Partnerships in the performance of their functions. It is a statutory function of the National Office to commission research and evaluations relating to the operation of Safety Partnerships. The National Office will also monitor the implementation of local community safety plans once they have been developed. The National Office for Community Safety can be contacted directly by email at the following address: info@communitysafety.ie

question: 2294. Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the current status of the proposed transfer of responsibility for coroner fees to his Department; the timeframe within which the transfer is expected to be completed; the steps that remain outstanding before the transfer can take place; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [57175/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration In October 2024, Government approval was given to draft a general scheme of a Bill to significantly reform the Coroner Service. The proposed legislation to reform the Coroner Service will provide for a national coronial service to be centrally funded, thereby removing the responsibility for paying for coronial services outside of the Dublin area (which are already paid by my Department) from the local authorities. It will also provide for the establishment of full-time salaried coroners and discontinue the existing fee-based system. Officials in my Department are currently working on drafting Heads of Bill in this regard, with the intention of bringing it to Government in the coming months.

question: 2295. Deputy James Geoghegan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the total value of non-compliant public procurement identified within his Department and in bodies under the aegis of his Department in 2025 and to date in 2026; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [57211/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I can assure the Deputy that my Department is fully committed to the principles of openness, transparency and the accountability of public bodies. Public procurement is governed by EU and national rules and my Department ensures that appropriate procedures are followed for procurement activity. Departments are obliged to ensure that public procurement is discharged in line with the standard accounting and procurement rules and that contract prices represent best value for money. Public procurement practices are subject to audit and scrutiny under the Comptroller and Auditor General (Amendment) Act 1993. Procurement is also subject to internal audit within my Department. The Deputy will be aware that under Department of Finance Circular 40/02, my Department makes an annual return to the Comptroller and Auditor General (C&AG) in respect of contracts above the applicable threshold which are awarded without a competitive process. These are detailed in my Department's annual Appropriation Accounts as published by the C&AG, and is subject to scrutiny by the Public Accounts Committee. While details for 2026 are yet to be compiled, my Department’s 2025 submission is currently being audited and verified by C&AG and will be published in the usual way as part of my Department’s Appropriation Account. Information relating to bodies under the aegis of my Department that are not subject to the Department's direct reporting requirements can be found in the relevant annual reports of those bodies, or in the published Appropriation Accounts for the relevant Vote.

question: 2296. Deputy James Geoghegan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the usage of artificial intelligence within his Department; the categories of usage; the usage of artificial intelligence within any bodies under the aegis of his Department; the categories of usage; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [57229/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2296 and 2409 together. I can confirm that there are artificial intelligence (AI) tools currently in use within my Department, primarily in the area of immigration services. My Department’s Immigration Service Delivery operates a Digital Contact Centre, which includes an AI enabled smart assistant and chatbot powered by Microsoft Copilot. This system assists users in navigating publicly available immigration information, checking application status, and submitting queries. The chatbot is trained exclusively on information published on the Immigration Service Delivery website, operates within a secure authenticated portal, and does not process or make decisions based on personal data. More complex issues can be referred to staff at any stage. In addition, the Department uses ID Pal, which employs machine learning based identity verification to authenticate applicants’ identity documents when establishing a customer account within the same service portal. My Department complies with the Guidelines for the Responsible Use of AI in the Public Service issued by the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation, as well as guidance from the National Cyber Security Centre. My Department is fully committed to transparency, including informing users whenever they are interacting with an AI system and has put in place appropriate governance, risk assessment and oversight structures to support the responsible use of these technologies. My Department does not currently use generative artificial intelligence tools for issuing responses to parliamentary questions. My Department will continue to assess emerging digital tools, including AI, but any future adoption will remain subject to appropriate governance processes, including risk assessment and human oversight. With regards to the use of AI tools in agencies under the aegis of my Department, I am informed of the following. The Gambling Regulatory Authority of Ireland uses AI in its regulatory function, where it is integrated into case management and provides case summary features to trained GRAI staff in specific case categories. The GRAI leverage advanced AI and ML techniques in their security operations, where AI enabled tooling is deployed to support – real time security monitoring of internet facing systems. The GRAI have published a dedicated AI Usage Guideline, which is a practical, advisory guideline that tells GRAI staff how the organisation’s existing security and data protection rules apply when using approved AI tools. The Legal Aid Board is at an early stage in its engagement with AI tools. Current use is limited to low risk, internal support functions and is governed by the Board’s Artificial Intelligence Policy Framework. No AI tools are used in decision making, eligibility assessments, or the provision of legal advice or representation. All access to justice decisions remains the responsibility of appropriately qualified staff. The Parole Board use a Case Management System which has limited use of AI integrated into it. I am informed only the Operations Team have access to it. The Judicial Council and Policing and Community Safety Authority have access to Microsoft Co-pilot, which is utilised as a general-purpose AI tool to assist with non-automated administrative tasks under human oversight. This is part of a suite of Microsoft 365 products available alongside other MS software and tools. The Data Protection Commission is conducting a pilot project to explore the use of AI. This project is limited to a small set of users using only publicly available/non-sensitive data. While no AI tools are currently in use in An Garda Síochána, I am informed that work is underway to develop a strategy for the deployment of AI within the organisation and to establish robust governance structures in relation to the use of such emerging technologies. It has not been possible for Fiosrú or the Courts Service to gather the necessary information in the given timeframe. I will write to the Deputy directly upon receipt of the information.

question: 2297. Deputy Pádraig Rice asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will review the non-EEA family reunification policy for essential healthcare assistants and home care assistants employed under the general employment permit system; if he will consider a proposal (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [57389/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I can advise the Deputy that on 26 November 2025, I published the review of the non-EEA Family Reunification Policy (available at www.assets.gov.ie/static/documents/160c592a/Final_Report_on_the_Review_of_the_Non-EEA_Family_Reunification_Policy.pdf) which had remained largely unchanged since 2013, and sets out how Irish citizens and most non-EEA Irish residents may apply to bring non-EEA family members to live with them in Ireland. Further changes to the policy were made on 12 June 2026 based on commitments made in the review, including an annual review of financial thresholds to keep them in line with the cost of living, and to align with the new Statutory family reunification scheme under the International Protection Act 2026. The latest version of the policy document is available here: www.irishimmigration.ie/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Family-Reunification-Policy-12-June-2026.pdf Critical Skills Employment Permit (CSEP) holders are deliberately dealt with more favourably under the Policy. Occupations on the critical skills list are promoted for migration to the State, based on skills shortages, and so preferential conditions apply to attract those key skills. Immediate reunification with nuclear family members is one of those conditions, and this is in the context that CSEP roles are generally skilled professions with higher starting salaries and considerable room for salary growth and promotion so will generally not need to have recourse to social protection. One of the most complex issues regarding the review into Family Reunification Policy was the level of income thresholds required for family reunification with minor children, in particular for General Employment Permit (GEP) holders. A key principle of the Policy is that sponsors should be able to support family members who join them in Ireland without recourse to State supports which is why income thresholds have historically been based on eligibility for Working Family Payment. There was extensive stakeholder engagement during the review which focused on the situation regarding lower paid holders of GEPs, such as Health Care Assistants (HCAs). Following detailed consultation with other departments and civil society groups, the review concluded that the levels of income thresholds for lower paid sponsors should be considered in the context of the sustainability of wage growth, as opposed to lowering income thresholds below the level of eligibility for Working Family Payment. The review also reduced the effective waiting period from 24 months to 12 months for GEP holders by reducing the requirement to produce two years evidence of income. It concluded that any further reduction in the 12-month waiting period would slow the processing of applications by creating a surge.

question: 2298. Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of crime incidents recorded by An Garda Síochána in each Garda division, together with the rate per 10,000 population in each division, in each of the years 2021 to date in 2026, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [57394/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2298, 2299 and 2300 together. The Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration does not collate or publish crime statistics. That responsibility rests with the Central Statistics Office (CSO), established under the Statistics Act 1993. Under Section 13 of the Statistics Act 1993, the Central Statistics Office (CSO) is fully independent in its role of issuing statistics. Recorded crime statistics are published quarterly and are available from the CSO website at www.cso.ie/en/statistics/crimeandjustice/ The CSO also publishes detailed information at www.data.cso.ie. The report titled CJQ06: Recorded Crime Incidents provides the information requested by the Deputy by type of offence and by Garda Division.

question: 2301. Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the value of assets seized or frozen by the Criminal Assets Bureau arising from operations in each county or Garda division in each of the years 2021 to date in 2026, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [57397/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2170, 2171, 2194, 2283 and 2301 together. CAB is a multi-agency statutory body established under the Criminal Assets Bureau Act, 1996. I am advised that all monies seized by CAB are remitted to the Central Fund of the Exchequer after the appropriate statutory time frame under the Proceeds of Crime Acts. I was pleased to secure an 8.2% increase on the Criminal Assets Bureau budget allocation for 2026. The Bureau’s budget allocation in 2026 is €13.8m, of which €11.25m is for Pay and €2.55m is for Non-Pay. A 15% uplift on the Criminal Assets Bureau’s total budget would equate to €2.07m additional in funding. This would provide a total budget in 2027 totalling €15.15m. I am committed to ensuring that the Criminal Assets Bureau have the powers and resources to continue their important work. The Proceeds of Crime and Related Matters Bill is making its way through the Oireachtas currently. Once passed into law, the Criminal Assets Bureau will have stronger investigative powers and will be able to dispose of assets much more quickly than is currently the case. Figures relating to asset recovery under the Proceeds of Crime Acts by CAB are available publicly in Chapters 3 and 4 of the annual reports published on the Bureau's website: www.cab.ie/annual-reports/ . The Criminal Assets Bureau have advised that they do not collate statistics by County. Statistics for 2026 are not yet available and can not be provided at this point in time. The disbursement of monies collected by the Criminal Assets Bureau is controlled by the Central Exchequer. However, the Deputy may be interested to note that the Community Safety Fund re-directs a portion of the proceeds of crime, seized by the Criminal Assets Bureau (CAB) and An Garda Síochána, back into communities in order to fund innovative local projects aimed at building stronger, safer communities. In 2025, €4.4 million was allocated through the Community Safety Fund to 42 community safety projects nationwide. This represented a 33% increase on the €3 million awarded to 33 community safety projects in 2024. I secured a further increase in funding to €4.75 million for 2026, which is reflective of the continued success of An Garda Síochána and CAB. The Fund has supported 127 community safety projects to date all across Ireland. Putting this money back into the community is a tangible way of showing that there can be a direct link between the activities of law enforcement and building stronger, safer communities. The below table provides a breakdown of the number of projects funded by the Community Safety Fund since it launched in 2022. Year Number of Funded Projects 2022 22 2023 30 2024 33 2025 42 Total 127 In 2025, the Community Safety Fund was transferred to the newly established National Office for Community Safety. The National Office for Community Safety, an office of my Department, is a central coordinating body to the new whole of government, collaborative, problem-solving approach to community safety. The final elements of this new community safety infrastructure are being established including: • The establishment of all 36 Safety Partnerships. • The publishing of the National Strategy for Improving Community Safety The National Office is currently conducting a review of the current operating model and criteria for the Community Safety Fund to ensure that projects funded in the future are consistent with the National Strategy for Community Safety and support the work of Local Community Safety Partnerships.

question: 2303. Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide greater investment in An Garda Síochána in rural areas; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [57425/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Under the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, the Garda Commissioner is responsible for the distribution and stationing of Garda personnel throughout the State. While I have no direct role in decisions relating to the allocation of Garda resources in rural areas, I remain committed to supporting the Garda Commissioner in ensuring that Garda infrastructure and resourcing needs are kept under ongoing review. The Garda Commissioner and his senior management team keep the distribution of resources under ongoing review and I understand that, when allocating and transferring Garda members to and from any Division, including in rural divisions, consideration is given to commitments and undertakings outlined in the Annual Policing Plan. The Commissioner also takes the requirements of all Garda Divisions nationwide into account, which include: • Local and national crime trends and workloads; • Policing arrangements and operational strategies; • Minimum establishment statistics; • Local population and trends, geographical area and size; • Transfer applications, including welfare, personnel issues and concerns. As Minister, my priority is getting more Gardaí into all our communities by supporting increased recruitment and appropriate civilianisation where possible. A Garda budget of €2.74 billion in 2026 will fund the recruitment of up to 1,000 new Gardaí, 200 more Garda staff and additional members of the Garda Reserve. This Government is committed to building stronger, safer communities across the country. Rural crime covers a range of issues that cause concern for people living in rural communities, ranging from burglary and theft, to animal crime and road traffic offences. Rural safety and community safety is not about policing alone of course – it requires a multi-agency, multi-sectoral and a whole-of-Government response. The Rural Safety Plan 2025-2027 brings together and strengthens all of the various strands of work being carried out in relation to rural safety. It has been developed by my Department, in conjunction with the National Rural Safety Forum. The Plan’s vision is to ensure people and communities in rural Ireland feel safe and are safe in their homes, places of work, and their local environments. It does this by identifying four key priority areas that we will focus on to achieve the overall goal. These areas are: Community Safety & Engagement, Property Crime, Roads Policing, and Animal & Wildlife Crime. A number of Garda operations are already supporting the plan, such as Operations Thor and Táirige, which tackle burglaries and thefts from homes, and retail crime respectively. Operation Thor actively targets organised crime groups through coordinated crime prevention and enforcement activity based on intelligence and the latest burglary trends. ‘Lock Up Light Up’ is An Garda Síochána's anti-burglary awareness campaign which encourages homeowners to protect their property from would-be criminals. In the 10 years since Operation Thor began, burglary and related offences have declined overall. The level of residential burglaries during the winter months, October to March, has fallen by a remarkable 75% since it started in 2015. Under Operation Thor, the Garda National Drugs and Organised Crime Bureau co-ordinates and supports Divisional resources with intelligence led-interventions that target organised crime gangs and repeat offenders, particularly involved in rural burglaries and crimes. Gardaí conduct high-visibility patrols and check-points at specific times of day in known ‘hot-spots’ to reduce the movement of burglars, gathering intelligence on known offenders and regularly communicating with the public about crime prevention measures. An Garda Síochána also provide the public with information and guidance on steps that can be taken by home owners to secure property and deter crime in rural areas. Local Garda Crime Prevention Officers provide practical guidance to a range of people and businesses on deterring crime including burglary and theft.

question: 2304. Deputy Mark Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of youth diversion projects per county, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [57495/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration (Deputy Catherine Ardagh) I propose to take Questions Nos. 2304, 2305, 2306 and 2307 together. The Government’s focus on diversion and early interventions is a keystone in the Youth Justice Strategy 2021-2027. The strategy emphasises early intervention, prevention, family support and community engagement. It is aimed at promoting positive behavioural change and targeting this behaviour so that we can break the cycle of offending by young people. This Department has, in recent years, significantly increased the funding for youth justice initiatives; the budget allocation for Youth Justice measures has almost doubled from 2020 to 2026, and the total allocation for youth justice measures is now €43 million. With these funds, Youth Diversion Projects employ dedicated Youth Justice workers who respond daily to the needs of young people across the country; over 570 fulltime equivalent youth justice workers have been recruited in recent years. Every young person in Ireland now has access to a youth diversion service. The following table outlines investment in Youth Justice since 2021: - 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 2026 Youth Justice €21.48m €27.74m €30.24m €34.52m €40.52m €43.0m There are currently 92 Youth Diversion Projects and 4 Targeted Youth Diversion Projects. The programmes offered by these YDPs primarily provide young people between the ages of 12 and 17 years with suitable activities to facilitate their personal development, promote civic responsibility, encourage pro-social behaviour in their communities and improve their educational outcomes and long-term employability prospects. The estimated full-year cost of a new YDP, comprised of all the elements provided for under the Youth Justice Strategy 2021-2027 (12-17 intervention, Early Intervention, Family Support and Harder-to-Reach programmes) is €400,000. The minimum core ‘package’ for a YDP now includes two Youth Justice Workers, together with what may be appropriate in the specific locality: a family support youth justice worker, an early intervention youth justice worker, an outreach youth justice worker to engage with harder-to-reach young people, and a team leader where the number of other staff requires such a post. The Department funds these posts based on the needs, size and population base of each YDP catchment area, and as feasible given the per annum budget allocation. Therefore, the actual cost of establishing new YDP projects varies from €200,000 to €400,000. There may also be additional start-up costs in the first year, which also vary based on the particular needs of each YDP. The average annual cost of a Targeted YDP, which are projects that aim to address the needs of children who are hard to reach, engaged in serious and prolific offending, and may not be deemed suitable for engagement with a YDP, was €650,000 in 2026. Targeted YDPs require, on average, 50% more funding as compared to a standard YDP, due to their more intensive programmes and provision of wraparound supports. The government has fulfilled the the commitment in the Youth Justice Strategy to ensure the full availability of Youth Diversion Projects throughout the Irish State. Funding for Youth Diversion Projects in 2027 will be allocated through the normal budgetary cycle. The following table outlines the number of YDPs and TYDPs by county by county. Carlow 1 Cavan 1 Clare 2 Cork 9 Donegal 1 Dublin 30 Galway 3 Kerry 1 Kildare 4 Kilkenny 1 Laois 1 Limerick 5 Longford 1 Louth 4 Mayo 3 Meath 3 Monaghan 1 Offaly 3 Roscommon 1 Sligo/Leitrim 1 Tipperary 6 Waterford 5 Westmeath 2 Wexford 3 Wicklow 2 The location of 2 TYDPs are confidential to protect the young people engaged with the TYDPs which disrupt the grooming of children into network-related criminal activity by adults.

question: 2313. Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the average completion time for Garda vetting applications, by year for the past five years and year to date in 2026, in tabular form; the steps his Department is taking to speed up the vetting process; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [57568/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under Section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024. This includes all operational matters, such as Garda vetting applications which are an operational matter for the Garda National Vetting Bureau (GNVB) under the National Vetting Bureau (Children and Vulnerable Persons) Act 2012 (as amended). The primary purpose of vetting carried out by the GNVB is to ensure the safety of children and vulnerable adults. This requires a robust Garda vetting process that reassures the public, and in particular parents, that appropriate checks are conducted on people taking on positions of trust. An Garda Síochána have provided the following table which shows the average completion time for over 85% of Garda vetting applications received over the last six years: Year Average Number of working days 2020 6 2021 6 2022 7 2023 7 2024 7 2025 9 2026 16 The Garda Authorities have advised that vetting turnaround times have steadily increased since April 2025 as demand has continued to rise significantly, with 633,563 vetting applications processed in 2025. The GNVB remains focused on reducing turnaround times and is taking ongoing steps to bring performance back within the target range of five to ten working days. The Government is aware of ongoing concerns regarding certain aspects of the vetting process and I have listened carefully to the views of affected sectors. I believe that the vetting system should be updated to ensure that the burden of seeking vetting disclosures is minimised to the greatest extent possible, while maintaining the high standards that are necessary. In practice, and subject to a general requirement that vetting be renewed every three years, it is envisaged that this will mean that when a person is vetted for the work they will be or are likely to be involved in as part of their employment or volunteering within identified risk categories, the person would not be required to repeat the process if they were to move to another role within the same risk category. My Department is actively engaging with the Garda National Vetting Bureau on the detailed work of developing the necessary legislative and technical steps to meet these goals in a way that is workable in practice. This includes an assessment of appropriate models for an expansion of digital service delivery, which is a very significant project that will necessarily take time to fully scope and implement.

question: 2314. Deputy Seán Crowe asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the medical reasons in which an individual would not be transferred from an IPAS centre to an alternative location; and if this would include ongoing cancer treatment. [57572/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration IPAS Accommodation is provided for in EU regulations and transposed into Irish law. Accommodation provided by IPAS is by its nature temporary, and residents may be relocated from one centre to another during their time in IPAS accommodation, for a range of reasons. This might include centre changes or closures, health and wellbeing matters, or operational reasons to manage the overall capacity of the system. IPAS acknowledges that relocating can be very disruptive for people. Where it is necessary for IPAS to transfer people from their accommodation for operational or other reasons, every effort is made to enable people with particular special reception needs or vulnerabilities to remain in the local area to maintain their links with medical care, special education, or other services they are receiving. If this is not possible, IPAS works with the National Social Inclusion Office in HSE and Tusla Education Support Service colleagues to assist with transfer of medical services or education in the new area. Due to the high demand for accommodation, IPAS can only consider transfer requests for international protection applicants that involve a medical priority, or otherwise exceptional cases at this time. To submit a transfer request on medical grounds, individuals and families are required to submit a referral form in accordance with the IPAS Protocol for Medical Transfer Requests[ ] (www.assets.gov.ie/static/documents/7027f7e8/IPAS_Medical_Transfer_Request_2026.pdf). Where a person or family requests to transfer to a particular location or to remain in a particular location if a centre is closing, IPAS can only consider such requests in exceptional cases where there are serious medical needs such as major physical or intellectual disabilities, acute health conditions requiring ongoing specialised care in a specialist hospital (for example, active cancer treatment or dialysis). While IPAS teams recognise that people may be integrating into the community, attending education or working, given the limitations within our accommodation options, new accommodation or availability may not be available in the same area. It is important to note that the majority of special reception needs, medical needs and vulnerabilities can be addressed in all IPAS accommodation and in most locations nationally. In addition, most people seeking international protection are entitled to a medical card and their treatment is provided in the same manner as Irish residents or citizens, through publicly funded health and social care services provided by the HSE or by organisations funded by the HSE.

question: 2315. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the date on which his Department was first notified of the intended retirement of a Deputy Garda Commissioner; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [57575/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2315 and 2316 together. My Department was first informed on 21 July 2026 of Deputy Garda Commissioner Shawna Coxon’s intention to leave An Garda Síochána. She has informed myself and the Garda Commissioner that she will retire from the Service in November 2026, following 30 years of policing service in Ireland and Canada. I wish to acknowledge the work and commitment of Deputy Commissioner Coxon and thank her for her distinguished service during her tenure. Under section 27 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024 sets out the statutory framework for the appointment of a Deputy Garda Commissioner. Under this section, I am required to consult both the Board of An Garda Síochána and the Policing and Community Safety Authority. My officials have written to the Chairs of the Board and the Authority seeking their views on the selection criteria and recruitment process. Once these are considered and concluded, I will request that the Public Appointments Service conduct a competition. Additionally, section 27(6) of the Act provides that the consent of the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation is required regarding to terms and conditions attaching to the post. My officials have engaged with this Department in this regard. Following completion of these processes, the Public Appointments Service will recommend a suitable candidate for appointment.

question: 2318. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if his Department has assessed the effect of the Standard Fund Threshold on the retention of senior members of An Garda Síochána at Assistant Commissioner rank and above; if any such assessment has been shared with the Department of Finance; the date of any such correspondence; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [57578/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Standard Funds Threshold (SFT) is part of the tax system which applies to all pension products or schemes for all public and private sector workers. The tax liability is based on the value of the pension. The Minister for Finance announced an independent examination of the SFT in 2023. The examination concluded in summer 2024, and the report was published in September 2024. Following consideration of this examination, the Government agreed to implement changes to the SFT in a phased manner. Finance Act 2024 provided for phased increases to the SFT beginning in 2026 with the SFT reaching €2.8 million by 2029. From 2030 future increases will take account of increases in average earnings. In 2025 an inter-Departmental implementation group was established to consider and examine the remaining recommendations in the report. The group is chaired by the Department of Finance with representatives from Revenue, the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration, the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation, and the Department of Social Protection. The group has commenced its consideration of the recommendations and any proposed changes to the SFT regime arising from the work of the group will be for the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance to consider as part of the annual Budget and Finance Bill process. Since my appointment, I have engaged with the Minister for Finance who has confirmed that his Department arranged for the above-mentioned evaluation to be undertaken by the Society of Actuaries in Ireland. Any changes recommended by inter-Departmental implementation group will be for the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance to consider.

question: 2320. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of Garda members assigned to Presidency related duties in each Garda division; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [57582/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2292 and 2320 together. The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under Section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024 which includes the distribution and stationing of Garda personnel throughout the State. Since January 2024, An Garda Síochána has been actively preparing to meet the policing and security requirements associated with the Presidency of the EU. I am informed that a comprehensive command, control and coordination framework is in place to support the delivery of Presidency-related policing operations, together with all other major and significant policing operations and events, while ensuring the continued provision of effective day-to-day policing services. I am advised by An Garda Síochána that specific operational arrangements and the deployment of Garda resources associated with Operation Brehon remain confidential for operational and security reasons. I understand that a small number of Gardaí have been temporarily transferred to Dublin Castle to effectively support and implement a robust policing and security operation for the duration of the EU Presidency, however the attestation of over 1000 Gardaí since March 2025 will ensure that An Garda Síochána have the necessary resources to maintain policing services in divisions nationwide while also providing for the security needs of the Presidency. While certain events may necessitate the deployment of a greater number of Garda personnel than others, I am assured that sufficient Garda resources will remain available to ensure the continued delivery of effective and consistent Garda services throughout the Presidency period. Continuity of core policing services across all functional areas remains a key organisational priority. Resource requirements for Presidency events are subject to continuous assessment through established governance, planning and coordination processes. Every effort is made to ensure that the delivery of normal policing services is maintained in parallel with the operational demands associated with the Presidency programme. The protection of frontline policing services, community engagement, crime prevention activity and emergency response capability remains a core consideration in all operational planning associated with the Presidency.

question: 2322. Deputy Aindrias Moynihan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration when an application for naturalisation will be completed (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [57595/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice The naturalisation application referred to by the Deputy continues to be processed by my Department. This application is based on Section 16 'Irish Association', which can take longer to process than applications based upon residency. Section 15 of the Act sets out the statutory conditions that must be fulfilled for a certificate of naturalisation to be granted. Section 16 of the Act gives discretion to waive the statutory conditions (including the 5 year residency requirement) in certain circumstances. This includes where the applicant is a direct descendant of someone who is or was an Irish citizen (for example, a grandparent), has a family connection to an Irish citizen (including by blood, adoption, or civil partnership), or is related by affinity, meaning a close relationship through a spouse’s family. Last year my Department published new guidelines for applications on the basis of Irish Associations under Section 16(1)(a) of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956. They set out the factors that may be considered when deciding whether to waive the statutory conditions in certain circumstances, including where the applicant is of Irish descent or Irish associations. Details of the guidelines are available on my Department’s website at the following link: How to Become an Irish Citizen Guide - Immigration Service Delivery (www.irishimmigration.ie/how-to-become-an-irish-citizen-guide/) Applicants can now directly check the status of their immigration application on the Immigration Service’s Customer Service Portal. They can register for, or log in to their existing account, at: www.irishimmigration.ie As an Oireachtas member, you can also request the status of individual immigration cases by e-mail, using the Oireachtas Mail facility at: IMoireachtasmail@justice.ie, which has been specifically established for this purpose. This service enables up to date information on such cases to be obtained without the need to seek information by way of the Parliamentary Question process.

question: 2329. Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will advise whether his Department is currently drafting a new explosives bill or is considering amendments to the existing explosives legislation (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [57619/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The General Scheme of an Explosives Bill was approved by Government in 2008. The aim of the General Scheme was to repeal the Explosives Act 1875 and replace it with a modern statutory framework for the control of the manufacture, storage, importation, transport and supply of explosives. This Bill would also provide for the reloading of ammunition by competent persons who are firearms dealers or licensed firearms holders under strict licensing and regulatory conditions. As you are aware, current Government policy is that, as a general rule, the reloading of ammunition by private individuals is not permitted. However, in certain circumstances it can be permitted where it is part of an approved pilot project. In order to be considered for a pilot project, it is necessary to submit a business case to my Department. question: 2334. Deputy Gillian Toole asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the efforts being made to work with airlines, taxi and bus regulatory authorities here and in Northern Ireland, to share passenger information for arriving migrants, in order to properly plan for services across international protection, housing, healthcare, community policing and education and to arrange the timely return of those with no demonstrably valid reason to remain in either the Republic of Ireland or Northern Ireland. [57678/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Ireland and the United Kingdom have a shared responsibility and a shared interest in protecting the Common Travel Area (CTA). It offers great advantages to our people on a social and economic level. The invisible border on the island of Ireland is among the most tangible gains of the peace process and is essential to the continuing normalisation of relationships. For security reasons and to protect the integrity of the immigration system, both I and my Department do not comment on specific operational channels of communication with UK immigration authorities. However, I can advise the Deputy that there is extensive engagement and cooperation at all levels between my Department officials and their Home Office counterparts, as well as significant operational cooperation between the Gardaí, UK Border Force, UK policing services and the Police Service of Northern Ireland. This strong practical engagement and cooperation serves the mutual interests of both Ireland and the UK and will continue. At the UK Ireland Summit in March it was agreed that further steps would be taken to ensure that the CTA remains secure by working together to expand immigration data sharing arrangements, particularly in preventing abuse of CTA free movement by those not entitled to its benefits. In June, I discussed the importance of cross border cooperation in protecting the CTA for both Ireland and the UK by phone with the Northern Ireland Minister for Justice, Naomi Long and the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland, Hillary Benn. I also spoke with UK Home Secretary, Shabana Mahmood; we discussed the ongoing need for cross border cooperation and our shared focus on protecting the Common Travel Area. Furthermore, I intend to meet with the Home Secretary at the earliest opportunity to discuss relevant matters, including returns.

question: 2335. Deputy Fionntán Ó Súilleabháin asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the initial projected implementation cost of the EU Migration Pact between 2026 and 2030; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [57796/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration As the Deputy will be aware, the International Protection Act 2026 entered into effect on 12 June 2026 and gives effect to the EU Migration and Asylum Pact. Estimated expenditure associated with implementation of the Pact in 2026 is €19.3 million, comprising €4.44 million in pay costs and €14.86 million in non-pay costs. Expenditure requirements for 2027 and subsequent years have not been fixed and will be determined annually through the Estimates process. Future costs will depend on a range of factors, including application volumes, operational demands across the international protection system and ongoing implementation requirements. In advance of the Pact coming into effect, significant investment was made in the international protection system. This included additional staffing, digitisation initiatives and process re-engineering measures which have substantially increased processing capacity. The objective of these investments is to support a fair, sustainable and efficient asylum system, including faster processing of applications and increased operational efficiency. In the medium to long term, these improvements are expected to reduce the amount of time applicants spend within the system and thereby help contain accommodation and other associated costs. These costs are being partly offset through EU funding: Ireland has also secured significant European Union funding to support implementation of the Pact. Approximately €21.5 million has been allocated under the Asylum, Migration and Integration Fund (AMIF) Thematic Facility Specific Action, and a further approximately €8.9 million is expected to become available following the AMIF mid-term review. Separately from implementation and operational expenditure, Ireland – along with all Member States - is also required under the Asylum and Migration Management Regulation to participate in the annual solidarity mechanism, either accepting relocations of asylum applicants from other Member States or pledge contributions to the Annual Solidarity Pool according to their fair share, based on 50% share of population and 50% share of GDP. In the first Annual Migration Management Cycle, Ireland was deemed ‘At Risk of Migratory Pressure’ and will have priority access to an EU Migration Support Toolbox. As part of this cycle, Ireland will not be accepting relocations of asylum applicants due to pressures on our current system. Ireland will make an expected payment of up to €9.26 million in 2027 as a support to countries under the most extreme pressure.

question: 2336. Deputy Fionntán Ó Súilleabháin asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of additional staff recruited to implement the EU Migration pact; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [57797/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration As the Deputy will be aware, the International Protection Act 2026 gives effect to the EU Migration and Asylum Pact and came into effect on 12 June 2026. The Pact provides a fair, sustainable and efficient asylum procedure. This will be achieved through convergence in asylum practices across the EU including standardised processing times for decisions: six months for a standard procedure, three months for accelerated and border procedures and two months for processing applicants who have applied for protection elsewhere in Europe. Having a common system across the EU makes sure that all applicants are treated the same in every Member State with no incentive to move from one to another. If Ireland had not opted into the Pact, it is likely that we would face higher levels of secondary movement, slower processing and a less efficient returns system. This would result in applicants staying in the system for much longer, at much greater cost to the State, in terms of the provision of accommodation and other supports. There has been significant investment in staff across the entire international protection process in recent years and this has increased with the introduction of the Pact. As of 30 June 2026, the International Protection Office (IPO) has 624 staff, an increase of 200% since 2022. In addition, 158 case processing panel members are also contracted by the IPO. There has also been a substantial increase in resourcing to IPAT. Administrative staff at IPAT have increased from 37 at the start of 2023 to 86 currently. In addition, a part time Appeals Officers competition is in progress. The successful Appeals Officers from these competitions will be assigned to the new international protection appeals body, the Tribunal for Asylum and Returns Appeals (TARA) which was established on June 12. Some successful candidates may be assigned to the IPAT. There is currently sanction for the appointment of 30 whole time decision makers, combining whole-time members in the IPAT and whole-time appeals officers in TARA. With 6 whole-time IPAT members currently, the remaining 24 posts are intended to be filled from the competition that recently concluded. There is a sanction for the appointment of 200 part-time decision makers, combining part time IPAT members and part time appeals officers in TARA. With 134 part time members of IPAT currently, the remaining 66 posts are intended to be filled through the current competition. It should be noted that the International Protection Appeals Tribunal will continue in existence to process appeals relating to applications under the International Protection Act 2015. Additional staff have also been assigned to related functions within the Department's Immigration Service Delivery function that deal with deportations and accommodation of international protection applicants. While projections for future levels of international protections applications are uncertain and impacted by a range of factors, the introduction of the Pact is expected to better respond as previously described. Staffing levels will be kept under review having regard to trends in application numbers and requirements across the international protection process.
