question: 2339. Deputy Marian Harkin asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if there is a mechanism under Irish immigration law by which a non-EEA national resident in Ireland on a Stamp 1G dependant visa can be granted permission to commence trading. [57806/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice I propose to take Questions Nos. 2339, 2340 and 2341 together. Spouses, de facto partners or minor children of Critical Skills Employment Permit, General Employment Permit or Intra-Company Transfer Employment Permit holders, or researchers on a Hosting Agreement, are granted a Stamp 1G immigration permission upon satisfying the relevant criteria. Such holders of a Stamp 1G permission are permitted to work and undertake a course of study in the State, but are not permitted to establish or operate a business. Further information on the different stamp types is available on my Departments website at the following link: www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/information-on-registering/immigration-permission-stamps/ I can advise the Deputy that after five years on a Stamp 1G permission as a dependent, these individuals may be eligible for a Stamp 4 permission, which permits the holder to establish and operate a business in the State. It is also open to any person to apply for a change of immigration status if they meet the criteria for doing so. Detailed information on how to change an immigration status is available on my Departments Immigration Service website at www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/changing-your-immigration-permission/ .

question: 2345. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide totals paid out in expenses for solicitors on the free legal aid scheme, for each of the past ten years and to date in 2026; and to provide a breakdown of those expenses into categories of expenses as applicable such as travel expenses/mileage, subsistence and incidentals. [57847/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Under the Criminal Justice (Legal Aid) Act 1962, it is the Courts, through the judiciary, that are responsible for the granting of legal aid. My Department is responsible for the administration of and has budgetary responsibility for the Statutory Criminal Legal Aid Scheme. As outlined in the Programme for Government 2025, the Government has committed to reforming the operation of Criminal Legal Aid, and work is continuing on the drafting of the Criminal Justice (Legal Aid) Bill 2023. The General Scheme of the Bill was published in 2023, and its key purpose is to transfer the administration of and budgetary responsibility for the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme from the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to the Legal Aid Board in order to strengthen oversight and governance structures for the Scheme. Under the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme, claims for payment for expenses including and not limited to, mileage, travel, parking, accommodation and consultation fees are received from any number of individuals associated with a case including, solicitors, barristers, interpreters, translators and witnesses. Therefore, the information is not available in such a way as to provide a breakdown of particular expenses claimed by one type of profession only. However, I can inform the Deputy, that the table below sets out the total cost of expenses paid under the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme for the years inclusive 2016 to 2025 and up to 22 July 2026. 2016 1,065,128.56 2017 975,083.59 2018 1,124,405.80 2019 1,169,181.86 2020 1,159,237.12 2021 1,398,868.38 2022 1,493,955.73 2023 1,555,621.71 2024 1,541,777.04 2025 1,747,712.13 2026 626,419.31 * *up to 22 July 2026

question: 2346. Deputy Paula Butterly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the current status of the recommendation contained in the study on familicide and domestic and family violence death reviews to establish a statutory domestic and family violence death review system; whether a preferred governance model has been identified; the timeline for bringing legislative proposals before Government; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [57921/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2346, 2347, 2348, 2349, 2350, 2351, 2352, 2353, 2354 and 2355 together. The independent Study on Familicide and Domestic & Family Violence Deaths Reviews was published in 2023. While there are no plans at present to publish any further reports on it, my Department is advancing work aimed at better understanding and aiming to prevent instances of familicide. This includes progressing recommendations arising from the Study which were prioritised following a subsequent consultation process. These consultations involved three dedicated groups; a cross functional Interdepartmental Group, an Advisory Group of relevant NGOs, and a family consultation group made up of the bereaved families of victims of familicide and domestic homicide who shared their experiences of the criminal justice system. The group met monthly over a six-month period to review each strand of recommendations. On the basis of a paper summarising these consultations, I directed that work be prioritised in respect of three key areas identified for action by the consultation groups; guardianship rights, multi-agency coordination and response, and establishment of a mechanism for review of domestic homicides. Work on implementing these actions is progressing. The Guardianship of Infants and Child Care (Amendment) Act 2026 was signed into law by President Connolly on 21 July 2026 and will allow for the removal of guardianship rights of a person who has been convicted of killing the other parent of their child. The primary aim of the legislative changes under the Act is the promotion of child protection and welfare. The Court will be required to consider in these cases whether a revocation of guardianship would be in the best interests of the child. In relation to the Study’s recommendations for the establishment of Multi-Agency Critical Planning and Response (MACPAR) teams in each Garda region to support close family members of victims in the most competent, caring and efficient way, further scoping is being carried out in partnership with relevant stakeholders. The purpose of MACPAR teams will be to co-ordinate agency critical incident responses and develop protocols to ensure that there is a consistency in responses across the country following incidents of domestic homicide or familicide. My Department is also developing a Domestic Homicide Review model for Ireland as per the recommendations made in the Study. The purpose of these reviews is to identify the circumstances surrounding the death in the context of intimate partner violence, lessons to be learned, and to make recommendations to improve systemic responses to those in need or at risk, aiming to help prevent similar deaths in future. At present, officials in my Department are seeking to determine if legislation is required to support a review mechanism. It is anticipated that the scope of the Domestic Homicide Review process will include cases where children have died by or through the actions of a relative where the cause and context of the death appears to be as a result of violence, abuse or neglect, as well as cases where the death of a child has, or appears to have, resulted from violence by someone to whom the deceased was not related but which occurred during an incident of domestic or family violence. In this regard, my Department is liaising with DCDE, as lead Department for the Child Death Review process, given the potential similarities of the two mechanisms, both aimed at attempting to draw learnings on how state agencies have performed their functions, in the interests of developing effective law and policy to better protect children in the future.

question: 2349. Deputy Paula Butterly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether consideration has been given to commencing a pilot domestic and family violence death review process in advance of primary legislation; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [57924/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2346, 2347, 2348, 2349, 2350, 2351, 2352, 2353, 2354 and 2355 together. The independent Study on Familicide and Domestic & Family Violence Deaths Reviews was published in 2023. While there are no plans at present to publish any further reports on it, my Department is advancing work aimed at better understanding and aiming to prevent instances of familicide. This includes progressing recommendations arising from the Study which were prioritised following a subsequent consultation process. These consultations involved three dedicated groups; a cross functional Interdepartmental Group, an Advisory Group of relevant NGOs, and a family consultation group made up of the bereaved families of victims of familicide and domestic homicide who shared their experiences of the criminal justice system. The group met monthly over a six-month period to review each strand of recommendations. question: 2356. Deputy Mark Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the details of the number of reports to the Gardaí of incidences of spiking another person with a drug or substance without the persons knowledge, for each of the past three years; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [57952/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Spiking is a crime that preys on vulnerability, that undermines consent and that can have devastating consequences for victims. As Minister, I am committed to fostering a zero-tolerance approach to all forms of domestic, sexual and gender-based violence (DSGBV). Spiking a person’s drink or spiking someone by injection are, in effect, poisoning, which is a criminal offence under section 12 of the Non-Fatal Offences Against the Person Act 1997. The offence carries a maximum penalty of three years imprisonment. Section 12 applies to anyone who intentionally or recklessly administers a substance which is capable of interfering substantially with another person’s bodily functions, which explicitly includes inducing unconsciousness or sleep. Depending on the nature of the substance that is administered, it may be possible to charge a perpetrator with endangerment under Section 13 of the Non-Fatal Offences against the Person Act 1997. Section 13 provides that it is an offence to intentionally or recklessly engage in conduct which creates a substantial risk of death or serious harm to another. The offence of endangerment carries a maximum penalty of seven years imprisonment. Where the drugging took place for the purposes of committing a substantive offence, the perpetrator may also be charged with that substantive offence (e.g. such as rape or sexual assault, theft etc.), or where that offence was not completed, an attempt to commit a substantive offence. While a complex area of law, an attempt in general terms can be considered to be committed where a person takes sufficiently proximate steps towards the commission of the offence, with intent to complete the crime. I am advised by the Garda authorities that the following analysis of spiking incidents, published on garda.ie in May 2024, may be of assistance: www.garda.ie/en/about-us/publications/general-reports/spiking-incidents-may-2024.pdf. It contains an overview of spiking incidents between 2010 and 2023. Per the published data, the total count of spiking incidents reported in 2023 was 52. I am further advised by An Garda Síochána that the total count of spiking incidents reported in 2024 was 61 and in 2025 was 58. An Garda Síochána take all reports of spiking seriously and thoroughly investigate to determine the exact nature of each incident including results of toxicology reports in each case. I would advise any victim of any form of spiking to come forward and report to local Gardaí..

question: 2357. Deputy Paul McAuliffe asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will commit to implementing Ask 2 of a framework (details supplied) by ensuring that bereaved families in manslaughter cases are entitled to receive a written explanation of sentencing decisions upon request, as operates in other jurisdictions such as England and Wales; whether this could be achieved through amendment to the Victims Act 2017 or through a direction to the DPP; the timeline proposed for implementation; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [58013/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration It is important to emphasise that the conduct of any court case is a matter entirely for the presiding judge. The courts are, subject only to the Constitution and the law, independent in the exercise of their judicial functions, including sentencing. While Judges are not required by statute to provide reasons for their sentencing decisions, they are required to have regard to certain factors, and typically explain how they balance the gravity of the crime, aggravating factors, and mitigating personal circumstances in reaching their decision. The Criminal Justice (Victims of Crime) Act 2017, which transposed the EU Victims’ Rights Directive into Irish law, sets out a framework of rights and entitlements for victims. This includes access to information, support services, and protection measures. Section 8 of the Act relates to a victim’s right to receive information in relation to their case and primarily concerns information provided during the investigation and prosecution phases of the criminal justice process. The section also distinguishes between general information about rights and supports, and additional case-specific information which may be provided where requested by a victim. The relevant competent authority is responsible for providing such information, depending on the nature of the information sought. While the Courts Service is not one of the bodies that are obliged to provide information directly under the 2017 Act, victims can obtain information relating to the courts process and outcomes where appropriate from responsible agencies including An Garda Síochána or the Director of Public Prosecutions. Directive (EU) 2026/1472, which amends and updates the Victims’ Rights Directive, came into force in July 2026. Ireland actively engaged in negotiations on this Directive, aiming to ensure at EU level that supports for victims are further entrenched. Ireland will be obliged to transpose the new Directive into Irish law by 2 July 2028 for most of its provisions, aside from those relating to the use of information and communication technologies to support victims, which have a transposition date of 2 July 2030. Officials in my Department will, as a matter of standard practice, review our victims’ rights legislation and policies during the transposition process. As Minister, it is not open to me to comment or intervene in any way in relation to how particular court proceedings are conducted, or on the outcome of those proceedings. The Judicial Council was established in 2019 to promote judicial independence as well as to ensure public confidence in the administration of justice. The Council is an independent body whose members are all of the judges in Ireland. In January 2026, I secured cabinet approval for the drafting of a Judicial Council (Amendment Bill) and to publish the General Scheme. The General Scheme also provides for the Programme for Government commitment to empower the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to ask the Judicial Council to draw up sentencing guidelines, for a particular crime area, within a certain timeframe and requires the Council to comply with such a request. The proposed provisions will support the work already carried out by the Council in relation to sentencing and in particular the work of its Sentencing Guidelines and Information Committee.

question: 2358. Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he is aware of the proposed relocation of Ukrainian residents from accommodation (details supplied) to other areas; whether he will advise on the way in which vulnerable residents are being assessed before relocation; the criteria being used to determine whether proposed accommodation is suitable; and the way in which medical, disability, and accessibility needs are being considered. [58029/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The ending of the provision of commercial accommodation at Citywest Hotel follows a Government decision of 26 May 2026. This forms part of a wider phased withdrawal of state-contracted commercial accommodation for individuals granted Temporary Protection who arrived in Ireland prior to March 2024. This approach is consistent with the Council Recommendation adopted by the European Union encouraging EU Member States to support an orderly transition from Temporary Protection, while providing protection to those displaced by the conflict. Recognising that this is a significant change for residents, my Department, the Irish Red Cross (IRC) and the International Organisation for Migration (IOM) undertook dedicated engagement with those affected. Information and practical support regarding available options was made available to all residents. This included supports to facilitate independent living where appropriate. The IRC and the IOM are conducting a series of information sessions for people granted Temporary Protection living in state-contracted commercial accommodation. My Department recognises that there are those who have a continued requirement for state accommodation due to individual circumstances. For this reason, a self-declaration application process was made available to residents who believe they continue to require temporary accommodation following the ending of accommodation at Citywest hotel. As part of this process, people were asked to self-declare their need for continued state-supported accommodation detailing the reasons why they would like to continue to avail of accommodation and providing supporting evidence, including medical evidence for individuals with highly complex medical needs. The information provided in the applications, including any supporting medical documentation, will be considered during the assessment for ongoing accommodation. My Department will endeavour to ensure those who continue to require state-supported accommodation are accommodated within the same HSE Community Health Organisation Area, to ensure continuity of care. A portion of the Department’s contracted accommodation portfolio is being retained to provide further accommodation. The identification of properties to be retained takes into consideration, among other criteria, the availability and capacity of accessible rooms.

question: 2359. Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration his response to the findings of the study funded by his Department and published by an organisation (details supplied) in January 2026, which found that most people in Ireland substantially overestimate the scale of immigration and that these misperceptions are strongly associated with negative attitudes and increased vulnerability to misinformation; and the steps his Department is taking to ensure accurate public information on migration is available; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [58160/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The ESRI research, which was funded by my Department, provides valuable insights into public attitudes and perceptions of migration in Ireland. It highlights the importance of ensuring that public discussion is informed by reliable evidence and accurate information. My Department is committed to supporting evidence-informed policymaking and to making factual information on migration readily available. This includes the regular publication of official statistics, information on immigration and international protection services, and updates on policy developments through the Department's website and other official channels. The Department has also supported public information programmes on migration and integration, including a national digital, social media and community information campaign on migration in 2024, and in 2026, supporting a series of community engagement sessions in each Local Authority area to hear community stakeholders' and service providers' experience of migration and integration. These meetings are ongoing at this time. By making factual information publicly available, the Department aims to support informed public debate and improve understanding of Ireland's migration system. This work will also be supported by the forthcoming National Migration and Integration Strategy, which will provide a long-term framework to guide Ireland's approach to migration and integration, based on evidence, collaboration across Government and engagement with stakeholders.

question: 2360. Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to update the House on progress made in implementing the recommendations on the Domestic Homicide Reviews in the Study on Familicide and Domestic and Family Violence Deaths, July 2023; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [58232/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The independent Study on Familicide and Domestic & Family Violence Deaths Reviews was published in 2023. While there are no plans at present to publish any further reports on it, my Department is advancing work aimed at better understanding and aiming to prevent instances of familicide. This includes progressing recommendations arising from the Study which were prioritised following a subsequent consultation process. These consultations involved three dedicated groups; a cross functional Interdepartmental Group, an Advisory Group of relevant NGOs, and a family consultation group made up of the bereaved families of victims of familicide and domestic homicide who shared their experiences of the criminal justice system. The group met monthly over a six-month period to review each strand of recommendations. On the basis of a paper summarising these consultations, I directed that work be prioritised in respect of three key areas identified for action by the consultation groups; guardianship rights, multi-agency coordination and response, and establishment of a mechanism for review of domestic homicides. Work on implementing these actions is progressing. The Guardianship of Infants and Child Care (Amendment) Act 2026 was signed into law by President Connolly on 21 July 2026 and will allow for the removal of guardianship rights of a person who has been convicted of killing the other parent of their child. The primary aim of the legislative changes under the Act is the promotion of child protection and welfare. The Court will be required to consider in these cases whether a revocation of guardianship would be in the best interests of the child. In relation to the Study’s recommendations for the establishment of Multi-Agency Critical Planning and Response (MACPAR) teams in each Garda region to support close family members of victims in the most competent, caring and efficient way, further scoping is being carried out in partnership with relevant stakeholders. The purpose of MACPAR teams will be to co-ordinate agency critical incident responses and develop protocols to ensure that there is a consistency in responses across the country following incidents of domestic homicide or familicide. My Department is also developing a Domestic Homicide Review model for Ireland as per the recommendations made in the Study. The purpose of these reviews is to identify the circumstances surrounding the death in the context of intimate partner violence, lessons to be learned, and to make recommendations to improve systemic responses to those in need or at risk, aiming to help prevent similar deaths in future. At present, officials in my Department are seeking to determine if legislation is required to support a review mechanism. It is anticipated that the scope of the Domestic Homicide Review process will include cases where children have died by or through the actions of a relative where the cause and context of the death appears to be as a result of violence, abuse or neglect, as well as cases where the death of a child has, or appears to have, resulted from violence by someone to whom the deceased was not related but which occurred during an incident of domestic or family violence. In this regard, my Department is liaising with DCDE, as lead Department for the Child Death Review process, given the potential similarities of the two mechanisms, both aimed at attempting to draw learnings on how state agencies have performed their functions, in the interests of developing effective law and policy to better protect children in the future.

question: 2361. Deputy Brendan Smith asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the progress to date in the provision of a refuge centre in County Cavan for victims of domestic abuse; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [58235/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2361 and 2362 together. One domestic violence refuge in the Cavan-Monaghan region was agreed as a priority area for refuge development under Zero Tolerance. Cuan actively engaged with the all stakeholders including Safe Ireland, the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage, Cavan and Monaghan County Councils and the Housing Agency, to progress the development of a 12-unit refuge in this region, which will also include community-facing ancillary support services. The Capital Assistance Scheme (CAS) Stage 1 application for a refuge site in Monaghan was approved by the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage last October 2025. Work is ongoing towards submitting a Stage 2 application, which will include further detail and costings on the full extent of works that will be required. The CAS process takes an average 75 weeks with construction typically taking a further 15 to 18 months. Safe Ireland is the lead Approved Housing Body on this development. This new refuge facility will include 12 independent units of refuge accommodation, along with essential ancillary services, thereby strengthening domestic violence support in the region. The following developments have been progressed with the support of the Minister for Justice, DHLGH, the Housing Agency, local authorities and Safe Ireland. An interim refuge with 5 family units will open in Monaghan this year. Cavan County Council will allocate three units to deliver three Safe Homes in the county this year, which will be run by Safe Ireland. Monaghan County Council will allocate three units to deliver three Safe Homes in the county this year, which will be run by Safe Ireland. All key stakeholders are working together to ensure there is a substantial uplift in service across the Cavan-Monaghan region. Safe Ireland is working with the stakeholder group to create a solid infrastructure and a coherent connected response across both counties.

question: 2366. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of applicants for international protection who were recorded as being in employment in each year from 2020 to date in 2026; and if a regional breakdown can be provided. [58300/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2366, 2367, 2368 and 2370 together. It is a central priority for me that Ireland’s immigration system is robust and rules based. Labour market access permission for international protection applicants gives eligible applicants the opportunity to work and helps them to integrate into Irish society while providing for themselves and their families outside of the State’s directly provided services and supports. It also helps people to plan and prepare for their future in Ireland if they receive a positive decision on their application for international protection. Under the European Communities (Reception Conditions) Regulations 2018 (S.I. No. 230 of 2018), people are eligible to apply for labour market access permission if: * They are an international protection applicant; and * They have waited at least 5 months from their “Application Received” date for their first instance recommendation; and * They are cooperating with the international protection process – delays in receiving a recommendation must not be attributable to the applicant. Following that, a person may be issued a permission for labour market access if, at 6 months, they have not yet received a first instance recommendation. This permission is valid for 12 months and may be renewed until a final decision is made on the person's international protection application. The permission allows a person to access both employment and self-employment. They may work for most employers, however they are not permitted to be employed in the Defence Forces, An Garda Síochána, the Civil Service, the Public Service, or one of the other bodies listed in Schedule 6 of the European Communities (Reception Conditions) Regulations 2018. The granting of a labour market access permission does not necessarily confirm that the applicant has found employment. Statistics on the number of international protection applicants that have achieved employment are not available. My Department does not have information regarding the type of employment international protection applicants are engaged in. The table below shows the number of labour market access permission applications made and granted from 2020 to 28 July 2026. Applications made Applications granted 2020 6,284 5,721 2021 6,688 6,091 2022 7,511 6,732 2023 10,939 10,102 2024 18,868 17,004 2025 23,748 20,336 2026* 12,113 10,534 *to 23 July 2026.

question: 2369. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of employed applicants for international protection residing in IPAS accommodation who are required to make financial contributions towards their accommodation; the amounts collected in each year since introduction of the scheme; and the average contribution paid. [58303/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration People resident in IPAS Accommodation do not currently make a contribution toward the cost of their accommodation. In line with a Programme for Government commitment, a scheme for working international protection applicants to contribute to the cost of IPAS accommodation is in development and is expected to be in place during 2026. IPAS Accommodation is provided for in EU regulations and transposed into Irish law. Statutory Instrument No 230/2018, European Communities (Reception Conditions) Regulations 2018, provides that all international protection applicants are entitled to material reception conditions. The regulations further provide that where a resident is in receipt of an income above a certain level, they may be required to make a contribution to the cost of providing reception condition services. The contribution rates are set out in a schedule to the regulations and are proportionate to the amount that people earn, as set out below. Weekly Income € Potential Contribution € % of weekly income €97.01 - €150 €15 15.5 -10% €150.01 - €210 €35.70 23.8 – 17% €210.01 - €275 €59.50 28.3 - 21.6% €275.01 - €340 €83.30 30.3 - 24.5% €340.01 - €405 €119 35 - 29.4% €405.01 - €470 €154.70 38.2 – 33% €470.01 - €535 €178.50 38 – 33% €535.01 - €600 €202.30 38 – 34% €600.01 + €238 39.60% Implementation of the contribution to cost scheme is underway and includes the development of systems and resources to assess eligibility, share data securely and collect and process payments. The implementation process includes procurement of an appropriate third-party provider service, and will involve further detailed analysis as the scheme comes into operation including determining the implementation cost. The introduction of this contribution is aligned with processes already in place in other EU member states. The scheme will have a review and appeals process incorporated into the process and introduction of the contribution model is expected later this year.

question: 2374. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the total expenditure incurred by the Legal Aid Board on legal aid and legal advice provided to non-Irish nationals in each year from 2020 to date in 2026, by immigration, asylum, international protection, judicial review, family reunification, deportation and citizenship-related matters. [58311/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2374 to 2378, inclusive, together. The Legal Aid Board (LAB) is the statutory body responsible for the provision of civil legal aid and advice to persons of modest means in the State, in accordance with the provisions of the Civil Legal Aid Act 1995 and the Civil Legal Aid Regulations 1996 to 2021. Section 3(3) of the 1995 Act provides that the Board shall, subject to the provisions of the Act, be independent in the exercise of its functions. However, to be of assistance to the Deputy I have had enquiries made with the Legal Aid Board. The civil legal aid scheme has two parts: a legal advice element and a legal representation element. Eligibility for the scheme is determined by reference to a financial assessment and the merits of the case being taken. Details on nationality of those receiving legal aid are not collated in a manner that allows for the breakdowns requested by the Deputy. The Legal Aid Board has confirmed that it releases available nationality/country of origin information of international protection applicants in its annual reports, available on the Board's website at: www.legalaidboard.ie/about-the-legal-aid-board/organisational-governance-compliance/annual-reports-financial-statements/.

question: 2379. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the expenditure incurred by his Department, and the International Protection Appeals Tribunal, arising from cases involving non-Irish nationals in each year from 2020 to date in 2026. [58316/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration It is a central priority for me that Ireland’s immigration system is robust and rules-based. International Protection is granted to people who have come to Ireland to escape persecution in their own country or cannot return to their own country because of a well-founded fear for their safety. The International Protection Office (IPO) within the Immigration Service Delivery function of my Department is responsible for processing applications for international protection. Under the International Protection Act 2015, all IPO first instance decisions other than Refugee Status grants can be appealed to the International Protection Appeals Tribunal (IPAT). There has been a significant increase in investment into the international protection appeal's system over the last number of years which, combined with digitisation and process reengineering, has facilitated a major increase in processing capacity. The table below details expenditure per year from 2020 to end of June 2026 for the International Protection Appeals Tribunal. Year €'000 2020 3,305 2021 3,369 2022 3,255 2023 3,805 2024 5,810 2025 8,449 2026* 4,977 *to end of June As the Deputy will be aware, the International Protection Act 2026 gives effect to the EU Migration and Asylum Pact and came into effect on 12 June 2026. The Pact provides a fair, sustainable and efficient asylum procedure. This will be achieved through convergence in asylum practices across the EU including standardised processing times for decisions: six months for a standard procedure, three months for accelerated and border procedures and two months for processing applicants who have applied for protection elsewhere in Europe. Having a common system across the EU makes sure that all applicants are treated the same in every Member State with no incentive to move from one to another. If Ireland had not opted into the Pact, it is likely that we would face higher levels of secondary movement, slower processing and a less efficient returns system. This would result in applicants staying in the system for much longer, at much greater cost to the State, in terms of the provision of accommodation and other supports. Under the International Protection Act 2026 the new appeals body, the Tribunal for Asylum and Returns Appeals (TARA) determines appeals arising post 12 June 2026. The International Protection Appeals Tribunal will continue in existence to hear appeals relating to applications under the International Protection Act 2015. TARA was allocated a budget of €5.052m in the 2026 Revised Estimates Volume. In future years costs for TARA will be settled as part of the normal Estimates process. I can also inform the Deputy that expenditure for the Chief State Solicitor's Office and the Attorney General's Office does not fall within my remit.

question: 2381. Deputy Brian Brennan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the supports that will be in place for a Ukrainian citizen of pension age with no other means who cannot return to Ukraine when the ARP payment is reduced, putting them at risk of eviction; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [58324/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Accommodation Recognition Payment (ARP) was introduced to recognise the generosity of hosts who have opened their homes, whether in its entirety or a room, at their own expense to provide accommodation to temporary protection beneficiaries arriving in Ireland under the EU Temporary Protection Directive. The scheme's payment rate is not, nor has it ever been, linked to the actual cost incurred by the person providing the accommodation. It is a recognition of the valued contribution of those who host. The payment is not intended to substitute rent, nor is it available where a rental agreement is in place. It is also not aligned with market rental rates. ARP does not create a landlord and tenant relationship between the accommodation host who has qualified for the financial contribution and the Ukrainians living in the accommodation, and it does not provide an automatic right to tenancy. Hosting arrangements are considered a private matter between the host and the person living in the accommodation. People with Temporary Protection continue to have access to public services in accordance with the Temporary Protection Directive and Irish law, including access to healthcare and, where eligible, social protection supports such as rent supplement administered by the relevant Departments. Integration supports are provided by a number of stakeholders and supports will be further mobilised and coordinated to harness inputs and support the integration of people with Temporary Protection and to assist them in moving to independent living. Local Authorities coordinate the supports of wider agencies through their Community Integration Forums. Supports are provided by: • The HSE on health • Department of Social Protection on PPSN and Social Welfare supports • Intreo on employment supports and jobs advice • Department of Education, ETBs and Regional Education and Language Teams (REALTs) for schooling, youth services and English Language supports Further supports are also provided by the Irish Red Cross (IRC) and the International Organisation for Migration (IOM). A blended model of online and in-person engagement will be delivered by the IRC and IOM to inform people of policy changes and give guidance on options available to people. For more information on these supports please visit State-Contracted Commercial Accommodation (EN) Where hosting arrangements are ending, people with Temporary Protection are entitled to make their own private arrangements for accommodation through their own means, using supports provided by the Department of Social Protection, or by asking their Local Authority or Irish Red Cross for alternative accommodation offered by hosts. Those wishing to avail of hosted accommodation in any given area should contact the Local Authority in that area or the Irish Red Cross. The Irish Red Cross can be contacted by email at migrationcrisis@redcross.ie or by phoning 1800 753 343.

question: 2387. Deputy Fionntán Ó Súilleabháin asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration his views on whether, if Ireland wants a sustainable immigration system that retains public confidence, policymakers must be prepared to have an honest conversation about immigration, integration, and citizenship; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [58345/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2389, 2124, 2125, 2126, 2387, 2388, 2390, 2391, 2395, 2396 and 2397 together. The granting of Irish citizenship through naturalisation is governed by the provisions of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956, as amended. All applications for a certificate of naturalisation are processed and assessed individually in accordance with the provisions of the Act, including the requirement that applicants satisfy the good character criterion under Section 15. As part of a naturalisation application, each applicant is required to detail any offences, regardless of where an incident occurred, or how long ago, including “spent” convictions. All adult applicants must also undertake Garda vetting. As part of the good character assessment, An Garda Síochána is requested to make enquiries into the applicant’s background, the detail and extent of which is a matter for An Garda Síochána. Last November I secured Government approval to introduce new policies and legislative changes to strengthen Ireland’s migration and asylum system to ensure it is rules-based, efficient and more aligned with EU Member States. As part of this my Department is reviewing aspects of Ireland’s citizenship legislation and developing proposed amendments. This includes examining the possibility of language and civics testing as a requirement for naturalisation and reviewing research in this area that the Department commissioned from the Economic and Social Research Institute. My Department is committed to supporting evidence-informed policymaking. My Department has also supported public information programmes on migration and integration, including a national digital, social media and community information campaign on migration in 2024, and in 2026, supporting a series of community engagement sessions in each Local Authority area to hear community stakeholders' and service providers' experience of migration and integration. These meetings are ongoing at this time. This work will also be supported by the forthcoming National Migration and Integration Strategy, which will provide a long-term framework to guide Ireland's approach to migration and integration, based on evidence, collaboration across Government, and engagement with stakeholders. To that end, a Strategic Migration Policy Group (SMPG) was established in December 2024 to support that work which now consists of ten Government Departments, meeting at senior official level. The key objective of the Strategy and the SMPG is to develop a whole-of-government approach to migration policy that is coherent across Departments and responsive in seeking to address Ireland’s current and future demographic, economic and social policy needs.

question: 2392. Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether a deportation order was made, considered, or in force in respect of a person (details supplied); if not, the reason no deportation order was put in place following that conviction or prior to his release from prison in January 2024; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [58410/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration As Minister, I do not comment on individual cases. In general, I can say that the removal of people who are involved in criminality and those who are a danger to society is a priority for me as Minister and my Department works closely with An Garda Síochána and the Irish Prison Service to ensure high risk persons are prioritised for removal from the State.

question: 2393. Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of foreign nationals convicted of serious sexual offences in each of the last five years; the number of those with such convictions in respect of whom deportation orders were made; the number removed from the State, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [58411/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The removal of people who are involved in criminality and those who are a danger to society is a priority for me as Minister and my Department works closely with An Garda Síochána and the Irish Prison Service to ensure high risk persons are prioritised for removal from Ireland. Under the European Communities (Free Movement of Persons) Regulations 2015, which transposes the Free Movement Directive (Directive 2004/38/EC) into Irish law, orders can be made for both the removal and exclusion of citizens of the European Union, European Economic Area and Switzerland who represent a danger to public policy or public security. These orders can be made on the grounds of that the individual’s personal conduct represents a genuine, present and sufficiently serious threat affecting one of the fundamental interests of society. These orders, and their legal basis, are distinct from deportation orders which are legal orders to leave the State and remain outside of it, apply in respect of non-EEA nationals only. Under Section 3 of the Immigration 1999, as amended, a Deportation Order may be issued on a number of grounds, including: • under Section 3(2)(a,) a person who has served or is serving a term of imprisonment imposed on him or her by a court in the State, • under Section 3(2)(b), a person whose deportation has been recommended by a court in the State before which such person was indicted for or charged with any crime or offence, • under Section 3(2)(i), a person whose deportation would, in the opinion of the Minister, be conducive to the common good. I can advise that the total number of people removed from the State due to criminality from 2021, up to 24 July 2026, is detailed in the table below. 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 2026 (up to 24 July) Deportations 5 13 15 23 76 58 EU Removals 42 37 21 18 56 100 Total 47 50 36 41 132 158 *Please note, figures are correct at time of issue, however, all statistics may be subject to data cleansing. It is not possible to provide a breakdown of the type of convictions for people removed from the State. As the Deputy may be aware, An Garda Siochana commenced Operation Moonridge in 2025 which is an operation focusing on the removal of convicted sex offenders, including by means of EU removal orders. The detailed management of this activity is a operational matter for the Garda authorities and I have been informed that 25 people were removed under the operation in 2025, with 42 removed so far this year.

question: 2394. Deputy James Geoghegan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the total number of persons who were deported on commercial flights in 2024, 2025, to date in 2026; the total costs associated with these deportations for each of the years and time periods specified; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [58425/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2227, 2228, 2394 and 2404 together. It is a central priority for me that Ireland’s immigration system is robust and rules based. The enforcement aspects of our laws, including deportation orders, are an essential requirement for the system to work effectively and to ensure that there is confidence in the application of our legislation in this area. Deportations are costly and complex to enforce. It is the preferred option to return people voluntarily and my Department has a voluntary return programme to assist people to return prior to the issuance of a deportation order. A person can only avail of voluntary return before a deportation order is issued and I have increased resources into this programme to enable individuals who wish to return before a deportation order is issued to them. If a person does not remove themselves from the State following the issuance of a deportation order, they will be removed, and my Department has taken action to significantly improve immigration enforcement measures and increase removals. In 2024, 1,122 people departed from the State under various mechanisms (i.e. enforced deportation, voluntary return etc.). In 2025, 2,111 people had their departure confirmed through these pathways, an increase of 88% compared to 2024. Up to 24 July 2026, 1,294 people have departed the State through these pathways. question: 2395. Deputy Fionntán Ó Súilleabháin asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the reason Ireland is the only European Union member state that does not require applicants for naturalised citizenship to demonstrate language proficiency or undergo a civics examination before becoming citizens; if he will consider such proposals; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [58430/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2389, 2124, 2125, 2126, 2387, 2388, 2390, 2391, 2395, 2396 and 2397 together. The granting of Irish citizenship through naturalisation is governed by the provisions of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956, as amended. All applications for a certificate of naturalisation are processed and assessed individually in accordance with the provisions of the Act, including the requirement that applicants satisfy the good character criterion under Section 15. As part of a naturalisation application, each applicant is required to detail any offences, regardless of where an incident occurred, or how long ago, including “spent” convictions. All adult applicants must also undertake Garda vetting. As part of the good character assessment, An Garda Síochána is requested to make enquiries into the applicant’s background, the detail and extent of which is a matter for An Garda Síochána. Last November I secured Government approval to introduce new policies and legislative changes to strengthen Ireland’s migration and asylum system to ensure it is rules-based, efficient and more aligned with EU Member States. As part of this my Department is reviewing aspects of Ireland’s citizenship legislation and developing proposed amendments. This includes examining the possibility of language and civics testing as a requirement for naturalisation and reviewing research in this area that the Department commissioned from the Economic and Social Research Institute. My Department is committed to supporting evidence-informed policymaking. My Department has also supported public information programmes on migration and integration, including a national digital, social media and community information campaign on migration in 2024, and in 2026, supporting a series of community engagement sessions in each Local Authority area to hear community stakeholders' and service providers' experience of migration and integration. These meetings are ongoing at this time. This work will also be supported by the forthcoming National Migration and Integration Strategy, which will provide a long-term framework to guide Ireland's approach to migration and integration, based on evidence, collaboration across Government, and engagement with stakeholders. To that end, a Strategic Migration Policy Group (SMPG) was established in December 2024 to support that work which now consists of ten Government Departments, meeting at senior official level. The key objective of the Strategy and the SMPG is to develop a whole-of-government approach to migration policy that is coherent across Departments and responsive in seeking to address Ireland’s current and future demographic, economic and social policy needs.

question: 2400. Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of outstanding IRP applications on 20 July 2026; the additional resources being allocated to clear the backlog; when he expects the backlog to be cleared; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [58465/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2447, 2152, 2162 and 2400 together. The Registration Office of my Department continues to experience an exceptionally high demand for first time registration appointments and immigration permission renewal applications. I understand that the extended wait times can be frustrating for applicants, and I can assure the Deputy that my Department is utilising every avenue available to facilitate as many applicants as quickly as possible and to increase processing capacity. The Registration Office is open seven days a week to facilitate customers to process both first time registration appointments and online renewals, with significant additional staff assigned to this work. This is having an impact and wait times are reducing, and I expect times to reduce further over the summer months. In the meantime, I can advise the Deputy that I recently published an updated interim employer notice and a notice to facilitate customers travelling during the summer months to alleviate pressure on applicants while the Department continues to reduce the wait times. Where an employee’s Irish Residence Permit (IRP) card has expired and they are unable to obtain a new one by the expiry date of their current IRP card, they are still permitted to work and to remain in the State until 31 August 2026. This applies to all expired IRP cards regardless of the number of weeks elapsed, but is subject to the applicant submitting their renewal application prior to their current IRP card expiring. Further information on this notice can be found at the following www.irishimmigration.ie/minster-announces-interim-notice-to-employers-regarding-renewal-of-registration/ It is important to note that the existing www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/how-to-renew-your-current-permission/notice-to-employers/.will continue to apply after 31 August 2026. Furthermore, the previous travel arrangements made for people awaiting a renewal of their IRP card who intend to travel has been reinstated until 31 August 2026. People may use their recently expired IRP card to travel until the end of August 2026, provided an application to renew their registration permission was submitted in advance of the expiry date of their IRP Card. Further information can be found on the ISD website at the following www.irishimmigration.ie/minster-announces-interim-notice-to-employers-regarding-renewal-of-registration/. While the Registration Office endeavours to process applications as quickly as possible, processing times for each stamp category may vary due to a number of factors, such as the number of applications on hand, individual circumstances, the complexity of applications, whether further information is required, and peak application periods. The objective is to reducing the timelines across all categories to more sustainable levels. The Registration Office provide a live application processing date broken down by stamp category, which is updated every Monday, and is available at the following link: www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/how-to-renew-your-current-permission/renewing-your-registration-permission-if-you-live-in-the-republic-of-ireland/. Applicants can now directly check the status of their immigration application on the Immigration Service’s Customer Service Portal. They can register for, or log in to their existing account, at www.portal.irishimmigration.ie/en/. It is also open to any person to request to have their renewal application expedited due to extenuating circumstances, and they can do so by contacting the Registration team of the Department via the Customer Service Portal. They will need to explain their circumstances and the urgent need to travel. All such requests are considered on a case by case basis. I can advise that as of 27 July 2026, there are approximately 59,000 renewal applications awaiting examination. The information requested on the number of Stamp 4 renewal applications submitted within 16 weeks that are yet to be processed is not readily available.

question: 2405. Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the average processing time of applications and appeals for international protection, by quarter in each of the years 2020 to date in 2026, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [58582/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration My Department takes all necessary steps to manage the international protection process efficiently and effectively, while ensuring the integrity of those processes is maintained at all times. There has been a significant increase in investment into the international protection system over the last number of years which, combined with digitisation and process reengineering, has facilitated a major increase in processing capacity and demonstrates a strong commitment to reducing cases on hand. In 2025, the International Protection Office (IPO) delivered over 20,200 first decisions compared to approximately 14,100 in 2024, a 44% increase. The International Protection Appeals Tribunal (IPAT) more than doubled the number of appeals closed from 3,100 in 2024 to nearly 6,300 in 2025. This year as of 19th July, IPAT has already closed 5,218 appeals and is on track to significantly exceed the number of appeals closed in 2025. answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration My Department is committed to playing its part in delivering a successful Irish Presidency of the Council of the European Union, which began on 01 July. This will continue to be a significant undertaking for Ireland over the remaining months of our Presidency. Under the estimates process for Budget 2026, my Department was allocated €5 million in respect of Presidency related costs. Of this, approximately €3.6m has been allocated to cover staffing costs, including in relation to an increased number of personnel seconded to the Permanent Representation of Ireland to the European Union for 2026. The remaining €1.4m is allocated to cover the cost of the hosting of Presidency specific events in Ireland and Brussels, as well as additional travel and related costs for officials travelling to Brussels to attend and chair meetings. During Presidency meetings in the host country, it is customary for a memento to be presented to Heads of Delegations. At the recent informal meeting of Justice and Home Affairs Ministers in Dublin Castle, I presented my EU counterparts with honey harvested from the beehives located on the roof of my Department, accompanied by a sample of local craft whiskey, glassware and a handcrafted enamel gift - the value of these gifts was €71. Other delegates were given the centrally sourced Presidency branded stationery which were procured by the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade. In relation to events, my Department will host a number of official level meetings in Ireland during our Presidency and more information on these events can be found here - irish-presidency.consilium.europa.eu/en/events/. At the majority of these meetings, delegates will be presented with the centrally sourced branded Presidency stationery referred to above. We will also host an informal meeting of Schengen Senior Officials, and a meeting of the European Union Administrative Approach, in the Irish College in Leuven.

question: 2409. Deputy John Brady asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide an overview of the AI policy in place within his Department; if AI has been incorporated into any work streams; if AI is ever used in reply to parliamentary questions; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [58665/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2296 and 2409 together. I can confirm that there are artificial intelligence (AI) tools currently in use within my Department, primarily in the area of immigration services. My Department’s Immigration Service Delivery operates a Digital Contact Centre, which includes an AI enabled smart assistant and chatbot powered by Microsoft Copilot. This system assists users in navigating publicly available immigration information, checking application status, and submitting queries. The chatbot is trained exclusively on information published on the Immigration Service Delivery website, operates within a secure authenticated portal, and does not process or make decisions based on personal data. More complex issues can be referred to staff at any stage. In addition, the Department uses ID Pal, which employs machine learning based identity verification to authenticate applicants’ identity documents when establishing a customer account within the same service portal. My Department complies with the Guidelines for the Responsible Use of AI in the Public Service issued by the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation, as well as guidance from the National Cyber Security Centre. My Department is fully committed to transparency, including informing users whenever they are interacting with an AI system and has put in place appropriate governance, risk assessment and oversight structures to support the responsible use of these technologies. My Department does not currently use generative artificial intelligence tools for issuing responses to parliamentary questions. My Department will continue to assess emerging digital tools, including AI, but any future adoption will remain subject to appropriate governance processes, including risk assessment and human oversight. With regards to the use of AI tools in agencies under the aegis of my Department, I am informed of the following. The Gambling Regulatory Authority of Ireland uses AI in its regulatory function, where it is integrated into case management and provides case summary features to trained GRAI staff in specific case categories. The GRAI leverage advanced AI and ML techniques in their security operations, where AI enabled tooling is deployed to support – real time security monitoring of internet facing systems. The GRAI have published a dedicated AI Usage Guideline, which is a practical, advisory guideline that tells GRAI staff how the organisation’s existing security and data protection rules apply when using approved AI tools. The Legal Aid Board is at an early stage in its engagement with AI tools. Current use is limited to low risk, internal support functions and is governed by the Board’s Artificial Intelligence Policy Framework. No AI tools are used in decision making, eligibility assessments, or the provision of legal advice or representation. All access to justice decisions remains the responsibility of appropriately qualified staff. The Parole Board use a Case Management System which has limited use of AI integrated into it. I am informed only the Operations Team have access to it. The Judicial Council and Policing and Community Safety Authority have access to Microsoft Co-pilot, which is utilised as a general-purpose AI tool to assist with non-automated administrative tasks under human oversight. This is part of a suite of Microsoft 365 products available alongside other MS software and tools. The Data Protection Commission is conducting a pilot project to explore the use of AI. This project is limited to a small set of users using only publicly available/non-sensitive data. While no AI tools are currently in use in An Garda Síochána, I am informed that work is underway to develop a strategy for the deployment of AI within the organisation and to establish robust governance structures in relation to the use of such emerging technologies. It has not been possible for Fiosrú or the Courts Service to gather the necessary information in the given timeframe. I will write to the Deputy directly upon receipt of the information.

question: 2413. Deputy Gary Gannon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether officials within his Department have undertaken research, prepared briefing papers, attended meetings with the European Commission or other member states, or received legal advice regarding the possible establishment or use of asylum return hubs outside the European Union; and if he will provide details of such work undertaken since 1 January 2025. [58725/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Returns Regulation will establish a Common European system for returns, with simpler, swifter and more effective returns procedures across the EU, and contains provisions relating to the establishment of return hubs. Following the publication of the regulation in March 2025 national experts attended EU Working Party meetings, where a detailed examination of the legislative text was conducted and agreement on a compromise text was reached by Member States. Article 17 of the Regulation provides for the legal possibility to establish return hubs in third countries. Under this provision, people who have received deportation orders and have no legal right to remain within the Member State may be returned to a third country with which there is a bilateral agreement or arrangement, provided certain conditions are met, including in particular the respect of international human rights standards and principles in accordance with international law. It should be noted that the establishment of return hubs under the regulation is not mandatory and that it will be up to individual Member States to determine whether they will seek to establish such an arrangement with a third country. Ireland has shown its commitment to a common EU-wide solution to migration through opting in to the Pact. Harmonisation in the area of returns is equally important and it is the Government’s preference that Ireland would participate in the Returns Regulation. Ireland considers that any proposed use of returns hubs must be sustainable, cost-effective and carried out in accordance with fundamental rights. A decision was taken to change the legal basis of the Regulation, meaning that it now forms part of the Schengen Acquis. Consideration of Ireland’s participation in the measure by way of an opt-in under Protocol 19 TFEU is ongoing and any such opt-in will be subject to approval by the Houses of the Oireachtas.

question: 2414. Deputy Gary Gannon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the average processing time for first-instance international protection decisions and subsequent appeals during each month since January 2025; the number of cases currently awaiting a first decision and appeal; and how many cases exceed the 12-week timeframe envisaged under the new EU asylum rules. [58726/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration My Department takes all necessary steps to manage the international protection process efficiently and effectively, while ensuring the integrity of those processes is maintained at all times. There has been a significant increase in investment into the international protection system over the last number of years which, combined with digitisation and process reengineering, has facilitated a major increase in processing capacity and demonstrates a strong commitment to reducing cases on hand. In 2025, the International Protection Office (IPO) delivered over 20,200 first decisions compared to approximately 14,100 in 2024, a 44% increase. The International Protection Appeals Tribunal (IPAT) more than doubled the number of appeals closed from 3,100 in 2024 to nearly 6,300 in 2025. This year as of 19th July, IPAT has already closed 5,218 appeals and is on track to significantly exceed the number of appeals closed in 2025. To date in 2026 the median processing time for IPO first instance decisions is 12 months (accelerated cases are processed in 3 months, while standard cases are processed in 16 months). The median processing time for International Protection appeals is 13.3 months. The median processing time under the accelerated procedure is 6.9 months and 16.5 months for all other appeals. The requested data in relation to median processing times of international protection and appeals decisions is outlined in the tables below. Table 1. Median processing time in months for first instance international protection decisions from 2025 to 2026 (up to 31/05). Currently, there are 11,259 international protection applicants awaiting a first instance decision from the IPO under the International Protection Act 2015. There are 20,772 number of appeals pending with the IPAT under the International Protection Act 2015. As the Deputy will be aware, the International Protection Act 2026 entered into effect on 12 June 2026 and gives effect to the EU Migration and Asylum Pact. The Pact will provide a fair, sustainable and efficient asylum procedure. This will be achieved through convergence in asylum practices across the EU including standardised processing times for decisions: six months for a standard procedure, three months for accelerated and border procedures and two months for processing applicants who have applied for protection elsewhere in Europe. While the new system has only been in place for over a month, it is running and in operation as intended. The Department engaged in significant amounts of preparation prior to commencement, particularly around staffing and processes, to ensure readiness for new timelines required under the Pact. 940 applications have been lodged since 12 June under the new International Protection Act 2026 and these are being processed in accordance with the requirements of the 2026 Act. There are no appeals currently pending with the Tribunal for Asylum and Returns Appeals (TARA) as of COB 19 July 2026.

question: 2416. Deputy Gary Gannon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of persons currently held on remand who are awaiting a psychiatric assessment, transfer to a hospital (details supplied) or another appropriate mental health facility, or access to addiction treatment services; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [58730/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Irish Prison Service does not hold data in relation to diversion waiting lists for those admitted to custody on remand and has no role in the Courts’ decisions to admit those with mental health or addiction needs into prison. In-reach mental health services are provided by the HSE’s National Forensic Mental Health Service. This involves the provision of weekly forensic mental health sessions led by consultant forensic psychiatrists, supported by non-consultant hospital doctors, community psychiatric nurses, and social workers. These HSE Psychiatric teams manage and control the waiting lists for admission to the Central Mental Hospital. The National Forensic Mental Health Service (NFMHS) provides the Irish Prison Service with data on their waiting list for access to the Central Mental Hospital (CMH) at Portance and as of the 20th July 2026 the number of prisoners in custody on the CMH waiting list was 33. The Irish Prison Service engages Merchants Quay Ireland (MQI) to provide a prison-based addiction counselling service across the entire Irish Prison Service estate (with the exception of Arbour Hill Prison and the Training Unit where the clinical need is currently under review). Merchants Quay Ireland (MQI) provides data in relation to waiting lists for Addiction Services and the waiting list was 1,302 at the end of May for the full prison estate.

question: 2420. Deputy John Brady asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide an update on the transfer of River Lodge, Newtownmountkennedy from his Department to the HSE; the timeline for the site to be returned to the HSE; the plans for future use of the site; the costs associated with the site since 2024; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [58737/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration River Lodge, Newtownmountkennedy, was offered to IPAS by the HSE in February 2024 and was used to provide tented emergency accommodation during a time of increased pressure on the international protection system. Accommodation was provided from early May to December 2024. The site provided tented accommodation with capacity for 96 residents. Due to severe weather conditions in December 2024, residents had to be moved from the site to alternative accommodation. A process to explore alternative development options to potentially repurpose River Lodge for other forms of accommodation was carried out. Following technical and financial assessments - particularly in relation to wastewater treatment infrastructure - it was deemed not possible to move forward with such proposals. It has been agreed with the HSE that the site will be returned to them, bringing the licensed use of this site for IPAS accommodation to a conclusion. Some minor works are required on site as part of the return process and the Department has now agreed the scope of this work with the HSE. It is intended that the site will be returned to the HSE as soon as possible pending these works being completed, and while a specific date for this return has not yet been finalised, this will be progressed as a soon as is practicable. The future use of the site after its return will be a matter for the HSE. Costs of the site 2024-2026 are provided below, including costs of establishing the site, utilities and services, accommodation costs, and security. The Department is maintaining security on the site while the transfer to the HSE is completed. In February 2026, the Department undertook a review of security services at River Lodge. Following appraisal, efficiencies were identified which resulted in cost savings at the site. Reference 2024 incl. VAT 2025 incl. VAT 2026 incl. question: 2422. Deputy John Brady asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide an update on ongoing litigation cases between his Department and accommodation providers for asylum seekers; the liabilities the State could face; the contingencies in place; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [58739/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The State is currently accommodating international protection applicants in over 300 accommodation centres around the country. A small number of accommodation providers, or potential providers, initiated High Court proceedings against the Minister between 2025 and 2026. Five such proceedings have been initiated where the Department had received an offer of international protection accommodation, had entered into a pre-contract arrangement, and subsequently made the decision not to proceed with those accommodation contracts. Three of these cases have now been settled and closed. Two sets of proceedings remain before the Courts. One additional set of proceedings has been initiated by an accommodation provider, where no contractual arrangements were in place, and this matter also remains before the Courts. Given that some of these matters remain before the courts, disclosing details of financial settlement amounts or other information, in respect of any case, may have the potential to limit the State in completing its defence of such claims, or in negotiations associated with these actions. In respect of potential liabilities, all expenditure by the Department will form part of the 2026 Appropriation Account and will be subject to review by the Comptroller and Auditor General in the usual manner. The existence of these cases has also been noted in the 2025 Appropriation Account which has been submitted to the C&AG.
