question: 54. Deputy Catherine Callaghan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for an update on the work being undertaken to establish a National Security Agency that can provide high-level vetting and security clearance services, amongst other functions; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [49367/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Programme for Government includes a commitment to bring the National Security Authority (NSA) under the remit of my Department. Work is well underway in my Department to design a new statutory NSA to support the security and protection of classified information, in line with our EU and international obligations. This includes the development of an NSA that can provide the full spectrum of security clearances required including personnel, facilities and ICT clearances. This priority project is a large-scale multi-year project, involving a number of departments and agencies. The Department is currently preparing a comprehensive plan and costings for the design, establishment, and operationalisation of the new National Security Authority on a statutory footing and I will be returning to government later in the year with my proposals. A Programme Board, comprising of senior representatives from a number of departments and bodies, and chaired by the Secretary General of the Department, has been established to provide input and guidance on the strategic direction of the NSA Programme. The NSA is currently supported by the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade and exists on an administrative basis only. Once the statutory NSA is established, responsibility for the National Security Authority will transfer to my Department.

question: 55. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the position regarding the Programme for Government commitment to "provide funding to recruit at least 5,000 new Garda recruits and additional Garda Staff over the next five years"; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [49290/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Getting more Gardaí on our streets to prevent and detect crime remains my priority as Minister. The Programme for Government commits to examining a range of further measures to enable An Garda Síochána to recruit 5,000 members across the five year term of this Government. I am fully committed to ensuring that An Garda Síochána has the resources it needs, with Budget 2026 providing unprecedented funding of €2.74 billion to support recruitment, training and staffing. At the end of May, total Garda personnel stood at over 18,200, which included 14,621 Gardaí, 3,498 Garda Staff, and 295 Reserves. Overall, just under 800 trainees entered the Garda College in 2025, the highest number since 2018. 619 Probationer Gardaí also attested from the College last year. Following two attestations this year, 360 probationer Gardaí have been assigned across the country. I look forward to seeing large numbers attesting from the Garda college in the remaining two attestations due to take place later this year, the first of which will be held in July. 223 and 215 trainees entered the college in intakes in November of last year and February this year so I expect to see in excess of 200 Gardaí attesting in each of the upcoming attestations. The number of Gardaí available to the Commissioner will continue to increase over the coming months as trainees currently in Templemore complete their training and attest from the Garda College. We are now regularly seeing groups of over 200 trainees entering Templemore. The most recent intake of 201 trainees on 4 May was the fourth intake in a row with 200 or more recruits entering the college. The most recent recruitment competition, which closed on 3 June 2026, attracted 4,115 applications. This brings the total applications received in the three Garda recruitment competitions that have been held since February 2025 to over 15,000. This demonstrates that there is a strong and sustained interest in a career as a Garda amongst the public and further recruitment competitions will be run to ensure that there is a steady pipeline of new recruits ready to enter the Garda College. The Garda authorities have advised that, in line with the Programme for Government, An Garda Síochána will continue to recruit Garda staff, embark upon the next phase of modernisation and specialisation, therein releasing Garda members from activity not requiring their powers and policing experience.

question: 56. Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the discussions he has had at EU level regarding the possible extension, including on a restricted or modified basis, of the Temporary Protection Directive beyond March 2027; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [49295/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Discussions to extend the EU Temporary Protection Directive are led by the Council of the European Union, following consideration of the situation in Ukraine and discussions between Member States and the European Commission. These discussions have intensified in recent weeks. On 26/06/2026 the Commission published a proposal to extend Temporary Protection until 04/03/2028. The proposal is currently under consideration by Member States and discussions have commenced under the current Presidency of the Council of the European Union. As these negotiations are ongoing, and as a final position has not yet been agreed by Member States, it is not possible to pre-empt the outcome. It can however be confirmed that there is broad recognition among Member States of the need to continue providing protection to people displaced by the war in Ukraine, while also advancing practical measures to support a coordinated transition from Temporary Protection over time. The Commission proposal also contains provisions relating to future arrivals from Ukraine and the circumstances under which Temporary Protection may apply. These elements are currently the subject of detailed consideration by Member States and legal analysis is ongoing. Ireland’s approach continues to be guided by the principle of alignment with a coordinated EU response. A harmonised approach is important to ensure consistency in the treatment of beneficiaries of temporary protection across the European Union. At national level, my Department is continuing to implement the Government decision of 26 May 2026 and to advance measures in line with the EU Council Recommendation on a coordinated approach to the transition from Temporary Protection. These measures include planning for alternative legal pathways, voluntary return arrangements, enhanced information provision and transition supports for beneficiaries of temporary protection. Ireland remains committed to supporting the people of Ukraine and to ensuring that any future arrangements are implemented in an orderly, fair and sustainable manner.

question: 57. Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will increase funding for the Legal Aid Board to reduce waiting times, increase the income limit and provide access to justice for people; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [49378/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 40 and 57 together. In June 2022, a Civil Legal Aid Review Group under the chairmanship of former Chief Justice Frank Clarke, SC, was established to review the current operation of the Civil Legal Aid Scheme. The outputs of the review were published in July 2025 and contained recommendations relating to eligibility for the Scheme, including income threshold and allowances, as well as recommendations aimed at improving access to justice for people. The Review also made recommendations extending the scheme to legal issues which are currently heard before tribunals. Any changes must be considered with regard to the potential implications that they might have on the operation of the Scheme, as well as forms of legal support available through different forums, such as administrative tribunals and other services. Officials in the Department are examining the recommendations and are working closely with the Legal Aid Board to ensure any proposed reforms are developed as part of the annual budgetary Estimates process and take account of potential implications on the operation of the Scheme and broader government policy. The recommendations from the Review will also have to be considered with due regard to the findings from Ireland’s first Legal Needs Survey, recently completed with the support of the European Commission and the OECD. This survey will provide invaluable insights into the extent of legal needs in Ireland. While preliminary results of the survey have been released on gov.ie., further analysis is underway, with the Department working closely with the OECD on final outputs. The Legal Aid Board provides a very important service to those who need its support in matters of civil dispute and in more general matters of civil law and operational practice. Given its wide remit and national reach my Department will continue to engage closely with the Legal Aid Board to ensure it has the resources necessary to meet its most immediate needs and the additional demands it will face going forward. Funding to the Board has increased in recent years, from €53 million in 2023, to €59 million in 2024, €64 million in 2025, and to €73 million in 2026. Funding for 2027 is being considered as part of the Estimates process in the usual way.

question: 58. Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide an update on Garda recruitment to meet increasing policing demands. [49846/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Programme for Government commits to examining a range of further measures to enable An Garda Síochána recruit 5,000 members across the term of this Government. The Garda Vote in Budget 2026 includes unprecedented funding of €2.74 billion which will support the continued recruitment of Garda members and staff. At the end of May, total Garda personnel stood at over 18,200, which included 14,621 Gardaí, 3,498 Garda Staff, and 295 Reserves. I will continue to support An Garda Síochána to increase this number further so that we can see more Gardaí assigned all across the country. Significant measures have been made to boost recruitment and retention including by increasing the Garda trainee allowance to €354 per week; increasing the age of entry from 35 to 50; and raising the mandatory retirement age to 62. Following two attestations this year, 360 probationer Gardaí have been assigned across the country. I look forward to seeing large numbers attesting from the Garda college in the remaining two attestations due to take place later this year, the first of which will be held in July. 223 and 215 trainees entered the college in intakes in November of last year and February this year so I expect to see high numbers attesting in each of the upcoming attestations. The number of Gardaí available to the Commissioner will continue to increase over the coming months as trainees currently in Templemore complete their training and attest from the Garda College. We are now regularly seeing groups of over 200 trainees entering Templemore. The most recent intake of 201 trainees on 4 May was the fourth intake in a row with 200 or more recruits entering the college. The most recent recruitment competition, which closed on 3 June 2026, attracted 4,115 applications. This further demonstrates that there is a strong and sustained interest in a career as a Garda amongst the public and further recruitment competitions will be run to ensure that there is a steady pipeline of new recruits ready to enter the Garda College.

question: 59. Deputy Gary Gannon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he accepts that the latest report by an organisation (details supplied) which recorded the highest demand in the organisation’s history, shows that the State is still failing to meet the scale of domestic violence in Ireland; and the urgent additional justice measures he will take to address this crisis. [49881/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 51 and 59 together. It was an honour to launch the Women’s Aid Impact Report 2025 last week. The figures and statistics in the report are extremely stark, and I’m very aware that behind these numbers are real women and children who have suffered, often due to the actions of someone close to them. While the figures are concerning, the increase in contact also reflects a growing awareness of the service provided, so that increasing numbers of victims know they do not have to face these experiences alone. The Report highlights the complexities of each disclosure, often involving repeated contact over time, and the accelerated demand for specialist services. I want to take this opportunity to recognise and commend the vital ongoing support provided by Women’s Aid to victims of domestic violence and abuse, as reflected in this important report. Combatting domestic violence is a priority for Government and our ‘Zero Tolerance’ DSGBV Strategy is the most ambitious strategy to date. It sets out a range of actions aimed at preventing domestic violence and abuse, improving protection for victims, and ensuring more effective access to justice. A key development in this regard has been the establishment of Cuan, the statutory agency responsible for coordinating and driving the implementation of the Zero Tolerance strategy. Under Budget 2026, funding of almost €80 million has been provided to support Cuan, frontline organisations working in the DSGBV sector and implementation of the Zero Tolerance Strategy. We continue to support Women’s Aid essential work through more than €2.2 million in funding (through Cuan) this year. Cuan is collaborating with various stakeholders, including domestic violence services, Approved Housing Bodies, the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage, the Housing Agency and Local Authorities to facilitate local action and support service development and the delivery of safe accommodation and ancillary services. At the commencement of the Zero Tolerance strategy, there were 49 safe homes and 141 DV refuge units in place. There are currently 181 domestic violence refuge units – which includes nine new units in Dublin south - and 60 safe home units, bringing the total safe accommodation at present to 241. By the end of this year it is expected that we will have 193 refuge units completed and 94 safe homes, bringing total safe accommodation to 287, with 50 further refuge units under construction. I have advanced a number of legislative changes in the area of domestic violence. The Domestic Violence (Judgments) Register Bill 2026 will set up a Register of Judgments, ensuring that relevant convictions for serious domestic violence offences are made public as part of the conviction process. The Guardianship of Infants and Child Care (Amendment) Bill 2026 provides for the removal of guardianship rights, in certain situations, from individuals convicted of killing their partner or the other parents of their child. My Department is actively considering further measures to better support and protect victims of domestic, sexual and gender-based violence. This process is informed by engagement with stakeholders, including Departments, agencies and civil society organisations. As the current Zero Tolerance Strategy approaches its conclusion, work is now underway on a fourth national strategy which will build on what we have learned and will address new and emerging threats such as technology-facilitated harms against women and children.

question: 60. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he can provide the Garda to population ratio per county; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [49840/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under Section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which includes the distribution and stationing of Garda personnel throughout the State. An Garda Síochána police on a Divisional basis, and not on the basis of population, using all resources in a Community Engagement area, supported by Divisional resources and units. This Operating Model has been designed to enable An Garda Síochána to meet the challenges of modern-day policing more consistently around the country by enabling specialisation in the delivery of key services and freeing up more Gardaí to focus on front line policing. Under this structure, each Division is organised into four Functional Areas: Community Engagement, Crime, Performance Assurance, and Business Services. The Operating Model, coupled with some realignment of responsibilities, is helping to deliver a consistent, community-focused policing service. I regularly engage with the Garda Commissioner to ensure our Gardaí have the resources they need. I am informed that when allocating and transferring Garda members to and from any Division, consideration is given to commitments and undertakings outlined in the Annual Policing Plan and priorities as determined in delivering ‘A Policing Service for The Future’. The Deputy may be interested to note that Garda authorities advise that the requirements of all Garda Divisions nationwide are also taken into account, which include: • Local and national crime trends and workloads; • Policing arrangements and operational strategies; • Minimum establishment statistics; • Local population and trends, geographical area and size; • Transfer applications, including welfare, personnel issues and concerns. An Garda Síochána publishes information in relation to the allocation of Gardaí nationally, including a breakdown of Garda allocated to divisions and stations nationwide. Historical data on the allocation of Gardaí can be found here: www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/human-resources-and-people-development/garda-hr-directorate/garda-strength-breakdown-2025/garda-strength-breakdown-2025.html The Deputy should select December 2025 and then select 'Garda Members by Division District Station'. The historical data is included in this file. Data for 2026 can be found here: Human Resources Statistics - Garda www.garda.ie/en/information-centre/garda-statistics/human%20resources/ The Deputy should select the relevant month and as above access the file on the nationwide allocation of Gardaí.

question: 61. Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he has had any engagement with the Department of Housing; Local Government and Heritage or Meath County Council with a view to transferring a property in County Meath (details supplied) to the local authority or an approved housing body so it can be used for social housing; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [48864/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration In line with the Programme for Government 2025 the State is working to develop more State-owned international protection accommodation and reduce reliance on commercially contracted accommodation. 37 in-community properties were purchased by the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth for the accommodation of more vulnerable applicants, for whom group accommodation would not be suitable. The property in the details provided is in this group and is currently being refurbished. Three of these properties are currently under review for alternative uses outside of international protection accommodation. I can confirm that the property listed by the Deputy has been the subject of local community engagement. The property is not being considered for use by the Department of Housing: Local Government and Heritage or Meath County Council.

question: 62. Deputy Catherine Callaghan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for an update on his work to combat online fraud and cyber threats, and to bring Ireland in line with the NIS2 Directive; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [49368/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration My Department continuously evaluates and adapts its strategies to deal with combatting cyber threats to Irish citizens and our critical national infrastructure. The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), which leads on the State’s response to cyber risk and comes under the remit of my Department, published Ireland’s National Cyber Emergency Plan in May 2026. The plan sets out the national approach for responding to serious cyber security incidents that affect nationally important systems and networks. As the plan has been developed in alignment with the Strategic Emergency Management National Structure and Framework, it establishes the structures for co-ordinating a "whole of society" approach to preparing for and responding to a cyber emergency. In addition, the NCSC regularly publishes alerts, advisories and guidance documents on a range of cyber security related topics to assist citizens in raising their cyber security awareness. The National Cyber Security Bill which is the legislative vehicle for the transposition of the NIS2 Directive will also establish the NCSC on a statutory basis and provide for related matters including clarity around its mandate and role in general and in relation to other actors in the cyber area. This legislation represents a significant step in strengthening the State’s cyber security and resilience. As the Deputy will appreciate, under the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, the detection and investigation of any form of criminal activity, including online cyber dependant crimes or cyber enabled crimes, is an operational matter for the Garda Commissioner who is independent in the performance of his functions under section 34(1) of that Act. As Minister, I have no direct role in these matters, but if anyone suspects they have been the victim of a cyber crime or fraud, I would encourage them to contact Gardaí to report this at the earliest possible time.

question: 63. Deputy Gary Gannon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the data his Department collects on the outcomes of women who engage with domestic violence services, including refuge access, repeat victimisation, protection orders and criminal justice outcomes; and whether he is satisfied that the State currently has sufficient data to assess whether victims are becoming safer after seeking help. [49880/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Deputy will appreciate that data on domestic, sexual and gender-based violence is collected across a range of agencies, including An Garda Síochána, the Courts Service, and service providers funded by the State. However, the data is not currently integrated in a way that allows for the tracking of individual outcomes over time, including refuge access, repeat victimisation, and longer-term safety outcomes following engagement with services. The Government’s Zero Tolerance strategy on domestic, sexual and gender-based violence (DSGBV), recognises the importance of improved data collection and analysis to support evidence-based policy development. In that context, Cuan, our statutory DSGBV agency is leading efforts to strengthen coordination and develop a more consistent evidence base in this area. Additional funding was made available to Cuan to expand the development of the national domestic violence helplines which also enables increased data collection. Government Departments, agencies and service providers gather and report data relevant to the implementation of the strategy to Cuan on key performance indicators to track and measure progress. For incidents of gender-based violence, An Garda Síochána have the lead role in recording details of such incidents in the PULSE system. I am advised that in July 2021, AGS introduced a mechanism to record the relationship between the victim and the offender. Since then, the Garda Information Service Centre (GISC) has implemented a data quality coherency check on the recording of the relationship, to improve the recording of the domestic abuse motive attached to PULSE incidents. The CSO conducted a Sexual Violence Survey which was published in 2023. The data gathered from that survey is used to inform policy and service provision. A further national survey is planned to take place in 2027. Cuan is represented on my Department's Analytics Steering Group and is engaging with the European Institute for Gender Equality (EIGE) on progressing aligned country data across EU member states. Early progress has been made on a Cuan/ESRI Joint Research Programme on Adult Sexual Violence in Ireland. This will include analysis of the 2023 CSO Sexual Violence Survey data, to examine patterns of victimisation among those that have experienced adult sexual violence and the profile of those that disclose experiencing adult sexual violence and use services. Alongside this, my Department is progressing work to develop a single unique identifier and standardising data categorisation across the Justice Sector which will facilitate better collation and sharing of data to support policy research and inform DSGBV service development. Through development of the National Service Development Plan (NSDP), Cuan is collaborating with services and stakeholders to strengthen data collection processes. An essential element to the NSDP is the establishment of robust monitoring structures for service delivery and outcomes. This monitoring process will identify critical areas for service and sector development. Monitoring on DSGBV service activity and outcome for 2024 and 2025 provides, for the first time, a national picture of service activity and impact across all DSGBV funded services. In 2025, 23,239 individuals were supported across Cuan funded Domestic Violence services. This along with the ongoing engagement with DSGBV funded services as part of annual funding process provides an evidence base on service delivery, outcomes and need. The range of data available, together with the enhanced monitoring being undertaken by Cuan, is significantly strengthening the State’s understanding of service delivery and outcomes and will continue to improve the evidence base over time.

question: 64. Deputy Brendan Smith asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he has had any recent discussions with his counterpart in the Northern Ireland Executive in relation to the introduction of additional measures to counteract cross-Border criminality; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [49843/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Significant engagement took place at Ministerial, senior official and operational level at the Cross Border Police Conference on Organised and Serious Crime in Co. Cavan in March of this year. I attended the event myself alongside Naomi Long MLA, Minister for Justice in the Northern Ireland Executive, the Garda Commissioner, the Chief Constable of the PSNI, senior officers from all the agencies and senior officials from Department of Justice Northern Ireland and my own Department. This is an annual event, aimed at enhancing understanding and cooperation between law enforcement agencies on both sides of the border, particularly in relation to cross border organised criminality and related issues. The objectives of the Conference include sharing experiences, identifying effective approaches and recommending actions to the Joint Agency Task Force aimed at enhancing cross-border working relationships to enhance our collective ability to tackle organised crime. The theme of the conference was: ‘Tackling the Business Model of Organised Crime: One Threat – Shared Responsibility’ . The message of the conference was clear in this regard. If we are to effectively tackle organised crime, we must address its entire business model – the ways it identifies demand, creates supply lines, generates profits and then reinvests those profits. Topics that were explored under this theme include ‘People’, ‘Finance’ and ‘Technology’ and ‘Merchandise’. As the Deputy will appreciate, the specific matters discussed at the Conference are sensitive and operational in nature, however I can advise the Deputy that robust and fruitful discussions around tackling cross border criminality and cross border co-operation between law enforcement agencies North and South took place. The conference also heard about actions taken on foot of last year's conference. Also discussed were learnings from recent successes of the task force, updates regarding Operation Tara, and discussion of the Proceeds of Crime (Amendment) Bill 2024 which is currently making its was through the Oireachtas. More recently I met with Minister long on 8 May for a meeting under the auspices of the Inter-Governmental Agreement on Co-operation on Criminal Justice Matters (IGA), in Armagh. At the meeting, Minister Long and I formally closed off the 2023-2025 IGA work plan and signed off on a new plan to run from January 2026 to January 2028. The new work plan contains shared goals and projected outcomes under five headings, each informed by its own Project Advisory Group • The Public Protection Group work centres on collaborative responses to emerging challenges, cross border seminars, research activity and leadership development. • The Support for Victims Group will continue to prioritise domestic abuse, sexual violence, human trafficking and Domestic Homicide Reviews, with further joint learning events and operational cooperation planned. • The Forensic Science Group priorities including joint strategic planning, business continuity support, knowledge exchange and collaboration on capital projects. • The Criminal Justice and Social Diversity Group is strengthening cooperation to address hate crime, protect minority communities and improve responses to radicalisation, violent extremism and paramilitarism. • The Youth Justice Group is focused on early intervention, diversion, bail support and addressing harmful attitudes and behaviours informed by the Stable Lives, Safer Streets joint research project funded by the Shared Island Initiative. The Joint agency Task Force is also reported on it operations. Key findings of the 19th JATF report include: • Ongoing disruptions of organised crime groups exploiting the Common Travel Areas. • The continued prevalence of rural crime, particularly burglaries and theft, driven by organised crime groups exploiting the border. • Significant drug trafficking activity, particularly cocaine and cannabis. • The increasing complexity in financial crime, with growth in online fraud and complex cross jurisdictional investigations. • Challenges law enforcement is facing in tackling human trafficking cases, particularly victim engagement and online exploitation. • Continued threat from excise fraud, including illicit fuel, alcohol and tobacco supply chain. Although organised crime groups continue to evolve, the report highlights the ongoing commitment of law enforcement agencies on both sides of the border, which has been effective in disrupting their activities.

question: 65. Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of asylum seekers that are currently sleeping rough; his plans to stop this from happening; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [49380/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Ireland is currently accommodating almost 33,000 people in approximately 303 International Protection Accommodation Service (IPAS) centres around the country. From the end of 2023, accommodation shortages meant that not all applicants could be offered an accommodation place. From that period on, IPAS prioritised women, children and those who were most vulnerable for the limited accommodation available. IPAS was unable to offer accommodation to all single male applicants for international protection from December 2023. People who were not offered accommodation are given a weekly allowance of €113.80 per week, an increase of €75 from the standard weekly allowance for asylum-seekers. Many applicants make their own accommodation arrangements and therefore are not rough-sleeping. IPAS has arrangements in place with a range of NGO partners to provide drop-in day services so people can access facilities including hot showers, meals and laundry services. IPAS teams can make offers of accommodation to any applicant who is rough-sleeping, identified through outreach. Since March 2025, IPAS has been able to review the cases of people who are awaiting an offer of accommodation and make offers to those who have been waiting longest, using the information they have provided to the International Protection Office (IPO). Through various actions taken since I have taken office, the number of people unaccommodated has reduced from over 3,500 to 914 currently. The new International Protection Act 2026 gives effect to the measures of the EU Migration and Asylum Pact and was passed into law last month. The new rules came into effect on 12 June. Reforming and speeding up processing of applications should also serve over time to reduce the scale of the demand for international protection accommodation. Additionally, my Department is working to increase the amount of State-owned international protection accommodation and creating a more stable and sustainable accommodation system. The purchase of the Citywest Reception Centre in 2025 was an important step in this strategy, and increased State-owned beds to 4,000 in 2025, compared to 900 in early 2024.

question: 66. Deputy Grace Boland asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the current status of legislative provisions to restrict the disclosure of counselling notes in rape and sexual offence trials; the expected timeline for enactment and commencement; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [49371/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 27 and 66 together. The Government recognises the deep distress that can be caused to victims and survivors by the disclosure of counselling records in criminal proceedings and is committed to minimising intrusion into their privacy to the greatest extent possible, while ensuring compliance with constitutional requirements, including the right to a fair trial and the presumption of innocence. The Criminal Law and Civil Law (Miscellaneous Provisions) Bill 2026 contains significant reforms to strengthen protections for counselling records. The Bill is currently at committee stage in the Seanad and is continuing through the legislative process. It is hoped the Bill will be enacted before the summer recess begins. Subject to the completion of that process, it is my intention that the relevant provisions will be commenced as soon as practicable following enactment. The Bill provides for the deletion of the waiver provision currently contained in section 19A of the Criminal Evidence Act 1992, as amended by the Criminal Law (Sexual Offences) Act 2017, thereby ensuring that no disclosure will take place without a disclosure hearing. The Government has also approved further amendments to introduce a statutory presumption of non-disclosure and to strengthen protections for other sensitive personal records. Under the proposed framework, counselling records will not be disclosed unless a court, following a disclosure hearing, is satisfied that disclosure is necessary in the interests of justice or to avoid an unfair trial. The court will be required to balance the privacy and dignity rights of the complainant against the accused person’s constitutional right to a fair trial. Disclosure will therefore be the exception rather than the rule, and will only arise where a judge determines that the statutory threshold has been met and that disclosure is strictly necessary.

question: 67. Deputy Brendan Smith asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will outline the proposals there are to increase the emphasis on community policing, which is a very highly regarded policing measure in communities throughout the country; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [49842/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which includes the distribution and stationing of Garda personnel throughout the State. As Minister, it is my role to support the Commissioner by ensuring he has the resources he needs. Budget 2026 provides unprecedented funding of €2.74 billion to support recruitment and staffing. I engage regularly with the Commissioner and I am assured that community policing remains at the heart of An Garda Síochána and is something that all Garda members have a role in. A member of An Garda Síochána is deemed to be a ‘Community Garda’ where that person is allocated to a Community Policing Team (CPT), and is responsible and accountable for applying a problem–solving approach to appropriate crime and policing quality-of-life issues in a specified geographic area through community partnership and engagement. Examples of this engagement can include working with Neighbourhood Watch, Community Alert or local business fora. I am advised by the Garda authorities that the Garda National Community Engagement Bureau have conducted a review of Community Policing nationwide and are currently drafting a new Garda Community Policing Policy document. Community Engagement Superintendents are also nominated representatives of An Garda Síochána to the Local Community Safety Partnerships. Community Policing is delivered across the country through a hybrid model of Community Engagement/frontline Garda members and dedicated full time Community Policing teams, depending on the demography and demands of the particular Garda Division/Community Engagement Area. The allocation of Garda members to Community Policing duties is managed at Divisional level by local Garda management. Figures from May 2026 show 600 Garda members assigned to Community Policing duties nationwide. An Garda Síochána publishes information in relation to the allocation of Gardaí including the allocation of Community Gardaí by Division. Information for 2026 can be found at the following link: [ ]www.garda.ie/en/information-centre/garda-statistics/human%20resources/ Information for previous years can be found at the following link: www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/human-resources-and-people-development/garda-hr-directorate/garda-strength-breakdown-2025/december-2025.html There is real momentum in Garda recruitment, which is providing more resources to the Garda Commissioner to deploy to frontline policing. This includes the roll out of high visibility policing initiatives in Dublin City Centre, as well as areas of South Dublin including Tallaght and Dún Laoghaire, and to Cork and Limerick Cities, which provide reassurance to the local communities. The Commissioner is committed to expand the rollout of the high visibility policing plan to other areas and I look forward to its further rollout.

question: 68. Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to outline progress on the Programme for Government commitment to construct a new prison at Thornton Hall; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [49839/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I am acutely aware of the capacity constraints in our prisons and the challenges faced by those who work and live in our prisons as a result. The Irish Prison Service (IPS) must accept into custody all people committed to prison by the courts and has no control over the numbers committed to custody at any given time. Since 2024, 258 spaces have been constructed across the prison estate, with 126 delivered in 2024,106 in 2025 and 26 finished so far in 2026. There are plans to build another 39 spaces in 2026 and 70 in 2027. In addition, Government has allocated funding for a significant building programme across the prison estate. On conclusion of the NDP Review in July 2025, I secured a record capital investment of €67.9 million for 2026, as part of a total investment of €528 million from 2026 to 2030, of which €495 million is being invested in building projects to further increase capacity. The IPS is delivering one of the most significant capital programmes in the justice sector, reflecting the Government’s commitment to increase prison capacity and modernise the estate in line with population growth, with an overall target of delivering over 1,500 spaces by 2031. This will include a large extension to the existing Cork Prison on the site of the old, decommissioned Cork Prison, a new block in Wheatfield, and an additional block extension at Midlands prison. This is in addition to spaces at Castlerea, Mountjoy and the Dóchas Centre. This record capital allocation will allow for work to start to plan and develop a new prison on the Thornton site in North County Dublin. A master plan for the site is planned to be developed in 2026, determining its future use as a combined site for use by the IPS, International Protection Accommodation Services and An Garda Síochána with plans to commence works in 2030.

question: 69. Deputy Noel McCarthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of long stay (join family) visa applications received, approved and rejected by his Department in each of the years 2023 to 2025 and to-data in 2026; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [49369/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I can advise the Deputy that my Department currently operates seven overseas Visa Offices in addition to the Visa Office in Dublin. These are located in Abuja, Beijing, London, Moscow, Ankara, Abu Dhabi and New Delhi. In addition, staff of the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade process certain visa applications in Irish Embassies abroad under delegated authority from my Department. Processing times and decisions at the Visa Offices in Dublin and overseas can be checked at the following link: www.irishimmigration.ie/visa-decisions In December 2025, the Immigration Service of my Department introduced online payment functionality to my Department's online visa system. This allows applicants to pay visa fees as part of the online application process. The initiative is being rolled out on a phased basis and is currently live in 40 countries, with South Africa added in January 2026. This reduces the administrative burden on Irish Missions and visa teams, and allows visa officers to dedicate more time to core application processing and decision-making, contributing to improved processing efficiency over time. Furthermore, the ongoing Immigration Service Delivery (ISD) modernisation programme is designed to support a more efficient, transparent and accessible immigration system. question: 70. Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of Garda stations in County Galway operating on a full time basis; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [48936/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under Section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which includes all operational policing matters such as the opening hours of Garda stations. The Commissioner is independent in his functions under Section 34 of the Act. The Garda Commissioner publishes full details of Garda stations including their opening hours in the Station Directory at the following link: www.garda.ie/en/contact-us/station-directory/. The Deputy should select the Galway Division and review the information using either the map or the list feature. It is important to emphasise that An Garda Síochána do not police on a station basis, but rather on a Divisional basis. Gardaí see stations as locations within communities for people to attend, and for resources to be accommodated. Policing for an area will be delivered using all resources in a Community Engagement area, supported by all Divisional resources and units.

question: 72. Deputy Mark Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for an update on "Grace's Law" in relation to scrambler use; how effective it is; if the incidents of scrambles driving recklessly in communities has decreased; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [49739/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration On 1 April, the Road Traffic (Control of Certain Vehicles) Regulations 2026, known as Grace's Law, were signed into law by my colleague Darragh O'Brien TD, the Minister for Transport. These regulations implement an explicit ban on scrambler use in any public place, to enhance community safety. The regulations prohibit the use of an off-road motorcycle, such as a scrambler or a quadbike, in any place, except on private land. They impose a requirement of consent where restricted vehicles are used on private land, and will make enforcement easier. The mere use of scramblers is now explicitly an offence, assisting An Garda Síochána operationally by ensuring that members no longer have to form a reasonable belief about dangerous use of the vehicle. It should be noted that the ban has only been in effect since the beginning April and as such the data on arrests, prosecutions and convictions made under this legislation are not yet available. Gardaí also have additional, and significant, legislative powers to combat the antisocial and dangerous misuse of scramblers, quad bikes, e-scooters and other such vehicles including under the Road Traffic Act 1961, the Non-Fatal Offences Against the Person Act 1997, and the Criminal Law Act 1997 and the Road Traffic and Roads Act 2023. I am assured that An Garda Síochána continues to adopt a proactive approach in addressing the illegal use of scramblers, quads, e-bikes and e-scooters. I informed by Garda authorities of a substantial increase in the seizure of these types of vehicles during the first quarter of 2026 when measured against the full year 2025. Garda authorities report 754 incidents in which an e-scooter has been seized in the first quarter of this year, compared to a full year figure of 931 for 2025. In respect of e-bikes, the 140 seizures recorded in Quarter 1 is already over half the 237 seized in the whole of 2025. Similarly, scrambler and quad bike seizures, at 94 and 17 incidents respectively for the first quarter of this year, are tracking well ahead of 2025 full-year figures of 159 and 40. Tackling dangerous driver behaviours and promoting compliance with road traffic laws will continue to be addressed through road safety education and public awareness campaigns and the enforcement of road traffic laws.

question: 73. Deputy Gary Gannon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration his views on whether the proposed changes to the criminal legal aid system risks delaying justice for victims and witnesses; and the updates, if any, on the changes to the scheme. [49883/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I welcome the opportunity to explain the changes to the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme in the District Court that I signed into law on Monday and that will come into effect on Wednesday 1 July. At the outset, I would like to acknowledge the critical role played by the legal professions in the effective administration of criminal justice and that Criminal Legal Aid is essential in upholding the right to a legal defence. I have progressed the Programme for Government commitments in relation to Criminal Legal Aid, of which there are three. The first is to reform the operation of the criminal legal aid scheme. The second is to restore the fees which were cut during the economic crisis. And the third is to enact the Criminal Justice (Legal Aid) Bill. The changes I am making to the fee structure address the first two commitments and I intend to progress the new legislation over the next year. The Bill will reform the overall system of legal aid; strengthening the provisions around eligibility and transferring responsibility for the operation of the system to the Legal Aid Board. The reform of the criminal legal aid fee structure in the District Court will not affect the ability of legal professionals to engage in criminal legal aid work. Neither is it intended to reduce the cost to the State of providing criminal legal aid. Rather, it will improve efficiencies, reduce unnecessary adjournments, simplify the administration of criminal legal aid, speed up case resolution and enable faster payments to practitioners. I expect that the improved efficiency and effectiveness of the system will be to the benefit of victims and witnesses. I can assure the Deputy that my officials will keep the operation of the new system under review over the coming months. This will allow any emerging issues to be identified without delay and addressed where necessary. The objective of these reforms is to provide a fair, sustainable and efficient framework for the delivery of criminal legal aid while maintaining access to high-quality legal representation.

question: 74. Deputy Tom Brabazon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of Gardaí that have been seconded to operational duties away from their base stations to Ireland's Presidency of the Council of the European Union. [49646/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which includes the distribution and stationing of Garda personnel throughout the State. The Commissioner is independent in his functions under section 34 of the Act. Since January 2024, An Garda Síochána has been actively preparing to meet the policing and security requirements associated with the Presidency of the EU. I am informed that a comprehensive command, control and coordination framework is in place to support the delivery of Presidency-related policing operations, together with all other major and significant policing operations and events, while ensuring the continued provision of effective day-to-day policing services. I am informed that at present, no significant disruption to normal Garda services is anticipated from EU Presidency-related policing operations. Garda authorities advise that it is expected that Garda clinics, community meetings, stakeholder engagement initiatives, victim support services, criminal investigations, case management functions, court-related duties and prosecution processes will continue to be delivered in the normal course. While certain events may necessitate the deployment of a greater number of Garda personnel than others, I am assured that sufficient Garda resources will remain available to ensure the continued delivery of effective and consistent Garda services throughout the Presidency period. Continuity of core policing services across all functional areas remains a key organisational priority. I understand that a small number of Gardaí have been temporarily transferred to Dublin Castle to effectively support and implement a robust policing and security operation for the duration of the EU Presidency however the attestation of 979 Gardaí since March 2025 will ensure that An Garda Síochána have the necessary resources to maintain policing services in divisions nationwide while also providing for the security needs of the Presidency.

question: 75. Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the consideration he is giving to strengthening knife crime legislation; the number of assaults and murders involving knives in each of the years 2023, 2024, 2025, and to date in 2026; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [49774/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration does not collate or publish crime statistics. That responsibility rests with the Central Statistics Office (CSO), established under the Statistics Act 1993. Under section 13 of the Statistics Act 1993, the Central Statistics Office (CSO) is fully independent in its role of issuing statistics. Recorded crime statistics are published quarterly and are available from the CSO website at www.cso.ie/en/statistics/crimeandjustice/ I can assure the Deputy that the Government is committed to ensuring that communities are safe and tackling knife crime remains an important part of that work. Ireland has a comprehensive and robust legal framework in place to address knife crime, with penalties for knife-related offences strengthened in recent years. In 2024, legislation increased the maximum penalty for offences including possession of a knife with intent to cause injury, trespassing with a knife and producing a knife to unlawfully intimidate another person from five years to seven years imprisonment. In addition, the Government doubled the maximum penalty for assault causing harm to ten years imprisonment in 2023. An Garda Síochána's report on Knife Related Crime for 2015-2024 provides detailed analysis of incidents involving the use of, and/or possession of, a knife. The report shows that assaults causing harm involving a knife accounted for, on average, less than 7% of all assault causing harm incidents over the past decade. The analysis also identified a 40% reduction in robberies involving a knife in retail spaces and a 35% reduction in robberies involving a knife in public spaces since 2020. The report is publicly available on the Garda website and I am informed by the Garda authorities that it will be updated later in 2026. The report can be viewed at the below link: www.garda.ie/en/about-us/publications/general-reports/knife-related-crime-2015-to-2024.pdf An Garda Síochána continues to undertake a range of proactive measures to tackle assaults in public places, including those involving knives. This is informed by a pro-arrest, early-investigation and high-visibility policing approach. Tackling knife crime requires a sustained, evidence-based approach that addresses wider issues such as anti-social behaviour, street violence and youth offending. The Department is supporting this work through youth justice measures and through the establishment of Local Community Safety Partnerships, which bring together a broad range of stakeholders including local communities, youth, education, new and minority communities, the business community and public services and An Garda Síochána to address community safety issues at local level. The Deputy may also be interested to note that An Garda Síochána are currently developing a new Crime Prevention and Reduction Strategy 2026-2029. Knife related crime will be encompassed with all violent crime within this new strategy.

question: 76. Deputy Peter Roche asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if his Department has assessed the delays being experienced by Irish citizens seeking to return to the State with non-Irish national spouses due to visa processing times (details supplied); whether any measures are being considered to prioritise spousal visa applications in such cases in order to facilitate family reunification; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [49849/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I can advise the Deputy that the Join Family visa application referred to was created 08 May 2025. Supporting documentation was received in the Ottawa office on 12 May 2025. The application was received in the Dublin Visa Office on 27 May 2025 where it awaits examination and processing. My Department's business target for join family visa applications is 12 months. It must be made clear that these are business targets for the immigration service and some applications can take longer than others. The business target reflects the detailed and often complex assessment that is required to be carried out in relation to applications for family reunification. While I acknowledge the personal difficulties an applicant might be experiencing; it is not possible to give a definitive date as to when this application will be finalised. All applications are processed in chronological order, based on date order of receipt. While every effort is made to process applications as soon as possible, processing times will vary having regard to the volume and complexity of applications, the possible need for the Immigration Service Delivery function of my Department to investigate, inquire into, or seek further information, and the resources available. The current processing times for Dublin visa decisions is available here: www.irishimmigration.ie/visa-decisions/ The date published on the website is the oldest date of application currently being processed under a given category. However, it should be noted that the Visa team continue to process and make decisions on applications received after the published processing date. If a particular application takes longer to consider this may result in the published processing date remaining unchanged. I can assure you that this does not indicate the processing of these applications has halted overall. I am acutely aware that join family applications are very important for the people impacted. I understand that people are eager to have their families join them in Ireland, and I am committed to improving the service my Department provides. The person concerned can now directly check the status of their visa application on the Immigration Service’s Customer Service Portal. They can register for, or log in to their existing account, at: www.portal.irishimmigration.ie/en/ As an Oireachtas member, you can also request the status of individual immigration cases by e-mail, using the Oireachtas Mail facility at: IMoireachtasmail@justice.ie, which has been specifically established for this purpose. This service enables up to date information on such cases to be obtained without the need to seek information by way of the Parliamentary Question process.

question: 112. Deputy Tom Brabazon asked the Minister for Defence if the holder of a Stamp 4 visa is eligible to serve in Óglaigh na hÉireann; if not, the plans to change this; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [50159/26]
answer: Minister for Defence (Deputy Helen McEntee) As Minister for Defence, I am fully committed to supporting the Defence Forces to increase numbers and strengthen the Defence Forces. It was positive to see the growth in numbers last year, with 790 inductions and I have set a target of 850 inductions for 2026. Indeed, overall application numbers for careers in the Defence Forces continue to grow, with a total of 16,510 applications received in 2025 and more than 10,000 received to end of May 2026. In relation to the Deputy's specific question, a Stamp 4 residence permission grants a non-EEA national the right to live and work in the State without an employment permit. However, under current regulations, holding a Stamp 4 visa is not an independent qualification for service in the Permanent Defence Force. Eligibility is instead determined by the specific legal status underlying the stamp. The Defence Forces accept applications from Stamp 4 holders if their permission was issued on the basis of being a recognised refugee, a recipient of subsidiary protection, or a non-EEA family member of an EEA or UK national. It should be noted that applicants to the Defence Forces must also meet the minimum eligibility criteria for service as laid down in Defence Forces regulations. These criteria are of general applicability to all candidates and may include age, residency, character, educational and medical/fitness requirements depending on the recruitment competition in question. Increases in application numbers and in the overall strength of the PDF demonstrate that the key enabling measures which the Government has introduced to support and drive Defence Forces recruitment and retention are yielding results, towards the pathway of LOA2.

question: 216. Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide an update on the Programme for Government Commitment to establish a cyber security centre of excellence around a cluster of third level education facilities and related industry; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [42218/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), in my Department, is leading on the development of a Cyber Security Research Centre of Excellence, as agreed in the Programme for Government. The Centre will: • operate from both a dedicated physical facility and a robust virtual platform; • provide a focal point for researchers across the State to collaborate; and • drive cutting-edge cybersecurity research, nurture emerging talent and accelerate innovation to address national challenges. The NCSC has established a Steering Group of key stakeholders to oversee and guide the project, including the Department of Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science, the Department of Enterprise, Trade and Employment, Research Ireland, Enterprise Ireland and the IDA. The NCSC is carrying out a strategic assessment of the project at present to validate an already advanced proposal, with a view to bringing a detailed project outline to Government.

question: 217. Deputy Michael Murphy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether his Department has engaged with the Department of Housing; Local Government and Heritage regarding the future use of modular accommodation developments currently being used to house persons under temporary protection, including the Haywood site in Clonmel, in light of the recent Government decision to wind down commercial accommodation contracts for Ukrainians; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [41559/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 217 and 218 together. The rapid build modular units, including those in the location referred to by the Deputy, were built to accommodate Beneficiaries of Temporary Protection fleeing the war in Ukraine. In total there are 654 units across 11 locations, accommodating 2,640 people in family units of four with children. Each of the 11 rapid build sites are currently exempt from planning permission requirements as the units are being used to accommodate families who are fleeing the war in Ukraine. The units can, therefore, only be used for this purpose currently. This exemption will apply for as long as the Temporary Protection Directive (TPD) is in place. The proposed winddown of this accommodation type will be in line with the ending of TPD to avoid pressures on areas where there may be local commercial accommodation in the midst of a winddown phase. The rapid build homes are durable units with an expected 60-year lifespan and are highly energy efficient, with an A2 rating. All 11 sites were developed in an environmentally sustainable way to ensure long-term use and to enhance the local areas. Future use of these units following the end of TPD has always been an integral element of the rapid build project in order to provide value to the State and local communities. To determine the long-term strategy for the sites post TPD, a multi-stakeholder process commenced in March 2025, chaired by officials from my department and including representation from the Office of Public Works (OPW) and the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage (DHLGH). In tandem with the consideration of the feasibility of potential future uses, this work involves exploring planning regularisation at each site. To date, there has been no final decision made on long term future use, as discussions are ongoing with the need to explore all potential options within the local areas. However, these options include Social Housing and lower cost affordable housing such as Cost Rental. While the units comply with social housing size requirements for a one-bedroom apartment, modifications are possible to convert two units into one larger three- bedroom unit to accommodate a family of five. One of the first steps to securing planning regularisation is to ensure that all sites are zoned as residential where this is not currently the case. I understand that the Local Authorities are in the process of completing this phase in their Local Development Plans under a variation process. Work is also underway to determine the appropriate planning application process for each of the sites.

question: 219. Deputy Paula Butterly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the current status of legislative provisions to restrict the disclosure of counselling notes in rape and sexual offence trials; the expected timeline for enactment and commencement; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [49373/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Government recognises the deep distress that can be caused to victims and survivors by the disclosure of counselling records in criminal proceedings and is committed to minimising intrusion into their privacy to the greatest extent possible, while ensuring compliance with constitutional requirements, including the right to a fair trial and the presumption of innocence. The Criminal Law and Civil Law (Miscellaneous Provisions) Bill 2026 contains significant reforms to strengthen protections for counselling records. The Bill is currently at committee stage in the Seanad and is continuing through the legislative process. It is hoped the Bill will be enacted before the summer recess begins. Subject to the completion of that process, it is my intention that the relevant provisions will be commenced as soon as practicable following enactment. The Bill provides for the deletion of the waiver provision currently contained in section 19A of the Criminal Evidence Act 1992, as amended by the Criminal Law (Sexual Offences) Act 2017, thereby ensuring that no disclosure will take place without a disclosure hearing. The Government has also approved further amendments to introduce a statutory presumption of non-disclosure and to strengthen protections for other sensitive personal records. Under the proposed framework, counselling records will not be disclosed unless a court, following a disclosure hearing, is satisfied that disclosure is necessary in the interests of justice or to avoid an unfair trial. The court will be required to balance the privacy and dignity rights of the complainant against the accused person’s constitutional right to a fair trial. Disclosure will therefore be the exception rather than the rule, and will only arise where a judge determines that the statutory threshold has been met and that disclosure is strictly necessary.

question: 220. Deputy John Brady asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the status of an IRP renewal application (details supplied); when the IRP card will issue to the applicant; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [49925/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The person referred to by the Deputy applied to renew their immigration permission on 31 March 2026 and this application is currently in the queue for consideration. The Registration Office within Immigration Service Delivery (ISD) of my Department provide a live application processing date broken down by stamp category, which is updated every Monday, and is available at the following link: Renewing your registration permission if you live in the Republic of Ireland - Immigration Service Delivery (www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/how-to-renew-your-current-permission/renewing-your-registration-permission-if-you-live-in-the-republic-of-ireland/) I understand that the extended wait times can be frustrating for applicants, and I can assure the Deputy that my Department is exploring every avenue available to facilitate as many customers as possible and to increase processing capacity. The Registration Office is open seven days a week to facilitate customers to process both first time registration appointments and online renewals. Additional staff have been assigned to this work, which has now begun to reduce the processing time for renewals. For certain categories of renewals, the processing time is now approximately 6 - 8 weeks from the time of initial application, with no category exceeding a wait time of 16 weeks. The Registration Office has also issued a notice to employers regarding the legality of employing someone awaiting renewal. This notice can be found here: Notice to Employers - Immigration Service Delivery (www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/how-to-renew-your-current-permission/notice-to-employers/) If the application is approved, the person concerned can expect to receive their new Irish Residence Permit (IRP) card within the following 10-15 working days. Applicants can now directly check the status of their immigration application on the Immigration Service’s Customer Service Portal. They can register for, or log in to their existing account, at www.portal.irishimmigration.ie/en/ As an Oireachtas member, you can also request the status of individual immigration cases by e-mail, using the Oireachtas Mail facility at: IMoireachtasmail@justice.ie, which has been specifically established for this purpose. This service enables up to date information on such cases to be obtained without the need to seek information by way of the Parliamentary Question process.

question: 221. Deputy John Brady asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the status of an IRP renewal application (details supplied); when the IRP card will issue to the applicant; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [49926/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The application from the person referred to by the Deputy has been approved.
